lens: Concreteness, examples and the ladder to abstraction

findings.observation: He opens with a manipulable object or scenario, never with a definition. The first thing on screen is something with parts you could point at, and the general claim is explicitly deferred to later in the same lesson.
findings.evidence: CLT video opens on a Galton board and a five-row idealised version of it; convolution opens on two lists of numbers and then a pair of dice; entropy opens on a robot on a moon receiving four movement instructions; Moser opens on a circle with dots; the Laplace video opens on cos(t); attention opens on the word 'mole' in three different phrases. In each case the formal statement arrives much later, and in the CLT video he says outright that the job of the rest of the lesson is to make the informally stated idea quantitative.
findings.why_it_works: A definition is a compressed answer to a question the learner has not yet asked. An object gives the learner something to hold in working memory that the later abstraction can be checked against, so the abstraction is received as a description of something already known rather than as new stipulated content.

findings.observation: He deliberately uses an IDEALISED version of the concrete object, announces the idealisation out loud at the moment he makes it, pre-empts the objection, and then later pays the idealisation off by showing that the simplifications he made were exactly the hypotheses of the theorem.
findings.evidence: CLT: the ball is assumed to land dead centre on each peg, to bounce ±1 with 50/50 odds, and the balls are assumed not to interact ('as if they're all ghosts'). He anticipates the complaint that this is not real physics and says the goal is illustration, not modelling. At the very end he reveals the three assumptions (independence, identical distribution, finite variance) and then shows that the real Galton board violates the first two — so his own opening example is retro-fitted as a NON-example, and the idealisations turn out to have been load-bearing. Blocks/pi does the same: perfectly elastic collisions, immovable wall, no relativity, all flagged, and at the end he gives two explicit justifications for idealising (start with the simplest variant; purity exposes hidden connections).
findings.why_it_works: An unannounced simplification is a lie the learner will later discover and distrust. An announced one is a contract. Discharging the contract at the end converts what looked like hand-waving into the actual content of the theorem — the learner retroactively learns that the fine print was visible from shot one.

findings.observation: Numbers are never arbitrary-but-plausible. Every numeric literal does one of exactly three jobs: (a) it is chosen so a hidden structure lands exactly, (b) it is deliberately ugly because the point is that its value does not matter, or (c) it is a real system's real value because the point is scale.
findings.evidence: (a) The robot's instruction probabilities are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 — dyadic so the information content of each symbol is an exact whole number of bits and the optimal code is exactly realisable; he calls the example contrived on purpose. Block mass ratios are powers of 100 (1, 100, 10^4, 10^6) so collision counts read 3, 31, 314, 3141. The die-roll worked example uses exactly 100 rolls so that the standard-deviation multiplier is √100 = 10 and the interval arithmetic is doable in the head. (b) The skewed die's mean is given as 2.24 — a deliberately unattractive number, used precisely at the moment when the claim is that the mean of the sum is n·mu regardless of what mu is; likewise in the Laplace video he uses e^{1.5t} and then immediately says there is nothing special about 1.5. (c) The attention video uses GPT-3's actual figures — 12,288 embedding dimension, 128 key/query dimension, 96 heads, 96 layers — and carries a running parameter tally to 58 billion out of 175 billion.
findings.why_it_works: Clean numbers make a structural claim verifiable by inspection rather than by trust. Ugly numbers make the invariance claim credible, because a viewer cannot suspect the result came from the number. Real numbers deliver a magnitude that a made-up number would understate. Arbitrary-but-plausible numbers do none of these and just add memory load.

findings.observation: He does not fully finish the concrete case before generalising. He states the general claim EARLY but informally, keeps working the concrete case, and only puts up the formal statement near the end — then immediately drops back to a concrete numeric example. The structure is a spiral around a fixed object, not a one-way ladder.
findings.evidence: CLT: after roughly one Galton-board pass he pauses to state the general idea in words (random variable, sum, tends to a bell curve), explicitly says the remaining job is to quantify it, runs more concrete simulations, builds mean and standard deviation, then presents the rigorous limit-of-a-probability-equals-an-integral statement, then says it is time to bring things back down to earth and works the 100-dice problem to the numbers 316 and 384. The three assumptions — the most abstract content — are placed last, after the concrete payoff.
findings.why_it_works: An early informal general statement gives the learner a target that makes the subsequent concrete work feel purposeful rather than aimless. Deferring the formal statement means it arrives as a tightening of something already believed. Returning to arithmetic afterwards is a self-test: the learner discovers whether they can actually use the abstraction.

findings.observation: He marks every change of abstraction level with an explicit verbal signpost — in BOTH directions — and the down-shift markers are as frequent as the up-shift ones.
findings.evidence: Up-shift markers recur across files: spelling something out more exactly, 'in general', putting notation to it, offering a formal statement if one is wanted. Down-shift markers are equally explicit: bringing things back down to earth before the 100-dice example; in the convolution video, immediately after the general index-sum notation he unpacks the case n = 6 into the specific pairs (1,5), (2,4), (3,3), (4,2), (5,1); in the Moser video, right after defining n-choose-4 he computes 6 choose 4 = 15 and says you can count 15 intersection points in the picture.
findings.why_it_works: Unmarked altitude changes are the main cause of a learner silently losing the thread — they keep trying to apply the last concrete referent to a sentence that is now universally quantified. A marker is cheap and resets the frame.

findings.observation: A general formula is almost never left standing alone: it is re-instantiated with the running example's own numbers within the same or the next beat.
findings.evidence: Convolution: the abstract 'sum over all i,j with i+j=n' is immediately followed by n=6 unpacked, and then by a fully worked micro-example, [1,2,3] convolved with [4,5,6] giving 4, 13, 28, 27, 18, computed slide by slide. Cross-entropy: the general weighted-sum definition is immediately followed by a two-outcome case (a 50/50 distribution against a 90/10 distribution) worked in both orders to give 1 bit versus about 1.74 bits.
findings.why_it_works: Symbols are only meaningful once the learner has watched values flow through them at least once. Substitution converts a formula from a thing to be memorised into a thing that has been executed.

findings.observation: The SECOND example is used in two sharply distinct roles, and he says which role it is playing. Role one: hold the procedure fixed and vary the input, to show what does NOT matter. Role two: push the input until the pattern visibly breaks, to locate the boundary.
findings.evidence: Role one, CLT: four simulations run side by side with sum sizes 2, 5, 10 and 15, and separately the underlying die distribution is changed live (skewed-left, then a bimodal one concentrated on 1 and 6) while the procedure stays fixed — the invariance is what the viewer watches. Role two, same video: at sum size 10 the bimodal distribution produces a visibly SPIKY bell curve — the pattern fails on screen — and he says 10 is not a large enough sum for the theorem to kick in, then raises it to 50 where the shape recovers regardless of input.
findings.why_it_works: A confirming second example that works by the same mechanism as the first teaches nothing new; a varying-input example teaches the scope of the claim; a breaking example teaches its boundary. Learners retain boundaries better than instances, because a boundary encodes both a yes and a no.

findings.observation: He flags an anomaly, explicitly leaves the question open, and resolves it later by a DIFFERENT method than the one that raised it.
findings.evidence: CLT: while running the Monte-Carlo simulation he points at the spikiness of the histogram and asks whether it is a real feature or an artefact of randomness, and notes he cannot tell from the simulation how many samples would be needed. He then switches to exact convolution-based computation of the distributions, and when the spiky case reappears he answers the earlier question directly: the spikiness was real, not noise.
findings.why_it_works: It models epistemic hygiene — a picture alone cannot distinguish signal from artefact — and it gives the second method a reason to exist beyond rigour for its own sake. The learner gets a demonstration that two independent routes agreeing is what confidence is made of.

findings.observation: He will deliberately induce a wrong generalisation, but only under strict conditions: the invitation to guess is explicit, the correction lands inside the same lesson, and — critically — the correction EXPLAINS why the wrong pattern held for the cases shown rather than merely denying it.
findings.evidence: Moser's circle problem: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and he explicitly dares the viewer to bet on the next term, which then comes out 31. He refuses to leave it at 'patterns can deceive': he derives 1 + C(n,2) + C(n,4) via Euler's formula, then situates that expression inside Pascal's triangle to show that for n ≤ 5 those three terms happen to sum to an entire previous row (hence a power of two), that at n = 6 the sum covers all but one entry of that row (hence exactly one short), and that at n = 10 it covers exactly half of a symmetric row (hence a power of two again). Milder controlled version in the CLT video: he announces that three assumptions exist, withholds them, and asks the viewer to try to spot them as the lesson runs.
findings.why_it_works: A prediction that fails creates a strong encoding slot; but a bare refutation leaves the learner with only distrust. Explaining the mechanism of the illusion converts the failure into structural understanding and — importantly — restores the learner's confidence in pattern-seeking as a method.

findings.observation: HIS OWN DIAGNOSED FAILURE: a toy example that is too simple can carry an accidental property the general case lacks, and viewers will generalise from the accident. Verbal disclaimers do not neutralise this — what is shown beats what is said.
findings.evidence: In the Grover post-mortem he identifies the cause of mass confusion: he opened by describing a mystery number being searched for, and briefly showed an example function that merely checks whether its input equals 12, while calling it a black box. Viewers concluded the algorithm must already know the answer. He notes he tried to forestall exactly that objection and failed, and takes the blame directly (short quote: 'That's on me.'). His prescribed fix is a better example, not a better disclaimer: Sudoku verification, where knowing the rules manifestly does not reveal the solution, and better still SHA-256, where irreversibility is the whole point.
findings.why_it_works: Learners induce from the salient visible features of the instance in front of them, not from the caveats attached to it. If the toy makes the answer visible, 'pretend you cannot see it' is an instruction the visual system will override. The only reliable fix is an example in which the misleading property is absent.

findings.observation: A single concrete visual object is carried across an entire multi-lesson arc, transformed but recognisable, while the abstraction level rises around it. New metaphors are not minted per topic.
findings.evidence: The pair-of-dice grid is introduced in the discrete convolution video as a 6x6 table of outcomes with constant-sum diagonals; it returns in the continuous convolution video as the xy-plane with a 3D probability-density surface sliced along x+y = s; it returns again in the Gaussian video as the same surface, now rotationally symmetric, where that symmetry is what makes the slice computable; and the same object underwrites the CLT video's sequence of distributions. Likewise the robot-instruction distribution introduced for entropy is reused, merely permuted, to motivate cross-entropy.
findings.why_it_works: Reuse means the cost of learning the visual grammar is paid once and amortised. It also makes cross-topic connections structural rather than asserted: the learner literally sees that two topics are the same picture at different altitudes.

findings.observation: When he offers two visualisations of one thing, he assigns each a specific job and says what each buys — and he names where a visualisation stops being useful.
findings.evidence: Convolution has a sliding-flipped-window view and a multiplication-table-diagonals view, presented as two ways of seeing one operation; he then points out that the sliding view makes the moving-average/blur interpretation obvious, while the diagonal-slice view makes commutativity obvious. In the Gaussian video he states that the diagonal-slice picture only buys you anything BECAUSE the surface is rotationally symmetric, that rotational symmetry uniquely characterises bell curves, and that for most other pairs of functions the picture reduces to just doing the original integral.
findings.why_it_works: A second picture without a distinct job is redundancy that costs attention. Naming the scope of a visual prevents the learner from over-applying it — the same failure mode as an over-simple example.

findings.observation: Rigour that would derail the main argument is pushed to a visibly separate side channel rather than into the narrative flow, and its existence is announced.
findings.evidence: The √2 factor relating diagonal-slice area to the convolution value is stated, briefly explained, declared absorbable into a constant, and left as an on-screen note for calculus enthusiasts. The Lagrange-multiplier argument for why the loss function must be a logarithm is explicitly withheld from the narration to avoid losing the forest for the trees and put on screen instead. The non-standard 'value up / value down' matrix naming in attention is flagged as differing from published convention, with the reconciliation left as a note.
findings.why_it_works: It preserves a single-threaded main argument while keeping the honest reader from concluding a gap was hidden. The announcement is the load-bearing part: an unmentioned omission reads as sloppiness, a mentioned one reads as editorial control.

findings.observation: Worked instances are cross-checked against something independently obtainable, and the check is shown or invited rather than asserted.
findings.evidence: After computing the convolution of [1,2,3] with [4,5,6] by hand he tells the viewer to run it in any numerical library and confirm he is not lying. The 100:1 mass ratio predicting 31 collisions is corroborated with real footage of a student demonstration and a reference to an independent physical attempt. The formula 24 / (number of lookalikes) is checked against the independently known fact that a cube has 12 edges, so removing one edge must give a family of 12. In Moser, 6 choose 4 = 15 is checked by counting 15 intersection points in the drawn diagram.
findings.why_it_works: A prediction that can be checked by a route the author does not control is the only kind that builds trust. It also teaches the habit rather than merely displaying the result.

findings.observation: Failed lines of attack are shown rather than edited out, and are labelled as failures before the successful route is presented.
findings.evidence: In the cube-counting video, an entire technique — counting lookalikes family-by-family — is developed at length and then explicitly declared useless in practice, because counting lookalikes is no easier than counting family sizes and you still have to traverse everything. Only afterwards comes the re-indexing insight (count per transformation instead of per object). The same video reports that the finished sculpture actually contains an error, a duplicated cube and a missing one.
findings.why_it_works: Showing the dead end makes the successful step legible as a choice rather than as magic, and calibrates the learner's expectation that being stuck is normal. Reporting the error costs nothing and buys the author's credibility on everything else.

findings.observation: Reader prompts are PREDICTIONS placed before a reveal, not recall questions placed after one.
findings.evidence: The CLT video asks the viewer, at the top, to watch for and predict the three assumptions, which are only revealed at the end. Moser dares the viewer to bet on the next term before showing 31. The convolution video shows an edge-detection kernel of positive-left/negative-right values and asks the viewer to predict its effect on the image before revealing it. The Gaussian video asks the viewer to predict what the 3D graph of two normal distributions looks like and what property of it could be exploited, before showing the rotational-symmetry argument.
findings.why_it_works: A prediction commits the learner to a position, which makes the subsequent reveal informative (it either confirms or corrects a held belief). A post-hoc recall question only measures attention.

findings.observation: INFERENCE, not directly observable in captions: wherever the narration references motion, it is always a swept parameter or a sequenced step, and the narration simultaneously names what varies and what stays fixed. I found no narrated instance of motion that is not tied to a variable being changed or a process being stepped.
findings.evidence: Recurring narration forms across files: as the underlying distribution is changed live, the viewer is told the bottom plot barely changes; in the cross-entropy video he says he is moving the fixed distribution P and tracing where the minimum of the resulting curve goes, which draws out a second curve (the entropy of P); in the Laplace video he says he is letting s wander the plane on autopilot and asks the viewer to think about why the resulting shape appears. This is an inference from what the narration references — the captions do not describe the visuals directly — but the consistency of the 'as X changes, notice Y' construction across five files is strong. Absence of counterexamples in narration is weaker evidence than presence, and I flag it as such.
findings.why_it_works: Motion is the perceptual channel with the highest salience; spending it on anything other than the one variable currently under argument steals attention from the argument. A swept parameter turns motion into the argument itself: invariance and dependence are literally visible as what moves and what does not.

candidate_rules.rule: Never open a knowledge point with a definition, a universally quantified statement, or a formula. The first shot must present one named instance with actual values that the reader could point at.
candidate_rules.rationale: Across the whole corpus the opening is always an object (Galton board, two blocks, a pair of dice, a robot with four instructions, six points on a circle, the word 'mole'). The general claim is stated informally later and formally later still. A definition first is a compressed answer to an unasked question.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Lint the narration of shot 1 of every knowledge point for: 'in general', 'for any', 'we define', 'let X be', and for a LaTeX/formula span. Any hit in shot 1 fails unless a preceding shot in the same knowledge point already showed a concrete instance with numeric values.

candidate_rules.rule: Every numeric literal in a shot must be tagged with one of exactly three jobs — EXACT (chosen so a structure lands exactly), UGLY (chosen so the reader sees the value does not matter), or REAL (an actual value from a real system, to convey scale). A number with no job tag is a defect.
candidate_rules.rationale: His numbers are dyadic probabilities, powers of 100, exactly 100 dice, or GPT-3's real 12,288 / 128 / 96 — plus deliberately unlovely values like a mean of 2.24 used precisely where the point is that the value is irrelevant. There is no fourth category of arbitrary-but-plausible numbers anywhere in the corpus.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require a source-level annotation next to each numeric literal in a drawFn or narration, e.g. `/* EXACT: gamma=0.5 so the geometric series is exactly 2 */`. A build script greps numeric literals in authored content and fails on any untagged one. Reviewer spot-check: for each EXACT number, confirm the claimed structure is actually visible on screen; for each UGLY number, confirm the surrounding narration says the value does not matter.

candidate_rules.rule: Announce every idealisation in the shot where you make it, and discharge it before the knowledge point ends — either by showing it was a hypothesis of the result, or by relaxing it. Never leave an unpaid simplification.
candidate_rules.rationale: The idealised Galton board is announced as unrealistic on introduction, and at the end the simplifications turn out to be exactly the theorem's independence and identical-distribution assumptions — the opening example is then re-cast as a non-example. The blocks video does the same with elastic collisions and an immovable wall.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain an explicit list per knowledge point: `idealisations: [{shot: 2, claim: 'deterministic transitions', discharged_at: shot 9}]`. Build fails on any entry with `discharged_at: null`. Reviewer confirms the discharging shot actually names the same simplification.

candidate_rules.rule: Never let a worked example possess a salient on-screen property that the general case lacks. Enumerate what a reader can read off the picture; for each such property that does not generalise, either change the example or add a shot showing a second instance where the property fails. A verbal disclaimer does not count as a fix.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is his own diagnosed failure. A toy verifier that just checked whether the input equalled 12 made viewers conclude the algorithm already knows the answer, and he states that he attempted to forestall that objection verbally and failed. His remedy was a structurally better example (Sudoku, then SHA-256), not a stronger caveat.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For every example, write a short 'accidental properties' list in the source: things visibly true of THIS instance (e.g. 'the optimal policy runs along the top row'; 'all rewards are zero except the terminal one'; 'the 4x4 grid is symmetric so V is symmetric'). For each, mark generalises: yes/no. Any `no` must reference either a replacement example or the shot id of the counter-instance. Untreated `no` fails review.

candidate_rules.rule: Every animated element must encode either a swept variable or a step of a process, and the narration must name what changes and what stays fixed. Ban any animation whose end state equals its start state and which sweeps no variable.
candidate_rules.rationale: Everywhere the corpus narration references motion, it is a parameter being changed (the input distribution being reshaped while the sum's distribution barely moves; the fixed distribution being dragged while the minimum traces out a new curve; s wandering the s-plane). This is an inference from narration, flagged as such — but it directly kills pulse rings, breathing circles, marching ants, and a token pacing back and forth, all of which sweep nothing and return to their start state.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Two mechanical tests. (1) CSS/JS lint: reject `animation-iteration-count: infinite`, `@keyframes` whose 0% and 100% frames are identical, and `stroke-dashoffset` marching-ants animations, unless the shot declares `sweep: {var: 'gamma', from: 0, to: 0.99}`. (2) Narration test: the shot's narration must contain a construction of the form 'as <var> …, notice/watch <what changes> while <what stays fixed>'. If deleting that sentence leaves the animation still doing exactly the same thing, the animation is decorative — cut it.

candidate_rules.rule: A second example must declare its job: CONFIRM-INVARIANCE (procedure fixed, input varied, to show what does not matter) or BREAK (input pushed until the pattern visibly fails, to locate the boundary). Two examples that support the same conclusion by the same mechanism is one example too many.
candidate_rules.rationale: The CLT video varies sum size across four panels and varies the underlying distribution live to show invariance, and separately pushes to a bimodal input at sum size 10 where the bell shape visibly fails — then repairs it at 50. Each extra example changes exactly one thing and answers a different question.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require `role: 'confirm-invariance' | 'break'` on every example after the first, plus a field naming which single variable differs from the previous example. Fail if two consecutive examples differ in more than one variable, or if a `confirm-invariance` example does not hold the procedure fixed.

candidate_rules.rule: If you invite a wrong generalisation, satisfy all three of: (a) the invitation to predict is explicit, (b) the correction lands inside the same knowledge point, (c) the correction explains WHY the wrong pattern held for the cases shown. Correction without mechanism is forbidden.
candidate_rules.rationale: Moser's circle is exactly this: an explicit dare to predict, an immediate break at 31, and then a full mechanistic account via Pascal's triangle of why the first five terms had to be powers of two, why n=6 falls short by exactly one, and why n=10 recovers a power of two. A bare 'patterns can deceive' would have taught distrust instead of structure.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Any knowledge point containing a QUIZ or shot flagged `invites_wrong_answer: true` must also contain a shot flagged `explains_illusion: true` before its SUM card, and the SUM card's misconception field must state both the wrong belief and the reason it looked right. Build fails on a missing pair.

candidate_rules.rule: After the general statement, the last non-quiz shot of a knowledge point must return to the opening instance and produce an actual number from it.
candidate_rules.rationale: After the formal limit statement, the CLT video comes back down to earth and grinds 100 dice all the way to mean 350, sd 17.1, interval 316 to 384. The Laplace video returns to cos(t) at three increasing depths. The concrete object is never abandoned once abstracted.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Each knowledge point declares `anchor_object`. Assert that the final non-quiz shot's drawFn references the same anchor_object as shot 1, and that its narration contains at least one computed numeric result. Fail otherwise.

candidate_rules.rule: Immediately after a formula appears, substitute the running example's own values into it in the same or the next shot. Never let a formula stand for more than one shot without an instantiation.
candidate_rules.rationale: The abstract convolution index-sum is immediately unpacked at n=6 into named pairs, then run end-to-end on [1,2,3] against [4,5,6]. The cross-entropy weighted sum is immediately run on a two-outcome case in both orders. Symbols only become meaningful after values have flowed through them once.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For every shot whose drawFn emits a formula, assert that the same or next shot contains numeric substitution of the anchor example's values. Automatable if formula terms carry ids: check that the following shot morphs at least one symbol span to a numeral.

candidate_rules.rule: Never ship a rendering primitive you have not personally watched render, with the exact content strings the deck actually uses. Before authoring any shot that uses a primitive, a smoke-test page must exist that renders every distinct formula/label string used anywhere in the deck, and it must be opened and read.
candidate_rules.rationale: This encodes the LaTeX failure directly, and it matches his practice of inviting external confirmation of a computed result rather than asserting it, and of corroborating the 31-collision prediction against real footage. Assertion without observation is the failure mode in both the aesthetic and the engineering register.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Build step: extract every distinct string passed to the formula-morph primitive across the whole deck into a single generated smoke-test page; render it; fail the build if any rendered text node matches /\\\\[a-zA-Z]+|\\{|\\}|\$/ (i.e. raw TeX control sequences or stray braces survived to the DOM). Additionally require a human-viewed screenshot of that page checked into the repo per release.

candidate_rules.rule: Every numeric claim shown on screen must be recomputable by an independent route, and that route must be recorded next to the claim.
candidate_rules.rationale: He tells the reader to run the convolution in a library and confirm he is not lying; corroborates the 31-collision figure against physical footage; checks a derived family-size formula against the independently known fact that a cube has 12 edges. The habit, not just the result, is part of the teaching.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Every shot with a numeric result carries `verified_by: '<script path or independent fact>'`. A test harness re-derives each such number (e.g. runs value iteration for the stated MDP and compares to the number in the narration) and fails on mismatch beyond a stated tolerance. Empty `verified_by` fails.

candidate_rules.rule: Carry one anchor visual object across a chapter rather than inventing a new metaphor per knowledge point. If a chapter uses more than two primary visual objects, justify each addition in writing.
candidate_rules.rationale: The dice grid becomes a 3D product surface becomes diagonal slices becomes the rotationally symmetric Gaussian, across four videos. The robot's instruction distribution is reused, merely permuted, to introduce cross-entropy. Reuse amortises the cost of learning the visual grammar and makes cross-topic connections structural instead of asserted.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Count distinct `anchor_object` values per chapter. More than two requires a `justification` string on each extra one. For CS234 this means, e.g., one grid world and one backup diagram carried through, not a new bespoke picture per lecture.

candidate_rules.rule: Every QUIZ must ask for a prediction about a case that has not yet been shown, and must be positioned BEFORE the reveal. Never place a recall question after the answer has been displayed.
candidate_rules.rationale: His prompts are consistently pre-reveal predictions: predict the three assumptions before they are given; bet on the next term before it is computed; predict what the edge-detection kernel does before the image appears; predict what the two-Gaussian surface looks like before the argument. A commitment makes the reveal informative.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Assert that every QUIZ's correct answer does not appear in any preceding shot's narration or drawFn output within the same knowledge point. Mechanically: string/semantic match of the answer text against prior narration; a hit means the quiz is recall, not prediction — move it earlier or rewrite it.

candidate_rules.rule: Keep rigour caveats out of the main narration flow: any caveat longer than one sentence goes into the SUM card or an explicitly-labelled aside, and its existence must still be announced in one clause.
candidate_rules.rationale: The √2 slice factor, the Lagrange-multiplier derivation, and the non-standard matrix naming are each announced in a clause and then pushed to an on-screen note. Unmentioned omissions read as sloppiness; in-line digressions break the single-threaded argument.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Lint narration for hedge-initiated sentences ('technically', 'strictly speaking', 'to be more precise', 'a small technical detail'). If the hedge block exceeds one sentence, fail and require relocation to the SUM card's caveat field, leaving a one-clause pointer in the narration.

anti_patterns: Opening a topic with the formal definition or the general formula, and only afterwards looking for an example to illustrate it. In every file the order is the reverse.

Motion that sweeps no variable and returns to its start state — infinite pulses, breathing, marching ants, pacing tokens. Nothing in the corpus narration corresponds to motion of this kind; every referenced motion is a parameter being changed or a process being stepped, with the narration naming what changes and what does not. (Flagged: this is an inference from narration, since captions do not describe visuals directly.)

Relying on a verbal disclaimer to cancel a misleading picture. He tried exactly this in the Grover video, states plainly that it failed, and prescribed a different EXAMPLE rather than a stronger caveat.

Using a toy so small that it has a property the real case lacks — e.g. a verifier that literally checks whether the input equals a visible constant. Simplicity that leaks accidental structure is worse than mild complexity.
Arbitrary-but-plausible numbers. Numbers in the corpus are exact-for-structure, deliberately-ugly-to-show-irrelevance, or real-system values. There is no fourth kind.
A second example that confirms the first by the same mechanism. Extra examples always change exactly one thing, and either demonstrate invariance or find the boundary.
Puncturing a wrong pattern without explaining why it looked right. Moser is emphatic that the near-miss powers of two are not coincidence and devotes the back half to the mechanism.
Abandoning the concrete case once the abstraction is stated. He always comes back down and computes a number.
Hiding a simplification, or making one and never paying it off. Every idealisation in the corpus is announced at the moment it is made and cashed in later.
Stating a computed result without any independently checkable route to it. He repeatedly invites the reader to verify, or corroborates against physical evidence or a separately-known fact.

Editing out the dead ends. He shows a whole technique being developed and then declares it practically useless before revealing the better route, and reports a real error in the artwork he is analysing.
Multiple visualisations of the same thing without assigning each a distinct job, and without saying where each one stops being valid.
Long rigour digressions inside the main narration, and equally, silently omitting them. Both are avoided by an announced side channel.
Recall-style questions placed after the answer has been shown; his prompts are always predictions made before the reveal.

lens: Building a concept from nothing — the move set that makes a definition feel inevitable rather than arbitrary

findings.observation: STEP 1 — Open with a design problem whose answer is a number, then explicitly demote the number. The concept is introduced as the thing you are forced to invent while trying to answer a concrete, askable question — not as an object to be defined. He states the contract out loud: definitions are the leftovers of an insight, and writing one down early would ruin the story.
findings.evidence: Reinventing Entropy opens with 'how efficiently can text be compressed?', promises the numeric answer only at the end, and says the approach matters more. Laplace opens by refusing to put the definition on screen until the problem it solves has been stated. Cross-entropy opens with a 2002 result about clustering languages by zipping files together — a puzzle, not a formula.
findings.why_it_works: A definition presented cold has no slot to go into; the reader has nowhere to attach it. A question creates an open slot, and the definition then arrives as the unique thing that fits it. Inevitability is manufactured by ordering, not by rhetoric.

findings.observation: STEP 2 — Warm up on a deliberately rigged miniature whose numbers come out clean, and say out loud that it is rigged. The rigging is what lets the coincidence at the heart of the concept become visible; the reader is told the rigging will later be removed.
findings.evidence: Entropy: a robot receiving four instructions with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 — every one a power of two, so bits come out whole. He calls the setup contrived and flags the independence assumption as an extra simplification. Central Limit Theorem: an idealised Galton board where balls are 'ghosts', later revealed to violate the theorem's own assumptions. Exploration & Epiphany: squares before cubes, with constraints deliberately relaxed and the resulting wrong count announced in advance.
findings.why_it_works: Clean numbers make a structural alignment legible that messy numbers would bury. Disclosing the rigging buys the right to generalise later without the reader feeling cheated, and it pre-empts the objection that the example was cherry-picked.

findings.observation: STEP 3 — Stage candidate answers as named voices of escalating sophistication, and let the escalation, not the author, do the arguing. Each voice proposes something defensible; the next voice names its shortfall.
findings.evidence: Entropy uses three students: a straightforward one (flat two bits per instruction), a clever one (variable-length code, 1.75 bits), and a theoretical one who asks what an optimal code must look like in principle. Convolution uses an imagined audience member who raises a hand and proposes flipping one row of dice probabilities around.
findings.why_it_works: Attributing a naive answer to a persona lets the reader hold it without embarrassment, and lets it be superseded without the reader feeling corrected. The escalation also models the actual search process rather than presenting a finished result.

findings.observation: STEP 4 — Correction to an expected pattern: the naive candidate is usually shown to be SUBOPTIMAL, not WRONG. I went looking for 'propose a broken definition, break it, patch it' and largely did not find it. What I found instead is a gap between a workable answer and a better one, and the gap itself is the engine that drags you toward the definition.
findings.evidence: In Entropy the flat two-bit code decodes perfectly — it is simply worse than 1.75. Nothing is patched; the second scheme is a different construction. The only true break-and-fix cases I found are elsewhere and are about candidate SHAPES or candidate EXPLANATIONS: the absolute-value exponent rejected in the CLT build because it produces a sharp corner, and the standard textbook story for cross-entropy loss which he calls unsatisfying and then replaces wholesale.
findings.why_it_works: A wrong-then-fixed definition teaches the reader that definitions are patched artefacts. A suboptimal-then-improved one teaches that a definition is the endpoint of an optimisation, which is what actually makes it feel non-arbitrary.

findings.observation: STEP 5 — Let the reader notice the coincidence before you state it. At the hinge of the argument he describes the SENSATION of a pattern rather than announcing the pattern, then confirms it a beat later.
findings.evidence: Entropy: after showing that allocating a one-bit codeword consumes half the space of all possible codewords, he notes that the consumed proportions match the probabilities exactly — and frames this as a bell resonating, a tickling sensation, before naming it as the founding insight of information theory. Cross-entropy: he traces a curve out of a moving minimum and asks the reader what the new curve represents before answering.
findings.why_it_works: Ownership. A pattern the reader spots one beat before it is named feels discovered; the same pattern named first feels asserted. The delay is short enough that no one is left behind.

findings.observation: STEP 6 — Raise the standard of proof yourself before the reader can. Having reached a good answer, he refuses it as merely good and demands a general argument, which is what forces the definition into existence.
findings.evidence: Entropy: after the clever code hits 1.75 bits and the alignment with probabilities is noticed, he says calling it perfect would be a bold claim and asks how you could rule out some fancier scheme over long sequences. Only that refusal produces the third student's principle (perfect compression must look like random noise) and hence the formula.
findings.why_it_works: The reader's residual doubt is voiced and honoured rather than ignored, so the eventual generality is felt as earned. It also converts a numerical result into a structural one.

findings.observation: STEP 7 — The formula's first appearance is a two-line algebraic restatement of a sentence the reader has already accepted. He never derives a formula; he transcribes an agreed claim into symbols.
findings.evidence: Entropy: the accepted sentence is 'a message using n bits must have probability 2^-n'. Take log base two of both sides, negate, and you have -log2(p) as the bit count — after which he says explicitly that everything preceding existed to make this feel like something you were drawn to rather than an arbitrary starting definition. Herschel's derivation of the Gaussian: two stated properties (radial symmetry; coordinate independence) collapse into a functional equation whose only continuous solutions are exponentials.
findings.why_it_works: The cognitive load of a formula is almost entirely in accepting its content, not in reading its syntax. If the content is already accepted, the symbols are free. This also means the formula cannot feel arbitrary — the reader watched it get written down from something they agreed to.

findings.observation: STEP 8 — A numeric instance always precedes the general symbolic form. The same weighted sum is computed with actual digits, given a name, and only then written with indices.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy: he recomputes the robot's average cost under a changed distribution to 2.625 bits, names that number as the cross-entropy, and only then says it is worth a few minutes to package it into formulas with P and Q. Entropy: the 1.75-bit weighted sum computed in the toy example turns out, pages later, to have been the entropy formula all along.
findings.why_it_works: The general form is then recognised rather than parsed — the reader is matching against an arithmetic step they personally performed, so the indices are decoration on a familiar act.

findings.observation: STEP 9 — Bind every symbol to a geometric feature before the formula is allowed to count as understood. Each term in the expression is assigned a specific visual role, and the whole expression is assigned a visual role too.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy: bar width is one probability, bar height is the negative log of the other, and the sum is the total area — stated term by term. Laplace: the definition is split into two named steps, multiply by an exponential and then integrate, and each step is motivated separately. Attention: the compact softmax expression from the paper is shown only after the grid of key-query dot products has been drawn, and is then read as a compact way to write the grid the reader already has.
findings.why_it_works: A formula with unbound symbols is a string; a formula whose every symbol points at something is a diagram. It also makes the formula editable in the reader's head — they can predict what happens if a term changes.

findings.observation: STEP 10 — Treat the surface awkwardness of the notation as a separate obstacle from the content, and dispatch it explicitly. He concedes when a symbol looks off-putting, offers alternate spellings, and sometimes says which convention he would have preferred.
findings.evidence: The negative logarithm is admitted to take getting used to; he offers 'how many times do you halve the space' as the reading, shows log of one over p as an alternative, and says he would personally lean toward writing it as a log base one-half. In the attention video he invents non-standard names for two factored matrices and immediately flags that papers write it differently and shows how.
findings.why_it_works: Readers routinely mistake notational discomfort for conceptual failure and conclude they do not understand. Naming the discomfort separates the two and prevents a false sense of not following.

findings.observation: STEP 11 — Every constant, sign, base, and normaliser is derived from a stated requirement, and the TYPE of justification is named: forced by mathematics, chosen for convenience, or deliberately deferred. I found no unexplained constant anywhere in the corpus.
findings.evidence: Gaussian: the sign of the exponent's constant is forced because a positive one makes the integral diverge, so the function could not be normalised into a probability distribution at all. The base e is shown to be a non-choice — any base gives the same family of curves — and is chosen only because it makes the free parameter readable and calculus clean. Cross-entropy: natural log versus log base two is dismissed as a constant factor absorbed by the learning rate, with derivative cleanliness given as the actual reason.
findings.why_it_works: An unexplained constant is where the reader silently concludes the whole thing was handed down by authority. Labelling the justification type also teaches the reader which parts of the formula they may safely renegotiate.

findings.observation: STEP 12 — Park the normalisation constant on purpose. Get the shape right while knowingly wrong by a constant factor, announce that you are doing so, and close the gap later with the requirement that made the constant necessary.
findings.evidence: Herschel derivation: he assumes a proportionality constant equals one, calls the move cheeky, states plainly that the resulting answer will be off by a constant, and says this is fine because probability distributions get rescaled to unit area anyway. The CLT video then builds the full normal-distribution formula as a chain of single-purpose edits — decay in both directions, then smoothness, then a width parameter, then a reparametrisation that gives the parameter a readable meaning, then division by the square root of pi for unit area, then a shift for the mean.
findings.why_it_works: Normalisation is bookkeeping that competes for attention with structure. Separating the two phases keeps the shape argument clean, and the later reunion turns the constant from a mystery into a receipt.

findings.observation: ANIMATION LAW — Every moving picture in this corpus has a controlled variable, a dependent variable, and a claim that the dependence establishes. The motion GENERATES the object under discussion; it is never ambience. (I am inferring the visuals from narration references, but the narration is unambiguous about what changes and why.)
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy: one distribution is held fixed, the other is dragged, the minimum of the resulting curve is traced, and the traced locus turns out to be the entropy curve — the animation is the proof. Entropy: a codeword is pushed lower on the binary tree and two others are forced upward, which he likens to flattening a bump in a rug — the motion is the trade-off argument. Convolution: sliding the flipped array one notch produces exactly one output entry per position, so the motion enumerates the answer. Laplace: dragging s around the plane makes a spiral sum converge or blow up, and its magnitude is plotted point by point as it moves.
findings.why_it_works: Motion is the most expensive attentional resource on a page. Spending it on a genuine dependency teaches a functional relationship that a static picture cannot. Spending it on anything else does not merely waste attention — it trains the reader to ignore motion, disarming the one channel you need later.

findings.observation: ANIMATION LAW, SPECIAL CASE — The invariance shot: vary the input aggressively and show that the output does NOT move. The claim is carried by the absence of change, which is impossible to make with a static picture.
findings.evidence: CLT: with a small sum size he changes the underlying die distribution and the bottom plot changes shape completely; with a sum size of fifty he changes the same distribution just as violently and the bottom plot stays put. He states that this stubbornness is what the theorem is.
findings.why_it_works: Robustness claims are exactly the claims a single frame cannot make. This is the highest-value use of animation in a technical explainer and the sharpest contrast with decorative looping, which is change without variation.

findings.observation: Give a central object two independent visualisations, assert that they are the same operation, and say which one is better for which job. He does not treat multiple views as redundancy.
findings.evidence: Convolution is presented both as flip-and-slide-and-dot-product and as a multiplication table summed along diagonals; he says they are two ways to see one thing, then later says the diagonal view makes commutativity obvious while the sliding view makes the moving-average reading obvious. In the continuous version he puts both on screen at once and drives the shared parameter to show the product graph and the diagonal slice changing in lockstep.
findings.why_it_works: A single representation is indistinguishable from the concept in a novice's mind; two force abstraction over what they share. Assigning each a comparative advantage also gives the reader a tool-selection rule rather than a preference.

findings.observation: Voice the strongest objection in the reader's own register before answering it — and do not assume that voicing it worked. The Grover post-mortem contains an explicit admission that he tried to head off exactly the objection that then flooded his comments.
findings.evidence: Entropy interrupts itself with the reader's complaint about how the robot knows where to split a variable-length bitstream. Convolution voices a reader calling the half-built polynomial-sampling algorithm foolish, by name, before the FFT rescues it. The Grover correction states he genuinely tried to forestall the confusion and failed, and takes the blame for the framing directly.
findings.why_it_works: An unvoiced objection keeps running in the background and blocks everything after it. But the failure case matters more: a forestalling sentence buried mid-paragraph does not neutralise a structural misimpression created by the opening framing. Objections must be answered at the level at which they were created.

findings.observation: REPAIR MOVE — When an explanation fails, diagnose the framing and the example before adding detail. He explicitly ranks missing low-level detail as NOT the cause, and identifies a too-small toy example as the culprit.
findings.evidence: Grover post-mortem: his original opening asked the viewer to imagine searching for a mystery number and briefly flashed a function that merely checks whether its input equals twelve. That example makes the answer look like it is hiding in the source code. His fix replaces it with a Sudoku verifier and a cryptographic hash — cases where the triggering input is a genuinely emergent property of the rules. He explicitly declines to add the quantum-compilation detail, arguing that knowing the logic gates for addition teaches you nothing about adding.
findings.why_it_works: An example whose target property holds by construction cannot demonstrate that the property is hard to obtain — it silently teaches the opposite. This is a mechanically avoidable class of error: check whether your example has the property emergently or by definition.

findings.observation: VISUAL HONESTY — Never let a choice made for presentation masquerade as part of the mechanism. Twice in the corpus a picture is explicitly quarantined from the thing it depicts.
findings.evidence: Grover: viewers concluded that picking a particular two-dimensional slice of the state space was a step of the algorithm; he corrects that the algorithm is indifferent to how anyone visualises it and that the state vector's confinement to that plane is an emergent consequence, not an instruction. Laplace: he says up front that the surface he is plotting is slightly distinct from the literal meaning of the integral, because the integral genuinely fails to converge over half the plane and what is drawn is its analytic continuation.
findings.why_it_works: Diagrams are read as ontology. Any framing, projection, colour-coding, ordering, or highlight introduced for legibility will be absorbed as a property of the object unless it is explicitly disowned in the same breath.

findings.observation: VERIFICATION — Cheap checks are performed on screen and the result is shown, including checks against an independent implementation. And critically: when an approximate visual raises a question about the exact object, he goes back to the exact computation to answer it.
findings.evidence: Convolution: he invites the reader to run the same convolution in a numerical library to confirm he is not lying, and separately times two library implementations (roughly five seconds versus four milliseconds) as evidence for an asymptotic claim. Laplace: he substitutes a value where the answer is already known from the earlier area picture and confirms the new complex-plane picture reproduces it. CLT: a simulation produces a spiky bell curve and he explicitly asks whether the spikiness is randomness or real, then answers it from the exact distribution — it was real. Exploration & Epiphany cites an independent computational paper confirming the count, and also reports an actual duplicate error in the artwork.
findings.why_it_works: This is the direct in-corpus grounding for verification discipline: a rendering can produce an artefact that looks exactly like a feature, and only an independent exact check distinguishes them. Assuming a rendering path behaves as expected is the same failure as assuming a simulation spike is meaningful.

findings.observation: Move rigour that would break the main line OFF the main line, into a marked aside, and say why you are doing it. The main narration holds one altitude throughout.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy: the constrained-optimisation argument proving that the loss function must be a logarithm is put on screen as a note for interested readers, with the stated reason that he does not want to lose the forest for the trees. Convolution: the square-root-of-two stretch factor between diagonal slices and the convolution's true values gets a screen note for calculus enthusiasts. Attention: the divisor under the dot products is disclosed as a numerical-stability detail he is not going to motivate, and marked as such.
findings.why_it_works: Altitude changes cost more than length. A reader who can see that the aside is optional does not have to decide whether they have fallen behind. This maps directly onto a summary-card or footnote slot in an authoring format.

findings.observation: Keep the dead ends in. A derived result is allowed to turn out useless, be named as a disappointment, and then be rescued by a reframing — and the emotional shape of that sequence is described directly.
findings.evidence: Exploration & Epiphany derives a correct relation between family counts and 'lookalikes', then states plainly that it does not help because both quantities are equally hard to count, and that you would still have to walk the whole hallway. The epiphany that follows is to count the same quantity along the other axis of the same grid. He also approvingly reports the artist dividing a running total by twelve for no reason other than optimistic probing.
findings.why_it_works: It calibrates what problem-solving actually costs, so the reader does not read their own dead ends as evidence of incapacity. It also makes the eventual reframing legible as a MOVE rather than as luck.

findings.observation: DEVIATION — When a concept is not derivable from a single requirement, he substitutes recurrence for inevitability: the concept is justified by how many unrelated places it independently arrives from.
findings.evidence: The discrete convolution video never poses a design problem. It opens with 'here are the obvious ways to combine two lists — here is a third, genuinely new one', then reaches the same operation from dice sums, moving averages, image blurring, edge detection, and polynomial multiplication. He notes that seeing an operation surface in seemingly unrelated areas is itself the reason to be excited. In the cross-entropy video he says a formula appearing in two separate contexts is mathematics hinting at a connection.
findings.why_it_works: Some concepts genuinely are not forced by any one requirement. Faking a derivation for them would be dishonest; multiple independent arrival points produce the same felt non-arbitrariness through a different mechanism.

findings.observation: DEVIATION — Where the object is empirical rather than derived, the derivation is dropped and the illustrative story is explicitly labelled as a story, repeatedly.
findings.evidence: The attention video presents the query, key, and value matrices as given, then narrates an invented adjective-modifies-noun example while stating more than once that he is making the example up, that the real learned behaviour is hard to parse, and that the parameters do whatever minimises the loss. The LLM overview separates what researchers designed (the framework) from what emerges (the specific behaviour), and says this is why the model's predictions are hard to explain.
findings.why_it_works: Presenting an empirical architecture with the rhetoric of inevitability would install a false belief that is expensive to remove later. The labelled story gets the reader a working mental image while marking exactly which parts are load-bearing. This matters directly for reinforcement learning, where many design choices are empirical rather than forced.

findings.observation: DEVIATION — Under extreme compression, the derivation is the first thing cut. What survives is one concrete framing, one quantitative shock, and the honesty markers.
findings.evidence: The 1.3k-word LLM overview keeps the torn-off-script framing, keeps one scale calculation (at a billion operations per second, training the largest models would take well over a hundred million years), keeps the designed-versus-emergent distinction — and derives nothing at all.
findings.why_it_works: Under a hard budget the framing and the calibration numbers are what a reader can still act on; a truncated derivation is worse than none, because a half-derivation implies a completeness it does not have.

findings.observation: Withhold a checkable fact and hold it open as a standing question across the whole piece, then close it explicitly at the end. This is his nearest analogue to a forced-answer checkpoint.
findings.evidence: The CLT video announces near the start that the theorem rests on three assumptions, declines to say what they are, and asks the viewer to try to spot them as the argument proceeds. All three are then stated and each is checked against the opening Galton-board example, which turns out to violate two of them.
findings.why_it_works: It converts passive watching into an active search with a definite answer, and the closing pass doubles as a consistency audit of the piece's own examples.

findings.observation: Name the thing last. The object is constructed, manipulated, and used before it acquires its standard name — and provenance stories attached to names are fact-checked rather than repeated.
findings.evidence: The entropy formula is built, visualised as total rectangle area, and played with by reshaping the distribution, before the name entropy appears via the von Neumann anecdote — which he checks and reports as probably apocryphal with a grain of truth. Exploration & Epiphany derives the whole counting argument and only then says it is an instance of Burnside's Lemma, immediately followed by what would still need proving for rigour.
findings.why_it_works: A name attached to an unbuilt object is a label to memorise; attached to a built one it is an index into something the reader owns. Fact-checking the anecdote costs one clause and protects the credibility of everything less checkable.

findings.observation: VIDEO-SPECIFIC — Some persuasion is done with elapsed duration, which a page cannot reproduce directly.
findings.evidence: Exploration & Epiphany moves the camera down a corridor holding all 4096 candidate cubes, speeds up, and remarks partway through that this is still only the halfway point — the tedium of watching IS the argument for why brute force is unacceptable. Nothing in a static or self-paced medium can impose that duration on a reader.
findings.why_it_works: Felt cost motivates the search for a better method more forcefully than a stated count. In a self-paced medium the nearest substitutes are a dense grid shown at true scale, or a stated comparison against something the reader already has a physical intuition for — a weaker but honest replacement.

candidate_rules.rule: Never let a formula appear in a knowledge point before an earlier shot in that same knowledge point has computed the same quantity with concrete numbers.
candidate_rules.rationale: Across the corpus the general symbolic form is always recognition of an arithmetic step the reader already performed, not an act of parsing. The 1.75-bit weighted sum is computed long before it is called entropy; 2.625 is computed before cross-entropy is written with indices.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each S() whose drawFn renders a formula, scan preceding S() calls in the same knowledge point for at least one numeric evaluation of the same expression. Automate as: a formula shot must carry a `derivesFrom` reference to an earlier numeric shot id; fail the build if absent.

candidate_rules.rule: Never introduce a symbol in a formula without binding it, in that shot's narration, to a named feature of the drawing.
candidate_rules.rationale: He binds every term: bar width is one probability, bar height is a negative log, total area is the sum. Unbound symbols make a formula a string rather than a diagram.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Extract the symbol set from the formula string. For each symbol, require the narration to contain it within the same sentence as one of a fixed vocabulary of visual nouns (width, height, axis, cell, arrow, row, column, area, position, length, node, edge). Report unbound symbols.

candidate_rules.rule: Never author an animation without declaring an independent variable, a dependent variable, and the claim the dependence establishes. If you cannot name all three in one sentence, delete the animation.
candidate_rules.rationale: Every animation in the corpus generates the object being explained: dragging one distribution traces out the entropy curve; sliding an array enumerates convolution outputs; pushing one codeword down the tree forces two others up. Motion without a controlled variable is what the reader correctly reported as meaningless.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require each animated drawFn to accept an explicit progress or parameter argument and to carry a one-line `claim` string. Fail any animation whose visual state is a function of wall-clock time only. Grep for `setInterval`, `requestAnimationFrame` loops with no bound parameter, and CSS `animation-iteration-count: infinite`.

candidate_rules.rule: Never animate a property that is not a quantity in the model being taught. Position along an axis, bar height, fill fraction, term position during a morph, and progress along a path are permitted; opacity pulsing, scale breathing, rotation for its own sake, dash-offset marching, and idle wandering tokens are forbidden.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is the direct encoding of the reported failure. Decorative motion does not merely waste attention; it trains the reader to filter motion out, which disarms the channel needed for the invariance and trade-off shots that actually carry arguments.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain an allowlist of animatable SVG/CSS properties per primitive. Lint the drawing layer for animated `opacity`, `stroke-dashoffset`, `filter`, and for `transform: scale()` whose scale factor is not a model quantity. Any violation fails.

candidate_rules.rule: Never leave an animation looping. Every animation must terminate in the state that is its point, and that final state must persist as the shot's resting frame.
candidate_rules.rationale: Inferred, but strongly: every narrated animation in the corpus resolves to a described end state — the traced curve that remains, the final offset, the converged spiral, the settled distribution. Nothing suggests perpetual motion anywhere.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Assert every animation has a finite duration and a defined end state. Snapshot the shot at t = duration + 1s and require it to be non-empty and stable across two consecutive samples. Flagged as inference: this rule extrapolates from narration, since the transcripts do not describe visuals directly.

candidate_rules.rule: Before publishing any shot that renders a formula, render it headlessly and read the resulting text back. Never assume a drawing primitive supports a notation you have not personally seen it render.
candidate_rules.rationale: The corpus's own verification habit is to check cheaply and show the check — timing two library implementations, substituting a known value to confirm a new picture reproduces an old answer, going back to the exact distribution to decide whether a simulated spike was real. Assuming a renderer handles LaTeX is the same class of error as assuming a simulation artefact is a feature.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: A build-time smoke test that renders every formula string in the content and asserts the resulting DOM text contains no backslash, no `\\frac`, no `$`, no `^{`, no `_{`, and no `\\left`. This is fully mechanical and should be a blocking test.

candidate_rules.rule: Never present a choice made for legibility as if it were part of the mechanism. Any projection, slice, ordering, colour-coding, highlight, or coordinate choice introduced for viewing must be disowned in the same shot's narration.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is the precise failure he diagnosed in the Grover video: viewers took the chosen two-dimensional slice to be a step of the algorithm, when the algorithm is indifferent to visualisation. He also flags that a Laplace plot is not literally what the integral says.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain a per-shot `viewingChoices` list. Any shot that introduces a slice, projection, reordering, or semantic colour must have a non-empty list, and each entry must appear in the narration text. Fail on mismatch.

candidate_rules.rule: Never write a constant, sign, base, or normalising factor into a formula without tagging its justification as one of: forced-by-requirement, convention-with-a-stated-reason, or deferred-with-a-named-debt.
candidate_rules.rationale: No unexplained constant appears anywhere in the corpus. The exponent's sign is forced because the alternative cannot be normalised; the base e is shown to be a free choice and then justified by readability and calculus; log base two versus natural log is dismissed as absorbed by the learning rate.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Tokenise each formula for numeric literals, sign changes, and base symbols. Require a matching entry in a per-shot `choices` map with one of the three tags plus a reason string, and require the reason to appear in the narration. Deferred entries must resolve in a later knowledge point or the build fails.

candidate_rules.rule: Never generalise a worked example without first stating that the example was rigged, and stating exactly which convenience is about to be removed.
candidate_rules.rationale: He calls the four-instruction robot contrived, names the independence assumption, and later removes exactly those conveniences — probabilities stop being powers of two, symbols stop being independent — with the consequences spelled out.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Any example whose inputs are powers of two, round decimals, or uniform must carry a `rigged` field naming the convenience. The generalising shot must reference that same field by name. Fail if a rigged example is generalised without the reference.

candidate_rules.rule: Never illustrate a concept with an example in which the target property holds by construction. The property must be emergent from the example's rules.
candidate_rules.rationale: The single self-diagnosed cause of his worst explanation failure: a toy verifier that merely checks whether its input equals twelve made the searched-for answer look like it was sitting in the source code. The repair was Sudoku and a cryptographic hash, where the triggering input is genuinely emergent.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each example, write one sentence answering 'could a reader read the answer off the setup?'. If yes, reject the example. In an RL setting this bites hard: never illustrate value iteration on a two-state chain where the optimal policy is obvious by inspection, and never illustrate exploration on a bandit whose best arm is visibly labelled.

candidate_rules.rule: Never respond to reader confusion by adding lower-level detail until you have first tested the framing and the example. Detail is the last fix attempted, not the first.
candidate_rules.rationale: He explicitly ranks missing low-level detail as NOT the cause of his failure, and declines to add the compilation step, arguing that knowing the gates that implement addition teaches nothing about adding.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Make it a required revision checklist, in order: (1) does the opening framing imply something false? (2) does the example have the property by construction? (3) is a needed principle under-emphasised? Only after all three are cleared may detail be added. Record which step fixed it.

candidate_rules.rule: Never let an approximate, sampled, or simulated visual stand as the answer to a question about the exact object. Follow it with the exact computation, or state explicitly which question it cannot answer.
candidate_rules.rationale: When his simulation produced a spiky bell curve he asked on the reader's behalf whether the spikiness was randomness or real, then answered it from the exact distribution — it was real. The same discipline applies to a rendering pipeline: an artefact and a feature look identical until checked independently.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Tag every shot whose data comes from sampling, simulation, or a random seed. Each tagged shot must be followed within the same knowledge point by an exact-computation shot or by a narration clause naming the question it cannot settle.

candidate_rules.rule: Never put a derivation of more than about three steps into the main narration line. Route it to a summary card or a marked aside, and say in one clause why it is being routed there.
candidate_rules.rationale: The constrained-optimisation proof that the loss must be a logarithm is deliberately placed on screen as an optional note rather than spoken, with the reason given. The square-root-of-two slice correction is handled the same way.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Count derivation steps per narration paragraph (lines containing an equals sign or a 'therefore'). Above the threshold, require the content to move to SUM() or an aside block carrying a `whyAside` string.

candidate_rules.rule: Never present a learned or empirically-chosen component as though it were derived. Any narrated story about what a component 'is doing' must carry an explicit hedge in the same shot.
candidate_rules.rationale: The attention video repeatedly marks its adjective-noun story as invented and states that real learned behaviour is hard to parse. This matters acutely for RL, where reward shaping, target networks, clipping ranges, and exploration schedules are empirical choices that a confident derivation would misrepresent.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain a `derivable: true|false` flag per concept. Where false, require the narration to contain an explicit hedge and require the corresponding SUM() misconception field to state that the component is empirical, not forced.

candidate_rules.rule: Never deliver a central object with only one visualisation. Give it two, assert in narration that they are the same thing, and state what each one is better for.
candidate_rules.rationale: Convolution is given as flip-and-slide and as a summed multiplication table, declared equivalent, and each assigned a comparative advantage — one makes symmetry obvious, the other makes the moving-average reading obvious.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each knowledge point flagged as central, require at least two structurally distinct drawFns plus one shot whose narration asserts equivalence and one that states the comparative advantage. In an RL context: a Bellman backup as both a backup diagram and a bar-chart value update.

candidate_rules.rule: Never state the general form before the special case has been reduced to at most two free parameters and varied.
candidate_rules.rationale: He collapses cross-entropy to a two-outcome distribution precisely so it can be graphed and dragged, and says the small number of free parameters is what makes the intuition-building possible. The Laplace warm-up strips the function away entirely and assumes the parameter is real before letting it be complex.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each concept, the first animated or interactive instance must expose at most two varying parameters. Count the arguments of the drawFn that change across the shot; fail above two.

candidate_rules.rule: Never hide a deferred question. Every question you raise and do not answer must be named as an open debt at the moment it is deferred, and either paid or explicitly declared out of scope by the end of the module.
candidate_rules.rationale: He names the pi in the normal distribution as a real question and hands it to a later video; he names entropy-rate generality as beyond exact calculation; he names what would still need rigorous proof after an informal derivation.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain a module-level debts register. Every narration clause matching a deferral pattern ('later', 'in the next', 'beyond what we') must add an entry with a target knowledge point. Fail the build on unresolved entries at module end.

candidate_rules.rule: Never let a naive candidate be dismissed by the author's assertion. It must be superseded by a stated shortfall that the reader can verify, ideally numerically.
candidate_rules.rationale: The flat two-bit code is not called wrong — it is beaten, 1.75 against 2.00, with the weighted sum shown. The rejected absolute-value exponent is rejected for a visible defect, a sharp corner, not for being inelegant.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Each shot that supersedes a candidate must contain either a numeric comparison or a named visible defect. Reject narration whose only ground is an aesthetic adjective.

candidate_rules.rule: Never assert that something is obvious, intuitive, or clear to the reader. Hedge, or restate the thing that makes it so.
candidate_rules.rationale: His claims about what the reader is feeling are consistently hedged — he guesses, he hopes, he suspects, and in the Grover post-mortem he admits he cannot tell whether he is over- or under-explaining. He is freely enthusiastic about the mathematics itself; the hedging is specifically about the reader's state.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Grep narration for bare 'obviously', 'clearly', 'it is easy to see', 'as you can see', 'trivially'. Each hit must either be removed or accompanied by a hedge or by the reason it is easy to see.

anti_patterns: Opening with a definition or formula. He states this as an explicit refusal in the Laplace video — the problem the tool solves comes before the tool. No formula in this corpus arrives before the question it answers.

Motion without a controlled variable. Nothing in the corpus moves except to show a dependence, generate an output point by point, or demonstrate an invariance. Pulsing, breathing, marching dashes, and idle wandering have no analogue anywhere.

Change without variation. Decorative loops are change, but the reader learns nothing because nothing is being varied against anything. The single most instructive shot in the corpus — varying the input distribution and showing the summed distribution refuse to move — is the exact inverse.
Unexplained constants, signs, bases, and normalisers. Every one is either derived from a requirement, marked as convention with a reason given, or explicitly deferred.

Toy examples whose target property holds by construction. The self-diagnosed cause of his worst failure: a verifier that just checks whether its input equals a fixed number, used to illustrate searching for an unknown input.
Fixing conceptual confusion with implementation detail. He explicitly declines to add the low-level translation step and argues it would not help.

Letting a chosen projection, slice, or coordinate frame read as part of the mechanism. He corrects this directly and calls the confinement to the chosen plane an emergent property, not an instruction.
Showing a picture that is not literally what the formula says without flagging it. He flags the analytic continuation rather than let a smooth plot imply convergence where there is none.
Claiming a pattern from small numbers. The Moser circle video exists as a cautionary tale about exactly this, and insists that both the apparent pattern and its failure need explaining.

Presenting an empirical architecture with the rhetoric of inevitability. Where the object is learned rather than derived, he labels his illustrative story as a story, repeatedly, within the same passage.
Hiding the dead ends. A derived result is allowed to be announced as useless before being rescued; the failed approach stays in the narrative.

Assuming that an attempted forestalling worked. He states plainly that he tried to head off the objection and failed — the attempt does not discharge the obligation, and an objection created by the framing must be answered at the framing level.
Asserting what the reader understands or finds obvious. Claims about the reader's state are consistently hedged, and calibration uncertainty is admitted outright.

Naming before building. The standard name arrives after the object has been constructed, visualised, and manipulated — and provenance anecdotes attached to names are fact-checked rather than repeated.

Letting a truncated derivation stand in for a full one under a budget. Under extreme compression he cuts derivation entirely and keeps framing, one calibration number, and the honesty markers, rather than shipping a half-argument that implies completeness.
