lens: What earns an animation — reconstructing 3Blue1Brown's motion-vs-static discipline from narration that references off-screen visual events

findings.observation: The dominant animation form is a SINGLE-PARAMETER SWEEP: one named scalar is dragged continuously, and every other object on screen is rendered as an explicit function of it. The motion's payload is not any one frame but the mapping parameter → response.
findings.evidence: Convolution X+Y: an interactive demo where he grabs the shift parameter s and slides it; the flipped graph translates, the product graph reshapes, its area changes, and the output curve is traced out point by point as 'whatever the area of the lower-left graph is'. Laplace: he moves s around the s-plane, watches the spiraling vector-sum converge to different points, then leaves it 'on autopilot' while s wanders and the magnitude surface is painted over the plane. Cross-entropy: he fixes P, graphs cross-entropy as a function of Q, then moves P and traces where the minimum goes — the traced locus IS a new curve (the entropy of P). Entropy: he sloshes the probability-bar widths around and the total rectangle area rises and falls.
findings.why_it_works: A continuous sweep delivers a derivative and a dependency directly to the visual system. Two static frames deliver two points and force the reader to hold both in working memory and diff them — an operation that costs attention and usually fails silently. Also: in the cross-entropy case the swept parameter literally CONSTRUCTS a new object (the locus of minima), which no pair of frames could do.

findings.observation: The single case where motion is not merely permitted but MANDATORY is an invariance claim. To assert 'the result does not depend on X' he perturbs X on screen and lets the reader watch the result fail to move.
findings.evidence: Central Limit Theorem: at sum-size 3 he changes the underlying distribution and the bottom plot changes shape completely; at sum-size 50 he changes it again and states that no matter how he changes it, there is essentially no effect on the bottom plot. Why-pi-in-the-normal: the bell surface has rotational symmetry about the z-axis, and the whole proof leans on that; the symmetry is shown by rotating and seeing no change. Colliding blocks: after highlighting two chords and the arc between them he says it did not matter which two he happened to highlight — the highlight is moved to prove the universality.
findings.why_it_works: An invariance is a negative, universally quantified claim. A static frame can only exhibit one instance, which the skeptical reader correctly reads as an example, not a law. Continuous perturbation with a non-responding output is the cheapest available demonstration of 'for all'.

findings.observation: The second-most common form is not continuous motion at all: it is SEQUENTIAL REVEAL WITH PERSISTENT OBJECT IDENTITY. Discrete steps, each one a state transition on an object that stays on screen and keeps its identity across the step.
findings.evidence: Discrete convolution: the flipped array slides one integer unit at a time, each stop producing one output entry which stays. Image blurring: the 3x3 kernel marches pixel by pixel, the output image fills in behind it. Attention: embeddings → query vectors → key vectors → grid of dot-product dots → softmax normalising each column → masking (entries set to negative infinity, then to zero) → value vectors weighted and summed → delta-e added back to the original embedding; each stage is a transition on a persistent diagram. Entropy: the robot decodes a bitstream one bit at a time and the set of still-possible instructions narrows as each bit lands. Moser's circle: one boundary point added at a time, chords drawn, regions recounted.
findings.why_it_works: The reader's real difficulty in a multi-step mechanism is re-identifying 'which thing is which' across the step boundary. Keeping the object on screen and mutating it in place carries that identity for free. Note this requires no continuous motion at all — the step boundaries are discrete and narrated as discrete.

findings.observation: He animates a rigid re-layout (flip, rotate, rescale axes, tilt an axis upright) only when the post-motion configuration exposes something the pre-motion one hid — and he states the payoff in the same breath as performing the motion.
findings.evidence: Convolutions: he flips the second distribution horizontally, immediately asks why one would do that, and answers by pointing at which pairs now line up vertically. Colliding blocks: he rescales the velocity axes by square roots of the masses specifically so the conservation-of-energy ellipse becomes a circle, having first said out loud that a circle would be more promising given that pi is the target. Gaussian+Gaussian: he rotates a diagonal slice 45 degrees so that the integration becomes an integration over a single variable with the other one constant — the rotation IS the proof step. Sol LeWitt: he tilts the corner axis to vertical because it makes the three-edge orbit structure easier to see.
findings.why_it_works: The motion answers 'why are we allowed to do this and what did we buy'. A before/after pair would have to be captioned; the motion is self-captioning because the reader watches the congruence being preserved.

findings.observation: The cheapest and most frequent visual device is HIGHLIGHT ON A FIXED LAYOUT — positions never change, only colour/size/opacity. He uses this wherever the claim is 'these particular elements are the relevant ones'.
findings.evidence: Dice grid: the 6x6 grid stays put while the highlighted diagonal moves from the sum-6 diagonal to the sum-7 diagonal. Attention: a grid where dot size encodes dot-product magnitude, then the column under a specific token is highlighted, then the upper-triangular mask region is marked. Moser: the 0th, 2nd and 4th entries of one Pascal row are highlighted, then visually related to a contiguous run in the row above. Colliding blocks: two chords and the single arc between them are highlighted.
findings.why_it_works: The reader's spatial map of the diagram stays stable, so no re-orientation cost is paid; all of the change budget goes to the attention pointer. This is the highest argument-per-unit-motion device in the corpus.

findings.observation: Two different visualizations of one object are proved equivalent by driving BOTH from the same parameter simultaneously and letting the reader watch them stay locked in step.
findings.evidence: Convolution X+Y: he pulls up both visualizations side by side and slowly decreases s — on the left this selects a different diagonal slice of the 3D surface, on the right it shifts the flipped graph — and points out that at all values of s the slice shape and the product-graph shape coincide. Colliding blocks: the physical block animation and the abstract state-space point are driven by the same clock, which is what makes the translation from physics to geometry believable.
findings.why_it_works: Simultaneity plus a shared driver is read by the visual system as identity. A single coincidence at one value of s would be an anecdote; coincidence maintained across a continuous sweep is the actual universally-quantified claim.

findings.observation: Formulae are built and transformed ONE SYMBOL AT A TIME, with the graph or diagram responding to each symbol change, and each change is verbally attributed to a specific visual consequence.
findings.evidence: CLT: the normal-distribution formula is assembled layer by layer — exponential, negated exponent, absolute value (rejected out loud for producing a sharp point), squared exponent, a constant inside to stretch and squish, the sigma reparametrisation, division by root-pi to fix the area, division by sigma-root-2, then the fractions combined. At every stage he names what the curve just did. Why-pi: the two-variable exponential is factored into a product of two one-variable exponentials and that factoring is immediately used as the argument that every slice is a rescaled copy. Moser: plugging into Euler's formula, he calls out specific terms that cancel — an n added and an n subtracted, two copies of one binomial minus one copy.
findings.why_it_works: In algebra the reader's difficulty is tracking which sub-expression became which. A morph that preserves term identity carries exactly the information a static before/after pair destroys. Pairing the symbol change with a simultaneous graph response also welds syntax to semantics.

findings.observation: He explicitly marks routine algebra as NOT deserving attention and lets it run without step-by-step narration.
findings.evidence: Laplace: before combining two partial fractions into the tabulated form he says he will just run some algebra on autopilot, and then only comments on the result. Gaussian+Gaussian: he acknowledges the direct route is an exercise in completing the square, says there is nothing wrong with that, and then declines to do it in favour of the geometric argument.
findings.why_it_works: Animating a manipulation implicitly promises 'something is happening here worth watching'. Spending that promise on bookkeeping devalues it everywhere else. Explicitly labelling a stretch as mechanical preserves the reader's trust that narrated motion is always load-bearing.

findings.observation: Stochastic/sampling animations are used to MOTIVATE and are then explicitly RETIRED in favour of exact computation, with the limitation named out loud.
findings.evidence: CLT: he runs a Galton board, then a sampled histogram of dice sums, then four such simulations in parallel at sum-sizes 2/5/10/15 — and then says illustrating with a simulation is fun but feels imprecise, asks whether the spikiness he sees is real or an artifact of randomness, and switches to computed exact distributions. He returns much later to confirm the spikiness was real. Convolution X+Y: repeated sampling of two weighted dice is shown to give a heuristic sense, then he states the real task is to compute the distribution precisely.
findings.why_it_works: A simulation shows a plausible-looking picture whose noise the reader cannot distinguish from signal. Naming that ambiguity and then resolving it converts the animation from a claim into a question that the exact computation answers — which is a stronger rhetorical position than either alone.

findings.observation: Rigor that would derail the main line is deliberately parked in a STATIC on-screen note addressed to a self-selected subset of readers. This is a recurring, named device, not an accident.
findings.evidence: Convolution X+Y: a note left on screen about the square-root-of-2 factor, for calculus enthusiasts who want to pause and ponder. Why-pi: the same device for the higher-dimensional-sphere derivation. Cross-entropy: the Lagrange-multiplier argument for why the loss must be a logarithm is pulled up as a screen note for multivariable calculus enthusiasts, plus a second note about overfitting. Gaussian+Gaussian: an exercise note for the unequal-standard-deviation case. Attention: the value-up/value-down naming convention is left as an on-screen note, with the explicit reason that it risks distracting from the main conceptual points.
findings.why_it_works: It resolves the tension between rigor and momentum without compromising either. Crucially the note is STATIC — motion would drag the whole audience's attention to material that only a minority wants.

findings.observation: Diagrams are treated as capital: a small vocabulary of scenes is introduced once, flagged as returning, and then amortised across an entire multi-video arc.
findings.evidence: The diagonal-slice picture is introduced in the convolutions video with an admission that he is having fun with the animation, plus an explicit promise that the diagonal-slice intuition will come back for a genuinely satisfying proof — and it then does the entire work of the Gaussian-convolution proof and connects to the pi-in-the-normal proof. The negative-log bar picture from the entropy video becomes the entropy area diagram, then becomes the cross-entropy area diagram with bar widths from one distribution and bar heights from another, then becomes the KL-divergence diagram. The state-space circle in the colliding-blocks video is announced as holding the key to a quantum-computing connection in a later video.
findings.why_it_works: Reuse converts the one-time cost of teaching a visual encoding into an asset. It also lets a later argument be carried almost entirely by a diagram the reader already fluently reads, which is where the genuinely hard steps get their headroom.

findings.observation: Before a load-bearing animation plays, he frequently asks the reader to PREDICT its outcome.
findings.evidence: Convolutions: before running the edge-detection kernel he asks the reader to take a moment to predict and understand what effect this kernel will have on the image. Convolution X+Y: before showing the two-normals surface he says many viewers may enjoy taking a moment to predict how it will look and what properties it has that could be exploited. Colliding blocks: before interpreting the conservation-of-energy equation in the abstract velocity space he asks for a moment's thought about what it is telling us.
findings.why_it_works: A prediction converts passive watching into a commitment the animation can confirm or violate, which is what makes the frames memorable. It is also a sharp authoring test: if you cannot write a one-sentence 'what do you expect to happen' prompt for an animation, that animation is not carrying an argument.

findings.observation: Every load-bearing animation TERMINATES, and its final frame is the claim. Nothing in the corpus is described as running indefinitely.
findings.evidence: The parameter sweep ends having traced out the entire convolution curve. The arc-dropping in the colliding-blocks circle ends exactly when one more arc would overlap — and that termination condition IS the count. The kernel march ends with the completed blurred image. The formula build ends at the finished normal-distribution expression. The repeated-convolution smoothing ends at the bell curve. The dice-sum simulation ends at a stated sample count and he then draws a conclusion from where it stopped.
findings.why_it_works: An argument has a conclusion; a conclusion is a final state. A motion with no final frame is structurally incapable of concluding anything, which is exactly why an endlessly looping decoration reads as noise no matter how tastefully it is drawn.

findings.observation: At most one independent thing moves per shot. Where multiple panels animate at once, they are small multiples of the SAME motion differing in one fixed constant, and that comparison is the argument.
findings.evidence: The convolution demo has three or four panels but exactly one driver (s); everything else is a declared function of it. The dice grid is static while only the highlight moves. The state-space circle is static while only the point moves. Pascal's triangle is static while only the highlighted entries move. The deliberate exception: the CLT video runs four simulations in parallel at sum-sizes 2, 5, 10 and 15, where the whole point is the cross-panel comparison of how bell-curve-like each becomes.
findings.why_it_works: Two independent motions force the reader to time-share attention and they will miss at least one. Small multiples do not violate this because the panels share a driver, so the reader tracks one motion and reads the differences spatially rather than temporally.

findings.observation: When motion is genuinely not load-bearing, he says so out loud, bounds it, and gives its remaining justification. There are only three such moments in fifteen transcripts.
findings.evidence: Colliding blocks: he admits the collision sounds are an artistic choice he simply likes — then adds the substantive reason, that it is otherwise hard to convey purely visually how dense the middle burst of collisions is. Convolution X+Y: he admits he is having a bit of fun with the animations and that nobody working this on paper would draw the 3D plot — but the fun collapse along the diagonal reproduces the already-known distribution, i.e. it is a consistency check, and he promises the picture will be load-bearing later. Sol LeWitt: the long tracking shot down a hallway of 4096 cubes exists only to make the size of the brute-force search felt, and he closes it by saying enough goofing around, let's make a plan.
findings.why_it_works: Bounding and justifying an indulgence keeps the reader's default assumption intact: that anything moving on screen is there for a reason. That default is the entire budget an explainer spends when it does animate.

findings.observation: He treats an animation as capable of INSTALLING a false belief, and the corrective is words, not a better animation.
findings.evidence: The Grover's-algorithm correction video: he diagnoses that briefly flashing an example function which merely checks whether the input equals a specific number made viewers believe the computer already knows the answer, and calls that framing his own fault. He also disowns his own visual choice of projecting the algorithm onto a two-dimensional slice that by construction contained the target axis — stating that the algorithm does not care how we choose to visualize it, and that the state vector staying in that plane is (short quote) 'a happy emergent property', not part of the instruction set. The entire remedy is a re-explanation with a better worked example (sudoku, then a cryptographic hash) plus an explicit statement of the property he had left implicit (linearity).
findings.why_it_works: Visual choices carry unstated implicatures. A frame that shows the answer sitting inside the machine implies the machine knows the answer; a frame that shows a conveniently chosen coordinate plane implies someone chose it. Neither implicature can be revoked by more motion — only by naming it. This is the corpus's own root-cause analysis of an explanation failure, and it is about what a picture SUGGESTS, not about what it depicts.

findings.observation: Whenever a visual encoding changes meaning, he announces the change at the exact moment it happens.
findings.evidence: CLT: he states that in anticipation of an animation he is about to build, the bottom plot now encodes probability as the AREA of each bar rather than its height, and that the reader should think of the y-axis as a probability density — precisely so it will align with how continuous distributions get read later. Convolution X+Y: at the transition to the continuous case he states that the y-axis no longer represents probability but probability density. Cross-entropy: he states that in the diagram, bar width comes from one distribution and bar height from the other.
findings.why_it_works: Silent re-encoding is the most expensive possible error, because the reader keeps confidently reading the old semantics off the new picture. The cost of announcing it is one sentence.

findings.observation: Cheap-to-check claims are CHECKED ON SCREEN rather than asserted, including running actual code and showing actual numbers.
findings.evidence: Convolutions: he invites the reader to open a numerical library and confirm he is not lying, then shows the actual convolution output for a small example; later he times a naive convolution against an FFT-based one on hundred-thousand-element arrays and reports the measured runtimes rather than claiming a speedup. Entropy: he shows an actual sampled instruction stream encoded both the naive way and the clever way, so the length difference is visible rather than only computed. Sol LeWitt: the artist's count was confirmed only after consulting mathematicians, an exhaustive computational search later re-verified it, and the video reports the actual residual error in the finished sculpture (a duplicated cube and a missing one). Colliding blocks: he refuses to call the pi result proved, because the required statement about runs of nines in the digits of pi is beyond current tools.
findings.why_it_works: Showing the check rather than asserting the result is what allows the reader to extend trust to the claims that cannot be cheaply checked. It also catches the author's own errors before shipping, which is the only reason it exists as a discipline.

findings.observation: The spoken pause instruction is his pacing gate; in a self-paced medium the structural equivalent is a mandatory question, best placed immediately before the animation whose outcome it asks the reader to predict.
findings.evidence: Explicit pause-and-try invitations recur throughout: pausing to work out the two-dice distribution, pausing to predict the kernel's effect, pausing to convince yourself a functional-equation property extends from two inputs to many, pausing over what the standard deviation of an empirical average does as the sample grows, pausing to check that two forms of the KL-divergence expression agree.
findings.why_it_works: In video the pause is the only available commitment device. In a self-paced medium the reader will simply not pause, so the commitment has to be enforced by a gate. Placing that gate immediately before the animation means the animation becomes feedback on an answer the reader has already committed to.

findings.observation: The one whole-video case of extreme compression contains essentially no described motion — it is a chain of conceptual claims with schematic illustrations.
findings.evidence: The brief LLM explainer (~1.3k words) walks through prediction, sampling, parameters, training, backpropagation, scale, pre-training vs RLHF, parallelism, embeddings, attention and feed-forward layers with no narration that references sliding, sweeping, highlighting or watching. The one dramatic beat is a rhetorical question about how long a billion operations per second would take, delivered as a question with a pause, not as motion.
findings.why_it_works: When the goal is coverage rather than mechanism, motion has nothing to do: there is no parameter to sweep and no invariance to demonstrate. This is direct evidence that his animation is driven by argument structure, not by a house style or a target motion density.

findings.observation: I could not find evidence of purely ambient or decorative motion anywhere in the narration — but the transcript is structurally incapable of ruling it out, and I want to be explicit about that limit.
findings.evidence: Across all fifteen files, every 'watch', 'notice', 'as I slide', 'let me pull up', 'take a look at' points at a state change that is a premise or a conclusion. The only borderline case is the opening of the convolution X+Y video, where repeated samples of a random variable animate underneath an explanation of what the density curve means. Even that loops over SAMPLES — each cycle delivers one new draw — rather than replaying an identical cycle.
findings.why_it_works: Ambient motion is by definition motion the narration does not mention, so a caption file cannot detect it. The honest, and more useful, positive claim is the narration-side one: he never asks the reader to attend to a motion that is not carrying a claim, and in the three places where motion is not load-bearing he says so. The sample-loop borderline case also suggests a mechanical discriminator: information delivered per loop iteration. A sampling loop delivers one new bit per cycle; a pulse ring delivers zero, forever.

candidate_rules.rule: Never ship an animation whose first frame and last frame are identical. If the visual state returns to where it started, delete the motion and draw the static frame.
candidate_rules.rationale: Every load-bearing animation in the corpus terminates in a final state that IS the claim: the traced convolution curve, the circle filled with arcs until one more won't fit, the completed blurred image, the finished formula. A motion that returns to its start has no conclusion and therefore cannot be an argument. This single test kills pulse rings, breathing circles, marching ants and a token pacing back and forth — all four of the reported failures — without requiring any taste judgement.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Mechanical. Grep the stylesheet and JS for `infinite`, `animation-iteration-count`, `alternate`, `setInterval` without a matching `clearInterval`, and any `requestAnimationFrame` recursion with no termination predicate. Additionally, in a test harness, render each shot's drawFn at t=0 and at t=duration and diff the serialized SVG/DOM; identical output is a hard failure.

candidate_rules.rule: Every animated shot must declare exactly one driver — a single named scalar (a parameter, a step index, a time step) — and every animated attribute on screen must be a pure function of it. Two independent timelines in one shot is a hard error; split the shot.
candidate_rules.rationale: In the corpus, one thing moves and everything else is derived: s drives the flipped graph, the product graph, the area, and the traced output point all at once; the dice grid is frozen while only the highlight moves; the state-space circle is frozen while only the point moves. Two independent motions force the reader to time-share attention and they will miss one.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Mechanical if the API requires it: make the animated form of S() take drawFn(ctx, driverValue) with a single scalar argument and forbid the drawFn from reading a wall clock. A lint rule can then flag any use of Date.now(), performance.now(), or a second animation timeline inside a drawFn.

candidate_rules.rule: The only permitted exception to one-driver-per-shot is small multiples: N panels sharing the same driver, differing in exactly one fixed constant, where the cross-panel comparison is the stated argument.
candidate_rules.rationale: He runs four sum-size simulations in parallel precisely because comparing how bell-curve-like each becomes is the claim. The panels do not compete for attention because the reader tracks one motion and reads the differences spatially.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Structurally checkable: a multi-panel shot must be authored as a single drawFn mapped over an array of constants, not as N hand-written panels. If the panels cannot be expressed as one function of one varying constant, they are not small multiples.

candidate_rules.rule: Every animated shot must carry a non-empty `watch` string that names, in advance, the specific thing the reader should look for and what would count as it happening. If `watch` is empty, the shot renders static.
candidate_rules.rationale: Before load-bearing animations he asks the reader to predict the outcome — the kernel's effect on the image, the shape of the two-normals surface, what the energy equation says in the abstract velocity space. If you cannot write one sentence saying what to watch and what it would mean, you have not got an argument, you have got motion. This is the closest thing to a mechanically enforceable taste rule.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Schema-level. Make `watch` a required field on any shot flagged animated; a build step fails on empty/whitespace/boilerplate values. A secondary heuristic check: reject `watch` strings that do not contain a concrete noun from the scene's own object vocabulary.

candidate_rules.rule: Animate a parameter sweep when and only when the narration must say 'because it moved this way, the following is true' — i.e. the dependency, the rate, or the invariance is itself a step in the argument. Otherwise use sequential reveal, highlight, or a static frame.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is the whole decision rule in one line. The sweep earns its cost when the payload is a mapping (how output depends on input), a rate (the area grows linearly, then shrinks linearly), or a non-response (changing the input distribution stops mattering past sum-size ~50). None of those survive being reduced to two frames.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Authoring-time question with a checkable artifact: require the shot to record which of three tags applies — DEPENDENCY, RATE, or INVARIANCE — and require the narration to contain the corresponding claim. A shot that cannot be tagged is not a sweep.

candidate_rules.rule: If the claim is 'X does not depend on Y', you MUST animate Y and show X not moving. In this one case motion is mandatory, not merely permitted.
candidate_rules.rationale: An invariance is a universally quantified negative. A static frame exhibits one instance, which a careful reader correctly discounts as an example. Perturbation-with-no-response is the cheapest honest demonstration of 'for all'. Directly applicable in RL: policy invariance to reward shifts, optimality of a greedy policy being unchanged under positive affine reward scaling, value iteration converging to the same fixed point from different initialisations.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Mechanical: for shots tagged INVARIANCE, the harness renders the shot at several driver values and asserts that the designated invariant sub-element's serialized geometry is unchanged across all of them while at least one other element does change. If the invariant moves, the visual is lying.

candidate_rules.rule: Use formula term-morphing only when a term on the left survives into a term on the right and the reader needs to know which became which. A morph must declare an explicit id map covering at least one surviving term; a morph with no id continuity is a cross-fade and must be a static replacement instead.
candidate_rules.rationale: The value of morphing is preserved term identity across a transformation — exactly the information a before/after pair destroys. He builds the normal-distribution formula one symbol at a time, naming the graph's response to each; he calls out which specific terms cancel in the Euler's-formula substitution. Since our engine morphs via FLIP on HTML spans, id continuity is literally the mechanism, so this rule is enforceable by construction.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Mechanical: the morph primitive should require a from→to id map as a parameter and throw at author time if the intersection of source and target ids is empty.

candidate_rules.rule: Mark routine manipulation as routine and do not animate it. Show the completed line and say in the narration that the intermediate steps are mechanical.
candidate_rules.rationale: He explicitly runs algebra on autopilot when combining partial fractions, and explicitly declines to walk through completing the square. Animating a manipulation implicitly promises something worth watching; spending that promise on bookkeeping devalues it everywhere else.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Reviewable, with a proxy: count morph steps per knowledge point and flag any morph whose narration string does not state a reason for that specific step (what it exposes, what it cancels, what it reparametrises). A morph with a purely procedural narration is a candidate for collapsing.

candidate_rules.rule: Prefer changing colour, opacity, size or stroke on a fixed layout over moving anything. If positions do not need to change for the claim, they must not change.
candidate_rules.rationale: Highlight-on-static is the highest argument-per-unit-motion device in the corpus and appears in nearly every video: the frozen dice grid with a travelling diagonal highlight, the frozen attention grid with a highlighted column and a marked mask region, the frozen Pascal triangle with highlighted entries. It preserves the reader's spatial map so the entire change budget goes to the attention pointer.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Mechanical: diff the serialized geometry (x/y/transform/d attributes) between consecutive frames. If the only differences are in fill, stroke, opacity, r, or font-weight, the shot passes cheaply. If positions change, the shot must be tagged with a re-layout justification (see next rule).

candidate_rules.rule: A re-layout animation (flip, rotate, rescale, reorder) must state in the same narration beat what the new configuration makes visible that the old one hid.
candidate_rules.rationale: He flips the second distribution and immediately asks why, then answers by pointing at which pairs now align; he rescales the velocity axes specifically so the ellipse becomes a circle, having already said a circle would be more promising; he rotates the diagonal slice 45 degrees because it turns the integral into one over a single variable. The motion is self-captioning only because the payoff is named.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Schema-level: shots tagged RELAYOUT require a `reveals` field. Reviewable check: the `reveals` text must describe a property of the POST state, not merely restate the operation.

candidate_rules.rule: Any stochastic or sampling animation must be followed, inside the same knowledge point and before the SUM card, by the exact or derived object — and the narration must name what the simulation cannot tell you.
candidate_rules.rationale: He runs Galton boards and sampled histograms, then says the simulation feels imprecise, asks aloud whether the spikiness he sees is real or an artifact of randomness, switches to computed exact distributions, and returns later to confirm. This is the disciplined form of exactly the failure mode we hit: an endlessly walking token is a sampling animation that never gets retired and never resolves into anything exact.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Mechanical: shots flagged `stochastic: true` require a subsequent shot in the same knowledge point flagged `exact: true`; build fails otherwise. Also assert that a stochastic shot terminates at a declared sample count rather than looping.

candidate_rules.rule: Put rigor that would derail the main line into a static, explicitly optional note card. Never animate a footnote.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is a recurring named device across at least five of the videos: the square-root-of-2 factor, the higher-dimensional-sphere derivation, the Lagrange-multiplier argument for why the loss must be a logarithm, the unequal-variance exercise, the value-matrix naming convention — each parked on screen for the self-selecting minority, with the explicit reason that it risks distracting from the main conceptual points. Motion would drag the whole audience's attention onto material most of them do not want. For a rigorous RL audience this channel is where the measure-theoretic caveats, the contraction-mapping proofs and the exact step-size conditions belong.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Mechanical: a NOTE-tagged block must contain no animated primitives; lint the block's subtree for any transition, transform, or morph call.

candidate_rules.rule: Whenever a visual channel changes meaning relative to the previous shot, the narration must declare the change at that exact moment.
candidate_rules.rationale: He announces that bar area rather than bar height now encodes probability, in anticipation of an animation he is about to build; he announces the switch from probability to probability density on the y-axis at the continuous transition; he announces that bar width comes from one distribution and height from another. Silent re-encoding is the most expensive possible error because the reader keeps confidently reading the old semantics off the new picture.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Semi-mechanical: maintain a per-scene-type encoding registry (what x, y, width, height, colour, size mean). A build step compares each shot's declared encoding against the previous shot's; on any diff it asserts the narration contains a declaration sentence and fails if not.

candidate_rules.rule: Before authoring any content that uses a rendering primitive, render the smallest possible instance of that primitive and inspect the actual rendered output. Never infer a primitive's capabilities from its name or signature.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is the discipline behind showing measured runtimes rather than claiming a speedup, showing the actual encoded bitstream rather than only its computed length, and inviting the reader to run the convolution themselves to confirm he is not lying. The LaTeX failure is exactly this rule's violation: a primitive's capability was assumed, never observed.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Fully mechanical and this one is worth building first. Generate a smoke-test page that renders every distinct formula string in the deck, then script the DOM and fail the build if any rendered text node contains a backslash, `$`, `\frac`, `\sum`, `\alpha`-style command tokens, `^{`, or `_{`. Extend the same scan to every drawFn's output. Run it in CI on every content change, not once.

candidate_rules.rule: Place a QUIZ immediately before the load-bearing animation whose outcome it asks the reader to predict, rather than after the explanation as a comprehension check.
candidate_rules.rationale: In video the spoken pause is the only commitment device; in a self-paced medium the reader will simply not pause, so the commitment must be gated. Placing the gate before the motion turns the animation into feedback on an answer the reader has already committed to — which is the mechanism behind his repeated pre-animation prediction invitations.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Structural: for each knowledge point, assert that at least one QUIZ precedes the first shot tagged DEPENDENCY, RATE or INVARIANCE. Reviewable check: the quiz options should be distinguishable by watching the animation, not only by having read the surrounding text.

candidate_rules.rule: Maintain a small fixed vocabulary of scene types and reuse them across knowledge points. When a scene will do work later, say so at its introduction; when it returns, say it is returning.
candidate_rules.rationale: The diagonal-slice picture is introduced with an explicit promise that it will return for a genuinely satisfying proof, and then carries an entire later proof. The negative-log bar diagram becomes the entropy diagram becomes the cross-entropy diagram becomes the KL-divergence diagram. Reuse converts the one-time cost of teaching an encoding into an asset, and lets hard later arguments run on a picture the reader already reads fluently. For CS234 the natural reusable primitives are the backup diagram, the MDP chain and the grid world.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Mechanical: each scene type has a stable id; a report lists ids by usage count. Any id used exactly once across the whole deck is flagged for review (either promote it to reusable or justify the one-off). Any id used two or more times must have a forward-reference string on first use and a back-reference on subsequent uses.

candidate_rules.rule: Within a single knowledge point, allow at most one continuous parameter sweep. Everything else must be sequential reveal, highlight, or static.
candidate_rules.rationale: Sequential reveal with persistent object identity — not continuous motion — is the workhorse form for mechanisms, and it is what a backup diagram, a value-iteration pass or a Bellman update naturally is. Reserving continuous sweep for the one genuinely continuous dependency in each knowledge point is what keeps it feeling significant. FLAGGING THIS AS EXTRAPOLATION: the corpus gives no explicit motion budget, so the specific cap of one is my inference from the observed pattern (one demo, many builds and highlights per video) plus the reader's exhaustion report — not a stated principle.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Mechanical: count shots tagged as continuous sweep per knowledge point; warn above one.

candidate_rules.rule: Do not animate anything that implies the mechanism knows something it does not know, or that a choice was made which no algorithm makes.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is the corpus's own root-cause analysis of an explanation failure. In the Grover correction he identifies that flashing a toy function which just checks for a specific value implied the computer already knew the answer, and that projecting onto a conveniently chosen plane implied someone chose it — and he insists the confinement to that plane is an emergent property, not an instruction. In RL this bites constantly: an agent glyph that visibly heads for the goal before learning, a value surface pre-shaped toward the optimum, a highlighted 'correct' action before the argmax has been computed. Every one of those installs the belief that the algorithm has foresight it does not have.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Reviewable, with a sharp prompt: for each shot, ask 'does anything on screen encode information the algorithm does not have at this step?' Semi-mechanical guard: assert that quantities derived from the optimal policy or optimal value function are never drawn in a shot depicting a pre-convergence iterate, unless explicitly labelled as an oracle overlay.

anti_patterns: Infinite loops of any kind — pulse rings, breathing circles, marching-ants dashes, a token pacing back and forth. Nothing in fifteen transcripts is described as running without end. Every animation he narrates terminates, and its final frame is the point. A loop delivers zero new information per cycle and, having no last frame, is structurally incapable of concluding an argument.
Motion that is identical run forwards and backwards. If reversal changes nothing, the motion encodes no direction and therefore no state transition; it should be a static diagram or a highlight.

Two or more independent things moving in one shot. He animates exactly one driver and derives everything else from it. The only exception is small multiples that share a driver, where the cross-panel comparison is the argument.

Animating what could be a highlight. He freezes the dice grid, the attention grid, the Pascal triangle and the state-space circle, and moves only the attention marker. Moving a layout that did not need to move burns the reader's spatial map for nothing.
Animating routine algebra. He explicitly runs bookkeeping steps on autopilot and declines to walk through completing the square. Morphing every line devalues the morph on the lines that matter.

Animating footnotes and caveats. Rigor he wants preserved but not centred goes onto a STATIC on-screen note addressed to whoever wants it — at least five separate instances. Motion would force the whole audience to attend to a minority's material.

Silently changing what a visual channel means. He announces the switch from height-encodes-probability to area-encodes-probability, and the switch from probability to density on the y-axis, at the exact moment each happens.

Leaving a simulation as the final word. He runs sampled histograms, then names the ambiguity out loud — is that spikiness real or an artifact of randomness — and replaces the simulation with an exact computation. A stochastic animation that is never retired is precisely the failure mode of an endlessly wandering token.

Depicting the mechanism as knowing more than it does. His own diagnosed failure: a toy verifier that just checked for a specific value implied the computer already had the answer; a conveniently chosen projection plane implied someone chose it. The remedy was a better example and an explicit statement of the omitted property, NOT a better animation.

Assuming a rendering primitive works without looking at its output. He shows measured timings instead of claiming a speedup, shows the actual encoded bitstream instead of only its length, and invites readers to run the computation themselves. The counterpart discipline is: render one instance, inspect the DOM, then author the other two hundred.

A novel bespoke graphic for every point. He builds a small vocabulary — diagonal slices, the negative-log bar diagram, the state-space circle — announces that each will return, and amortises it across a whole series.
Unannounced motion. Every 'watch', 'notice' and 'as I slide' in the corpus points at a specific state change that is a premise or a conclusion. Motion the narration cannot name is motion with no job.

Time-based spectacle in a text medium. The one indulgent stretch in the corpus — a long tracking shot down a hallway of 4096 objects to make brute-force tedium felt — depends on elapsed time and a voice filling it, and he still bounds it explicitly. It does not transfer to a self-paced page; a count and a comparison do the same work.

Reaching for animation when there is no parameter to sweep and no invariance to demonstrate. His most compressed video is a chain of conceptual claims with essentially no described motion, which is direct evidence that the animation is driven by argument structure rather than by a house style or a target motion density.

lens: Openings and motivation — how each video earns attention in its first minute or two, how it states the question it answers, how it sets up and later discharges a payoff, and what survives extreme compression.

findings.observation: Naming happens early; defining happens late; and the deferral of the definition is stated out loud as a deliberate choice. The topic word appears in the first ~30 seconds, but the formula that defines it is withheld until after the viewer has watched an instance of it being computed by hand.
findings.evidence: Laplace (j0wJBEZdwLs): before showing the definition he explicitly says he first wants to talk about what problem the transform is trying to solve. CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo): names the normal distribution, says there's a very specific function for it, and defers it explicitly to later. Entropy (l6DKRf-fAAM): says defining information and entropy too early would spoil the story, and calls great definitions the residue of an insight. Convolution (KuXjwB4LzSA): the word appears in sentence 3, the summation formula arrives only after the dice grid and the sliding-flipped-array picture.
findings.why_it_works: A definition is a compression of experience the reader hasn't had yet, so it decompresses into nothing. Delaying it converts it from an arbitrary stipulation into a summary of something already witnessed. Announcing the delay stops the reader from feeling they missed the definition.

findings.observation: Every opening in the corpus puts a specific object or a specific case under manipulation before any general statement. Not one video in this corpus opens with a definition, a field survey, or a historical chronology.
findings.evidence: Galton board already dropping balls (zeJD6dqJ5lo); two blocks colliding with a running collision count (6dTyOl1fmDo); chords being added to a circle one at a time (YtkIWDE36qU); the finished s-plane plot displayed and declared to be what will be built (j0wJBEZdwLs); a torn movie script and a next-word machine (LPZh9BOjkQs); two sampled normal distributions and a running sum (IaSGqQa5O-M); a museum table of cube fragments (_BrFKp-U8GI).
findings.why_it_works: A manipulable instance gives the reader something to hold predictions about. Generalities give nothing to be wrong about, so they generate no engagement and no memory hooks.

findings.observation: The dominant hook structure is a short ordered ladder of concrete cases, where the reader is explicitly invited to guess the next entry before it is revealed — and the reveal violates the guess or lands on something eerily familiar.
findings.evidence: Moser's circle (YtkIWDE36qU): 2, 4, 8, 16, then a direct challenge about whether you'd bet your life on the next one, then 31. Blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo): 3 collisions, then 31, then 314, then 3141. Entropy (l6DKRf-fAAM): 8 bits per character, then about 4, then better still, then the open question of the limit. LLM briefly (LPZh9BOjkQs): offers two wrong anchors for the training compute (a year? ten thousand years?) before revealing over 100 million years. Attention (eMlx5fFNoYc): mole, then tower, then Eiffel tower, then miniature Eiffel tower, each added word forcing a further update.
findings.why_it_works: Committing to a prediction creates a debt the reader wants settled, and a violated prediction marks the exact location where the reader's model is wrong — which is the only place explanation can attach. The ladder also silently teaches the parameter that matters before naming it.

findings.observation: The question the video answers is stated as a gradable task with a determinate answer, not as a topic. Frequently it is phrased as something the reader should be able to do by the end.
findings.evidence: CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo) states the target task explicitly: roll a die 100 times, sum the results, find the narrowest range you're 95% confident the sum falls in — and the video literally works that problem at the end (350 ± 2·17.1 → about 316 to 384). Moser (YtkIWDE36qU): if it isn't a power of two, what function of n is it? Entropy (l6DKRf-fAAM): what is the limit of text compression? Gaussian (d_qvLDhkg00): why this function and not any other bump-shaped one?
findings.why_it_works: A gradable task lets the reader self-assess, which converts passive watching into monitored progress. A topic label ("today: the central limit theorem") gives no such signal.

findings.observation: He plants open loops in the opening — items explicitly withheld with a promise of when they return — and the corpus shows these are actually closed, in the same terms, at the promised time.
findings.evidence: CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo): announces the theorem has three assumptions, refuses to say what they are, and instructs the viewer to try to spot them; all three are delivered in the final section. Entropy (l6DKRf-fAAM): says he'll share a numerical estimate at the end and does (about one bit per character). Blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo): opens by admitting the pi connection is technically an unsolved problem, explained at the end via the digits-of-pi nines condition. X+Y (IaSGqQa5O-M): opens with a quiz and promises to return to it with an unusually satisfying answer.
findings.why_it_works: An unclosed loop is a low-cost attention debt; discharging it in the promised terms is what builds the reader's willingness to accept the next deferral. The instruction to watch for the withheld item also converts the middle of the piece into active search.

findings.observation: Motivation is overwhelmingly by unexplained surprise or by an unanswered question — not by usefulness. This corrects an expectation I went in with: an applications survey appears in only a minority of openings and is never the sole justification.
findings.evidence: Convolution (KuXjwB4LzSA) and Transformers (wjZofJX0v4M) do list application domains, but each pairs it with something else (a gap in a list of familiar operations; unpacking the acronym the reader already says). CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo) lists heights and prime-factor counts as places the shape *occurs*, not as things it's useful for. Moser (YtkIWDE36qU), X+Y (IaSGqQa5O-M), Gaussian (d_qvLDhkg00), pi-in-the-normal (cy8r7WSuT1I) and LLM briefly (LPZh9BOjkQs) contain no utility pitch at all in their openings.
findings.why_it_works: Usefulness is a claim about the reader's future; surprise is an event in the reader's present. Only the second creates immediate need. For a rigor-seeking audience, an unresolved discrepancy is a stronger draw than an argument that they'll need this someday.

findings.observation: He shows the destination as an image before it has been earned, and describes what to look for in it, so the reader has a target silhouette to fill in.
findings.evidence: Laplace (j0wJBEZdwLs) literally opens on the final complicated diagram and says it's what will be built; well before the definition he previews that the transformed function will show sharp spikes over particular values of s, and names them poles. CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo) previews the core visual intuition — realign all the distributions to a common mean, rescale to unit standard deviation, and watch them converge on one universal shape — before deriving any of it. (Inference: I'm reading the on-screen content off the narration in both cases.)
findings.why_it_works: A preview turns subsequent detail into recognition rather than accumulation. The reader knows which features are load-bearing and stops trying to memorize everything equally.

findings.observation: He states the wish before the machine: describes the properties an ideal tool would have, in plain language, and only then reveals that the named tool is the thing that has those properties. The tool arrives as the answer to a need the reader now feels.
findings.evidence: Laplace (j0wJBEZdwLs): describes wanting a machine you could pump a function into that would reveal which exponential pieces it decomposes into, and only afterwards says that machine is the Laplace transform. Entropy (l6DKRf-fAAM): the third, theoretical student doesn't propose a code at all — they ask what properties a perfect code must have, which is what leads to the negative-log formula. Blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo): notes that pi is about circles and that an ellipse is tantalizingly close, then changes coordinates specifically to force a circle.
findings.why_it_works: It inverts the usual order (here is a tool, here is what it does), which leaves the reader unable to evaluate the tool. Specifying the target property first gives the reader a criterion, so the tool's design choices read as forced rather than arbitrary.

findings.observation: Every simplification is declared at the moment it is made, with its reason, and — in the strongest instances — the simplification is later revealed to have been load-bearing rather than merely convenient.
findings.evidence: CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo): the idealized Galton board is flagged as unrealistic, with the reason that the goal is not to model physics; at the end he returns and shows the real Galton board violates both independence and identical distribution, so the idealization was *necessary* for it to be an instance of the theorem at all. Blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo): itemizes perfectly elastic collisions, immovable wall, ignored relativistic effects. Entropy (l6DKRf-fAAM): calls the four-instruction robot contrived and says so. Cubes (_BrFKp-U8GI): does explicit housekeeping, relaxing two of three constraints and warning the running count will exceed the target 122 until they're restored.
findings.why_it_works: An undeclared simplification is indistinguishable from an error, and a rigorous reader will stop to check. Declaring it converts a potential objection into a shared premise; discharging it later converts the premise into a result.

findings.observation: Objections are pre-empted in the reader's own register — staged as a raised hand or a complaint — immediately after the move that provokes them, and he often concedes the objection is right before fixing it.
findings.evidence: Moser (YtkIWDE36qU): raises the does-it-depend-on-point-placement objection himself right after the count. Blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo): raises the no-energy-loss-means-no-sound complaint himself. CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo): pre-empts the complaint about the unrealistic Galton board. Convolution (KuXjwB4LzSA): voices the reader calling his sampling plan idiotic because computing the samples already costs n-squared — concedes it, then produces the FFT fix. Transformers (wjZofJX0v4M): states in first person that it doesn't feel like next-word prediction should actually work, then demonstrates GPT-2 versus GPT-3.
findings.why_it_works: An unvoiced objection blocks all downstream reasoning while the reader silently argues. Voicing it in the reader's register signals that the author is aware of the same difficulty, which is what buys permission to keep going.

findings.observation: But a pre-empting sentence cannot repair a motivating example that visibly has the wrong property. In his own postmortem he identifies the root cause of mass confusion as the framing example in the opening, not as missing technical detail — and reports that he had tried to forestall exactly that objection in words and failed.
findings.evidence: Grover postmortem (Dlsa9EBKDGI): he had opened by asking viewers to imagine a mystery number being searched for, and briefly flashed a toy function that just checks whether its input equals 12. That example *contains the answer in its own source*, so it looked like the computer already knew what it was searching for. He calls that a misleading way to open, and replaces it with Sudoku verification and SHA-256 — examples where knowing the rules manifestly does not reveal the solution. He compresses the fix into a single reframing line about the logic gates distilling the rules of the game but not the strategy.
findings.why_it_works: Readers reason from the instance, not the disclaimer. Whatever property the example visibly has is the property they will generalize, and a verbal denial arrives too late and too weakly to overwrite it. This also means comprehension failures reported at step N are often caused at step 0.

findings.observation: He legitimizes the standard or boring route before offering his own, and refers readers to other people's treatments rather than positioning against them. Where he complains about conventional teaching, the complaint is about a gap in understanding, never about other explainers.
findings.evidence: Laplace (j0wJBEZdwLs): the drive-a-car versus understand-the-engine analogy, with the explicit caveat that neither is better and driving is probably more practical, plus an admission that most of the video isn't necessary if you only want to solve equations. Gaussian (d_qvLDhkg00): says the direct route of plugging in and completing the square is fine and will get you the answer, before offering the visual route. Convolution (KuXjwB4LzSA), blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo), pi-in-the-normal (cy8r7WSuT1I): each points to other channels', other authors', or other online treatments of the same material as good.
findings.why_it_works: Attacking the standard treatment makes the reader defend it, since they usually learned it that way. Granting its validity first frees them to be curious about the supplement instead of being asked to renounce something.

findings.observation: He grades his own claims in the opening, including downgrading his own headline, and states confidence levels explicitly rather than uniformly asserting.
findings.evidence: Blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo): opens by admitting the pi connection is technically an unsolved problem. Entropy (l6DKRf-fAAM): raises the provocative claim that compression is intelligence, then immediately says it's hard to judge rigorously since intelligence is ill-defined, and offers a safer version. Gaussian (d_qvLDhkg00): promises "something like a satisfying answer" (quoted phrase — the hedge is the point). Moser (YtkIWDE36qU): says he doesn't know whether n=10 is the last power of two and offers it as an open challenge.
findings.why_it_works: For a reader seeking rigor, a uniformly confident voice is unusable because they cannot tell which claims to check. Explicit grading tells them where to spend scrutiny, and makes the ungraded claims more credible.

findings.observation: Alternative and wrong answers are personified as characters, which stages the escalation and turns a misconception into someone with a position rather than an error to be avoided.
findings.evidence: Entropy (l6DKRf-fAAM): three students — straightforward (two flat bits), clever (variable-length prefix-free code, 1.75 bits), and theoretical (asks what a perfect code must look like) — each answer is better and each is attributed. Convolution (KuXjwB4LzSA): stages a hypothetical audience member raising a hand to propose the flip-and-slide picture, after he has praised the first, grid-based answer. Pi-in-the-normal (cy8r7WSuT1I): adopts the incredulous friend from Wigner's anecdote as the standard the explanation must satisfy, and explicitly says the classic proof leaves the task incomplete until that friend's disbelief is addressed.
findings.why_it_works: A character's answer can be inhabited and then outgrown without the reader feeling personally corrected. It also lets the piece show the *space* of reasonable answers, which is what makes the chosen one feel selected rather than handed down.

findings.observation: He calibrates difficulty and the emotional shape of the journey in advance, including naming stretches that will feel like failure.
findings.evidence: Attention (eMlx5fFNoYc): warns up front that many people find the attention mechanism confusing and not to worry if it takes time. Cubes (_BrFKp-U8GI): promises playful exploration that nonetheless ends in a highly non-trivial result; later flags a whole segment as a dead end, defends spending time there, and names the sequence as disappointment preceding epiphany. Grover postmortem (Dlsa9EBKDGI): says the starting point is a genuinely weird place to start from and that everyone finds the state-vector picture weird.
findings.why_it_works: Unexpected difficulty reads as the reader's own failure and causes them to quit; predicted difficulty reads as terrain. Naming a dead end in advance also lets him include an instructive failure without the reader concluding the argument broke.

findings.observation: Under extreme compression (1,305 words), the elements that survive are: an imagined concrete scenario in second person, the identification of that scenario with the real object, one guess-then-reveal magnitude, one micro-example of the key mechanism, and one honest limitation. Everything I would have called "motivation" is cut.
findings.evidence: LLM briefly (LPZh9BOjkQs) opens with a torn movie script and a hypothetical next-word machine, then states that this is exactly what happens when you use a chatbot, and only then gives a one-sentence definition. It keeps the training-compute guess ladder, one disambiguation example (bank becoming riverbank in context), and the caveat that the specific behavior is emergent and hard to attribute. It carries no application survey, no importance rhetoric, no prerequisite or scope statement, no complaint about standard treatments, no withheld-item hook, no named characters, no meta-commentary about the explanation, and — notably — no explicit driving question at all.
findings.why_it_works: The runnable scenario is what lets a reader simulate the object; the identification is what transfers that simulation onto the real thing. The pitch is a wrapper around that transfer, so it's the first thing that can be removed without loss. This is the strongest available evidence about what he considers load-bearing.

findings.observation: Every motion he narrates does one of three jobs: it advances a ladder of concrete cases, it sweeps a parameter to demonstrate a dependence or an invariance, or it reconciles a new representation with a result already established. The claim is stated in the same breath as the motion.
findings.evidence: Ladder: chords added one at a time with the region count recomputed (YtkIWDE36qU); balls accumulating into buckets (zeJD6dqJ5lo). Sweep: changing the underlying die distribution while the sum's distribution visibly refuses to change shape once n=50 (zeJD6dqJ5lo); moving s around the s-plane and watching the spiraling vector sum grow or cancel (j0wJBEZdwLs); sliding the flipped array to successive offsets, each offset producing one output entry (KuXjwB4LzSA); redistributing probability mass and watching total entropy rise and fall (l6DKRf-fAAM). Reconcile: moving s to 1 in the complex picture and confirming the arrows stack to the value 1 already derived from the area-under-a-curve picture (j0wJBEZdwLs). CAVEAT — inference: transcripts cannot show motion he did not narrate, so this is evidence that narrated motion is load-bearing, not proof that no ambient motion exists.
findings.why_it_works: Motion draws the eye involuntarily. If what the eye is drawn to is not the thing the argument is about, attention is spent and no claim is delivered — the reader pays the cost and gets nothing, which is worse than a still image. Binding each motion to an asserted change makes the eye's involuntary tracking do the argumentative work.

findings.observation: Where a presentational element carries no information, he names it as such and justifies it on communicative grounds rather than leaving it unremarked.
findings.evidence: Blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo): explicitly says the collision sounds are an artistic choice — physically wrong given perfectly elastic collisions — and defends them because the density of the mid-experiment burst is otherwise very hard to convey visually. He also stages a deliberate pause before the 314 reveal and comments on it.
findings.why_it_works: Declaring a non-informational element forces the author to identify what fact it is the sole carrier of. Anything that fails that test has no defence and gets cut. It also prevents the reader from hunting for meaning in something that has none.

findings.observation: Numbers and claims are checked against an independent second route, and the check is shown rather than asserted; assertions that were not proved are itemized rather than hidden.
findings.evidence: Cubes (_BrFKp-U8GI): derives family size 12 for a one-edge-removed cube from the lookalike formula and immediately corroborates it against the independently known fact that a cube has 12 edges; closes by naming two specific results the argument assumed but did not prove (that the cube rotation group has order 24, and the orbit-stabilizer theorem). CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo): flags that the spiky look of a 3,000-sample simulation might be a sampling artifact, then computes the exact distribution and confirms the spikiness is real. Convolution (KuXjwB4LzSA): invites the reader to run the convolution of [1,2,3] with [4,5,6] in any library to confirm he isn't lying, and reports measured runtimes (about 4.87 s versus 4.3 ms) rather than only asserting the asymptotic improvement.
findings.why_it_works: Two independent routes agreeing is the cheapest available proof that neither is a rendering or transcription artifact. Itemizing what was not verified tells a rigorous reader exactly where the argument is soft, which is what makes the rest trustworthy.

findings.observation: Openings and endings are bound: the question posed at the start is returned to and answered in the same words, often as the final beat.
findings.evidence: CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo): the 100-dice 95% range question posed near the start is worked at the end; the three withheld assumptions are delivered last. X+Y (IaSGqQa5O-M): explicitly promises to return to the opening quiz. Blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo): the opening admission about the unsolved status is discharged in the final third. Laplace (j0wJBEZdwLs): the opening drive-a-car/understand-the-engine analogy is extended at the end into a third level — build the car yourself — which becomes the next chapter's premise.
findings.why_it_works: Closure is what retrospectively justifies the opening's demand for attention. Answering in the same words (rather than a paraphrase) lets the reader verify the debt was paid, which is what makes them extend credit next time.

candidate_rules.rule: The first shot of a knowledge point must never introduce a definition, a new symbol, or a formula. It must show one specific instance being manipulated, with concrete values.
candidate_rules.rationale: No video in the corpus opens with a definition; several announce the deferral explicitly. A definition read before the experience it summarizes decompresses into nothing.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Lint S[0].narration for definitional markers ("is defined as", "we define", "is called", "let X denote") and lint S[0].drawFn for formula-morph primitives. Fail the build if either is present in the first shot of any knowledge point.

candidate_rules.rule: Every knowledge point must contain, within its first two shots, exactly one interrogative sentence naming the quantity to be determined — and the same question must be answered by that point's SUM core claim and probed by at least one QUIZ.
candidate_rules.rationale: The gradable-task pattern (the 100-dice 95% range; what function of n; what is the compression limit) is what lets a reader self-assess. A topic label gives no such signal, and unanswered openings leave the attention debt outstanding.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require a `question` field per knowledge point. Assert it appears verbatim (or as a declared alias) in one of the first two narrations, and that SUM.core and at least one QUIZ.stem are linked to that same question id. Fail on missing or orphaned links.

candidate_rules.rule: Before the first universally quantified sentence in a knowledge point, at least two concrete instances with actual numbers must have appeared, and the reader must have been invited to predict the next one.
candidate_rules.rationale: The escalating-ladder-with-invited-guess hook is the single most consistent opening device in the corpus (2/4/8/16→31; 3/31/314; a year?/10,000 years?→100 million). A violated or confirmed prediction is what marks where the reader's model is wrong.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Scan narrations in order; find the first sentence containing a quantifier ("in general", "for any", "always", "every", "all"). Count distinct numeric literals or named instances appearing before it — require ≥2 — and require at least one second-person prediction prompt ("what do you think", "guess", "before I show you") in that prefix.

candidate_rules.rule: Delete the decorative animation primitives from the drawing API entirely — pulse rings, breathing circles, marching-ants dashes, idle back-and-forth walkers. Do not merely stop calling them.
candidate_rules.rationale: The corpus contains no narrated motion that lacks an argumentative job, and the one non-informational element he keeps (collision sounds) he names and defends out loud. Capability that exists will be reached for under deadline; the cheapest enforcement is removal.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Grep the projector source for those primitive names and remove the definitions. Add a CI grep that fails if any of the removed names reappear in the codebase or in any knowledge-point file.

candidate_rules.rule: Every remaining animated primitive must carry a required `role` (LADDER | SWEEP | RECONCILE) and a required `claim` string, and that claim's text must appear in the narration of the same shot.
candidate_rules.rationale: Narrated motion in the corpus always does exactly one of these three jobs — advance a case ladder, sweep a parameter to show a dependence or invariance, or cross-check a new representation against an already-established value — and the claim is always stated in the same breath as the motion.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Enum-validate `role` at build time. Assert `claim` is a non-empty substring (or declared paraphrase-alias) of the shot's narration. Fail the build on any animated call missing either field.

candidate_rules.rule: No animation may loop. Every animation has a finite step count, ends on an explicitly declared resting frame, and that resting frame stays on screen for the remainder of the shot.
candidate_rules.rationale: An unbounded loop has no final state, so it can carry no claim — it can only consume attention. He stages the opposite: motion resolves and then holds (the long pause before the 314 reveal), so the held frame is what the narration's claim points at.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Forbid `repeat: Infinity` / `iterations: -1` / CSS `animation-iteration-count: infinite` at the API boundary and via a CSS grep in CI. Require every animated call to declare `restFrame`; assert the timeline's last keyframe equals it and that no later keyframe exists.

candidate_rules.rule: Any element that carries no information must declare, in a required `justification` field, the single fact it is the sole carrier of — and the narration must acknowledge it as a presentational choice. Default: not allowed.
candidate_rules.rationale: The collision-sounds precedent: physically wrong, kept only because burst density is otherwise invisible, and explicitly flagged as an artistic choice. Anything that cannot pass the sole-carrier test has no defence.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require `justification` on any element not bound to a LADDER/SWEEP/RECONCILE role. Assert the shot's narration contains an acknowledgement marker. Reject empty or generic justifications ("looks better", "for emphasis") via a denylist.

candidate_rules.rule: Every simplification must be registered at the shot that introduces it — ASSUME(id, what_is_idealized_away, why, returns_in) — and the build fails if any registered id is never discharged by a later shot.
candidate_rules.rationale: He declares every idealization with its reason, and in the strongest case (the Galton board) later reveals the idealization was necessary rather than convenient. For a rigorous reader an undeclared simplification is indistinguishable from an error and stops all downstream reasoning.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain an assumption registry across the module. Fail on any ASSUME whose `returns_in` shot id does not exist or whose discharging shot does not reference the id.

candidate_rules.rule: Every forward reference in narration ("we'll see later", "at the end", "coming up", "I'll explain shortly") must carry a linked `resolves` id pointing at a real later shot that discharges it in the same terms.
candidate_rules.rationale: Every open loop planted in the corpus openings is actually closed at the promised time, in the same words — the three CLT assumptions, the one-bit-per-character estimate, the unsolved-problem admission, the return to the opening quiz. An unclosed loop spends the reader's credit and doesn't repay it.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Grep narration for forward-reference phrases; require an adjacent `resolves` annotation; assert the target shot exists and its narration references the same question id. Fail the build otherwise.

candidate_rules.rule: Within one shot of any registered assumption or any counterintuitive claim, include an objection written in the reader's voice and answer it. If the answer is 'you're right, and here's the fix', say so.
candidate_rules.rationale: He voices objections in the reader's register immediately after the provoking move, and concedes when the objection is correct (the idiotic-plan concession before the FFT fix). An unvoiced objection blocks all downstream reasoning while the reader argues silently.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each ASSUME id and each shot flagged `counterintuitive: true`, assert a shot within distance 1 contains a narration segment tagged `objection` and one tagged `response`. Fail on missing pairs.

candidate_rules.rule: Every motivating example must declare `must_not_reveal`: the property that makes the real problem hard. Reject any example whose own construction contains the answer literally. A reported reader confusion at step N triggers a mandatory audit of shot 0's framing before any edit is made to step N.
candidate_rules.rationale: The Grover postmortem: a toy verifier that just checked equality against 12 visibly contained its own answer, which is exactly the property the real oracle lacks — and his verbal attempt to forestall that objection failed. Readers generalize from the instance, not the disclaimer.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require the `must_not_reveal` field on every motivating example. Mechanical partial check: reject motivating examples implemented as a literal equality/lookup against the sought value. Process check: a confusion report opens a required review of the knowledge point's first shot before the implicated shot may be edited.

candidate_rules.rule: Never narrate a rendering capability you have not observed rendering. Every formula string must pass a rendered-DOM assertion in CI before publish: the visible text may contain no backslash, no `\frac`, no `^{`, no `_{`, and no unmatched brace.
candidate_rules.rationale: Directly addresses the LaTeX failure. The corpus analogue is his habit of showing a measurement rather than asserting it — inviting the reader to run the convolution themselves, reporting actual timings — rather than trusting that the thing works.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Snapshot-test every formula-morph call: render headless, read `textContent`, assert against the character denylist, and store the rendered image. CI fails on any match. Run over all formulas in all shots, not a sample.

candidate_rules.rule: Every numeral spoken in narration must be interpolated from the same computed value the drawing uses. Hand-typed numerals in narration are a build error.
candidate_rules.rationale: He cross-checks numbers by a second independent route and shows the agreement — the 12-edges corroboration of the family-size formula, the exact computation confirming the simulation's spikiness was real. Two routes agreeing is the cheapest proof that neither is an artifact.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Narration templating: numbers must appear as `${value}` references resolving to the shot's data object. Lint for bare numeric literals in narration strings and fail, with an allowlist for numbers that are part of the problem statement itself.

candidate_rules.rule: Every knowledge point must carry a non-empty `caveats` field naming what was asserted but not proved or verified in that point. `none` must be written explicitly, not left blank.
candidate_rules.rationale: He closes the cubes video by itemizing exactly which assertions the informal argument assumed without proof (group order 24; orbit-stabilizer), and grades claims throughout — the technically-unsolved pi connection, the hedged 'something like a satisfying answer'. A uniformly confident voice is unusable to a reader who wants to know where to check.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Schema-require the field; reject empty strings; surface it on the SUM card so it cannot be silently omitted at authoring time.

candidate_rules.rule: An application list may never be the sole motivation of an opening shot. The opening must contain either an interrogative or a concrete surprising instance.
candidate_rules.rationale: Motivation by usefulness is the minority pattern and is never used alone; the majority open on an unexplained surprise or an unanswered question. Usefulness is a claim about the reader's future, which creates no present need.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For the first shot, assert the narration contains either a `?` or a shot flagged `surprising_instance: true`. Fail if the only justification clause matches an application pattern ("is used in", "shows up in", "is important for") with neither present.

candidate_rules.rule: If an opening criticizes the standard treatment, an adjacent clause must state what that treatment does well, and any alternative source referenced must be referenced neutrally or positively.
candidate_rules.rationale: I found no instance in the corpus of disparaging another explanation; the opposite is routine (the drive-a-car caveat, the endorsement of completing the square, links to other people's treatments of the same proof). Attacking the standard treatment makes a reader defend what they already learned instead of being curious.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Grep openings for criticism markers ("never explain", "textbooks just", "nobody tells you", "the usual treatment fails"); require a concession clause in the same or adjacent sentence. Flag for review rather than hard-failing, since this one needs a human read.

candidate_rules.rule: Each knowledge point's final shot or SUM must answer the opening question in the same terms it was posed, and the module's final knowledge point must discharge every module-level open loop planted in its opening.
