candidate_rules.rationale: Openings and endings are bound throughout the corpus — the 100-dice problem worked at the end, the three withheld assumptions delivered last, the opening quiz returned to. Closure in the same words is what lets the reader verify the debt was paid.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Assert the `question` id declared in the opening appears in the closing SUM. At module level, assert the assumption registry and the forward-reference registry are both fully discharged before publish.

anti_patterns: Opening with a definition, a symbol, or a formula. Zero of the fifteen videos do this; three explicitly announce that they are deferring the definition on purpose.

Opening with a bullet-list agenda of subtopics. Where a roadmap appears it is short and framed around what will be surprising about the structure — e.g. warning that the second half will look unrelated and that the payoff is reconciling the two halves — never a table of contents.
Motivating by usefulness alone. Application lists are a minority device and always appear alongside a surprise, an unanswered question, or a familiar-thing-you-already-do hook.

Opening with historical chronology. History appears mid-piece as evidence or as a character (Shannon and his wife's guessing game; the naming-entropy anecdote; the 2002 gzip paper) — never as "first X did A, then Y did B".

Disparaging other explanations or textbooks. I found no instance. He links to and praises competing treatments of the same material, and legitimizes the boring standard method before offering the elegant one.

Choosing the flashiest example for the opening. He explicitly rejects opening the convolution video with the visually striking image-processing case because it is unrepresentative of the operation, and picks dice instead for familiarity and representativeness.

Toy examples that smuggle in a property the real object lacks. His own diagnosed failure: a verifier defined as "input == 12" contains its own answer, which is exactly what the real oracle does not do.
Relying on a disclaimer to fix a misleading visual. He states directly that he tried to forestall the objection in words and failed. The example wins.
Undeclared idealizations. Every simplification in the corpus is announced with its reason at the moment it is made.
Unclosed open loops. Every withheld item planted in an opening is discharged in the same terms at the promised point.

Motion without a claim attached in the same breath. Every narrated motion is a case-ladder step, a parameter sweep with a stated dependence or invariance, or a cross-check against an already-established value.

Unbounded looping motion. Motion in the corpus resolves and then holds; the held frame is what the claim points at. (Honest caveat: transcripts cannot prove the absence of unnarrated ambient motion — this is inference from the fact that every motion he narrates is load-bearing.)
Uniform confidence. He grades claims explicitly, including downgrading his own headline to "technically an unsolved problem" in the first minute.

Asserting a number or a capability instead of showing the check. He reports measured timings, invites the reader to reproduce a computation, cross-checks a formula against an independently known count, and itemizes what he did not prove.

lens: Formulas, notation and symbol manipulation — how 3Blue1Brown makes mathematical notation survivable in a medium where the audience cannot pause to parse, and what that implies for a term-morphing SVG/HTML projector.

findings.observation: The referent always precedes the symbol. A concrete instance is fully worked in words and pictures, and only then is a letter introduced as an act of *naming something already on the table* — the introducing sentence is grammatically an assignment ("let's label X with the letter Y"), never a definition the reader must hold on faith.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy (GlYgs6v2YfU): the four-instruction robot distribution, its optimal code, and the mismatch scenario are all worked numerically to 2.625 bits BEFORE P and Q are introduced, which happens as an explicit relabelling of the two distributions already discussed. Attention (eMlx5fFNoYc): the mole / Eiffel-tower / miniature examples establish contextual embedding before "let's denote these embeddings with the letter e". Convolutions (IaSGqQa5O-M): the dice grid and the sliding-and-multiplying procedure are demonstrated before p_x, p_y, p_{x+y} are named. Colliding blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo): m1, v1 are named while pointing at a specific block on screen.
findings.why_it_works: A symbol is a compression pointer. If nothing is in memory for it to point at, the reader must hold an unbound token in working memory while also parsing the syntax around it — two costs at once. Introducing the referent first means the symbol costs nothing to install; it only shortens what the reader can already say in longhand.

findings.observation: Symbol introduction carries an explicit type/range declaration, and the declaration is deliberately re-asserted rather than assumed to stick.
findings.evidence: Laplace (j0wJBEZdwLs): on introducing s he states it is a number that selects which exponential, then that it is permitted to be complex, then says outright that every occurrence of s in the whole video is a complex number — a pre-emptive re-binding for later shots. CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo): he pauses on variance-vs-standard-deviation specifically because variance's units are squared and therefore cannot be read as a distance on the diagram.
findings.why_it_works: Type errors are the dominant silent failure in formula reading: a reader who thinks s is real, or that a value is a probability when it is a log-probability, will follow every subsequent step and arrive at nonsense without noticing. A stated type gives the reader a cheap local check on every later line.

findings.observation: The choice of glyph is itself explained, either by mnemonic or by convention, so the letter is not arbitrary noise.
findings.evidence: CLT: mu for mean and sigma for standard deviation are justified as the Greek initials of the English words. Laplace: the transformed function is capitalised because that is the standard convention for naming a transform after its input function. Entropy (l6DKRf-fAAM): Shannon's h is introduced with the (probably apocryphal) von Neumann anecdote about why the quantity was named entropy at all.
findings.why_it_works: An arbitrary glyph must be memorised; a motivated glyph can be reconstructed. It also converts the notation from something imposed on the reader into something with a history, which lowers the sense of gatekeeping.

findings.observation: He refuses standard notation when the standard is bad, says he is refusing it, substitutes something clearer, and then provides an explicit crosswalk so the reader is not ambushed by the literature later.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy: he says the conventions in the wild are inconsistent and announces that he and the viewer will just work with the sum and its bar diagram instead. Attention: he coins "value down" and "value up" matrices, flags that this is not the conventional naming, and then explains that papers staple all the value-up matrices into one output matrix and call only the first factor "the value matrix". Laplace: he shows his poles-form answer for the cosine transform and then shows the combined s/(s²+ω²) form that a table would actually list.
findings.why_it_works: Two separate failures are avoided at once. Adopting bad notation for authority's sake taxes every subsequent line; abandoning it silently leaves the reader unable to connect to the source material. The crosswalk is a one-time cost that buys both.

findings.observation: When notation is awkward, he names the awkwardness as a property of the *notation*, not of the concept — so the reader does not conclude the idea is broken.
findings.evidence: Convolutions (IaSGqQa5O-M): he flags that writing the sum over x with g(s−x) gives artificial emphasis to one variable, and states this is because we lack good notation for iterating symmetrically over pairs with a fixed sum. He separately flags that the index can run outside the defined domain (negative die faces) and resolves it as harmless zeros. Entropy: he says the negative-log form takes getting used to and offers log base one-half as the reading he personally prefers.
findings.why_it_works: Readers who hit an oddity default to assuming they misunderstood. Attributing the oddity to the writing system converts a confidence-destroying moment into a shared complaint, and pre-empts the specific wrong inference ("the operation must be asymmetric").

findings.observation: Large formulas are assembled in layers, where each added piece is introduced as the fix to a named defect of the previous version — including at least one layer that is tried and visibly rejected.
findings.evidence: CLT: the normal density is built as e^x → negate the exponent for decay → negative absolute value (explicitly rejected for its sharp corner) → negative square → constant inside for horizontal scale → reparameterised as −½(x/σ)² so that σ reads as the standard deviation → divide by √π because the area is √π → divide by σ√2 → combine into 1/(σ√(2π)) → subtract μ to slide the centre. He announces the method as peeling back layers and building it up a piece at a time.
findings.why_it_works: Each layer is individually motivated, so the final formula is not memorised but derived on demand. The rejected layer is the crucial part: it shows the constraint that the accepted layer satisfies, which is what makes the choice feel forced rather than decreed.

findings.observation: The inverse move is equally deliberate: strip a formula to its skeleton, run the whole argument on the skeleton, then restore the constants and assert (rather than redo) that the argument survives.
findings.evidence: Gaussian+Gaussian (d_qvLDhkg00): he explicitly peels away every normalising constant and the σ and μ parameters, argues the whole rotational-symmetry proof on e^{-x²}, then says reintroducing the constants leads by essentially identical reasoning to the √2·σ result. Laplace: he removes f(t) entirely and additionally assumes s is real, each simplification announced, to study the bare integral of e^{-st}.
findings.why_it_works: Constants are load-bearing for correctness but never for insight. Carrying them through an argument multiplies the glyph count on screen while adding nothing the reader is supposed to notice, and it hides which structural feature is actually doing the work.

findings.observation: A compact published formula is shown whole only *after* the mechanism it summarises has been walked through in pictures; the first full appearance is then immediately decoded glyph-by-glyph back onto the picture, and any glyph not yet earned is explicitly deferred rather than left silent.
findings.evidence: Attention: the softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V expression appears only after keys, queries, dot-product grid, softmax-per-column and masking have all been shown. He then maps the numerator to the grid of all key-query dot products, explains √d as a numerical-stability detail, states that softmax applies column by column — and says of the V term that they will get to it shortly. Laplace: the definition is shown, immediately split into two named steps (multiply, then integrate), and then he narrows to the inner expression and spends the next ten minutes there.
findings.why_it_works: The compact form is a summary, and a summary of nothing is a wall. Decoding it afterwards converts it from an obstacle into a compression the reader can verify. The explicit deferral matters independently: an unremarked symbol reads as a comprehension failure, whereas a deferred one reads as a scheduled appointment.

findings.observation: Every summation or integral is narrated as a loop with three named parts: what the index runs over, what a single term of the body means in plain words, and what the weights mean.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy: the weighted sum is read as going through each symbol, taking how often it comes up (the probability) times its information content (the negative log base 2 of its probability). Convolutions (IaSGqQa5O-M): the integral is described as wanting to iterate over all pairs x and y constrained to a given sum s, with x ranging over all reals and s−x being whatever it must be. Entropy: the entropy sum is read as adding p times negative-log-p over each probability in the distribution.
findings.why_it_works: A summation sign is the single densest glyph in applied maths — it encodes a domain, a body and an accumulation in one mark. Unpacking it into three plain-language slots turns one unparseable symbol into three ordinary sentences, at reading speed.

findings.observation: Algebra that carries no argument is skipped out loud rather than animated. He announces the skip, shows only the endpoint, and moves on.
findings.evidence: Laplace: combining the two pole-fractions into the table form is done by, in his words, running some algebra "on autopilot" (quoted fragment), after which he shows only where the dust settles. Cross-entropy: he declines to walk the Lagrange-multiplier derivation in the spoken line at all, giving only its high-level shape.
findings.why_it_works: Animating a step that carries no claim spends the reader's attention budget and teaches them that motion is meaningless, which then devalues the motion that does mean something. Announcing the skip preserves honesty — the reader knows a gap exists and where it is — without paying to cross it.

findings.observation: Conversely, when a manipulation IS the argument, it is motivated by a stated wish *before* it happens and narrated by its structural consequence rather than its mechanics.
findings.evidence: Gaussian+Gaussian: after rotating the slice, the constant factors out of the integral and he stops to say this is the important point — the s-dependence is now entirely separate from the integration variable. Colliding blocks: he says outright that it would be more promising if the ellipse were a circle, and only then redefines the axes as √m·v so that the energy equation becomes x²+y²=const. Why-pi (cy8r7WSuT1I): the Herschel derivation says it would be nice if the proportionality constant were one, and then assumes it, flagging that the answer will be off by a constant that renormalisation will absorb.
findings.why_it_works: Unmotivated algebra reads as a trick and cannot be reconstructed. Stating the goal first converts the step from "watch me do this" into "here is what we need; here is the only move that gets it", which is the difference between a magic trick and a method.

findings.observation: Closely related formulas are presented in identical layout and their relationship stated as a single replacement — a diff, not a re-derivation.
findings.evidence: Laplace: the transform of e^{1.5t} is described as the previous integral with s replaced by s−1.5, and the general cosine as the earlier result with every i replaced by ωi. Convolutions (IaSGqQa5O-M): the continuous convolution is asserted to be one hundred per cent analogous to the discrete one, differing only in swapping the sum for an integral. Attention: cross-attention is described as almost identical to self-attention with the single change that keys and queries act on different data.
findings.why_it_works: Naming the one difference tells the reader exactly how much of their existing understanding transfers — everything but this. It also makes the claim falsifiable: the reader can check the two layouts glyph by glyph and confirm nothing else moved.

findings.observation: Any index-heavy or abstract expression is instantiated at a small concrete value within seconds of appearing, and the instantiation is chosen so its value is independently visible in a drawn object.
findings.evidence: Convolutions (KuXjwB4LzSA): after admitting the index-pair notation is a mouthful, he immediately sets n=6 and enumerates the five pairs. Moser (YtkIWDE36qU): 6-choose-4 is computed as 15 and then the 15 intersection points are counted in the drawn diagram. Laplace: s is set to 1, and the spiralling vector sum is shown landing on 1, matching the area-under-the-graph computation done earlier; separately s→i is checked against 1/i = −i. Colliding blocks: the family-size formula is checked against the fact that a cube has 12 edges.
findings.why_it_works: It is a cheap correctness oracle the reader can run themselves. It also converts an existential claim ("this formula computes something") into a verified one, and it catches the reader who has silently mis-parsed the general form.

findings.observation: When a formula has too many free parameters to visualise, he reduces the parameter count until the formula becomes a graph, then sweeps ONE parameter and makes the envelope or locus traced by that sweep into a second, separately-named object.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy: he restricts to two-outcome distributions so that P and Q each have one free parameter, plots cross-entropy as a function of q with p fixed, notes the minimum sits where q equals p, then moves p and traces the path of that minimum — and the traced curve turns out to be the entropy of P. He explicitly asks the viewer what the new curve represents before revealing it.
findings.why_it_works: This is the highest-value motion in the entire corpus and the template for what animation is for: motion with a named independent variable, a named dependent quantity, and a claim about the relationship, whose *residue* is a new object. The reader ends up holding a relationship between two quantities rather than a picture of one.

findings.observation: Each symbol is given a persistent visual degree of freedom, and the resulting diagram is reused across the whole arc so that reading the formula and reading the picture become the same act.
findings.evidence: Entropy and cross-entropy: bar width is locked to the probability p, bar height is locked to the information −log₂q, and total area is the sum. The same diagram is then reused unchanged for entropy, for cross-entropy (widths from P, heights from Q), for the minimum-at-P=Q claim, and finally for KL divergence, where he asks the viewer to convince themselves the variant diagram represents the expression. Laplace: s is a *place* on the s-plane, the transform is a *height* over that plane, and a pole is a *spike*, sustained for the entire video.
findings.why_it_works: Meaning decays fastest right after introduction. Binding a symbol to a geometric role that is visible in every subsequent frame re-teaches the binding continuously at zero narration cost, and lets the reader check an algebraic claim by looking at the picture.

findings.observation: Multi-glyph subexpressions are given a single plain-English name and thereafter referred to by that name, not by their syntax.
findings.evidence: CLT: the standardised sum (S−nμ)/(σ√n) is introduced as looking more complicated but having a highly readable meaning — how many standard deviations from the mean the sum is — and is then referred to that way for the rest of the lesson. Cross-entropy: the whole formula is repeatedly re-glossed by its question — how well a code optimised for one setting performs in another. Laplace: poles are named as the things that expose the exponential pieces, and that gloss is repeated on each reappearance.
findings.why_it_works: It converts a chunk of syntax into a single unit in working memory, which is the only way a reader can manipulate a formula with more terms than they can hold. The gloss also survives when the syntax is forgotten, which is the durable half.

findings.observation: He explicitly disowns properties of his own rendering that are not properties of the object — distinguishing artefacts of the visualisation from features of the mechanism, sometimes as an emergency correction.
findings.evidence: Grover post-mortem (Dlsa9EBKDGI): he states flatly that the two-dimensional slice he chose for the visualisation is not part of the algorithm, that the algorithm does not care how anyone chooses to view it, and that the state vector staying in that plane is (quoted fragment) "a happy emergent property". CLT: he raises the question of whether the spikiness of a 3000-sample simulation is an artefact of randomness or a real feature, and later returns to answer that in that case it is real.
findings.why_it_works: Readers attribute every salient visual choice to the mechanism, because they have no way to tell authorial choices from object properties. Any framing, ordering, coordinate system, highlight or motion introduced for legibility will be learned as content unless explicitly renounced. This is the strongest available argument against decorative motion: motion that is not in the object will be attributed to the object.

findings.observation: His own diagnosed failure was that a toy example accidentally possessed the very property whose absence was the point, and the fix was to replace the toy with examples where the absence is manifest.
findings.evidence: Grover post-mortem: he identifies the cause of mass confusion not as missing low-level detail but as his framing — opening with a mystery number to be searched for, and flashing a sample function that merely checks whether the input equals 12. He takes responsibility for this in one short sentence and replaces it with Sudoku verification and SHA-256, where nobody, including the computer, knows the triggering input. He also notes that he had tried to forestall the objection and that trying was not enough.
findings.why_it_works: A toy example teaches its incidental properties as strongly as its intended ones, and simplifications are chosen precisely for properties the real object lacks. The audit is mechanical: for each simplification, list what it added, and check none of the additions is the thing being explained.

findings.observation: He warns when a formula's structure must not be read as a procedure.
findings.evidence: Grover post-mortem: after showing the verifier acting on a superposition as a weighted sum over basis vectors, he explicitly declines to endorse the reading that the function is evaluated on all bit strings in parallel, and uses a hiker rotating north-east to argue that linearity is a property of the transformation and not a set of instructions for carrying it out.
findings.why_it_works: Notation for a characterisation and notation for an algorithm look identical. Readers default to the procedural reading because it is more concrete, and then build a wrong mental model of cost, of causality, and of what the system actually does at runtime.

findings.observation: Each lesson designates one sentence as the thing to remember, announces it as such, and restates it later almost verbatim; and misreadings are named explicitly and rejected rather than merely avoided.
findings.evidence: Laplace: he says that if only one fact is retained it should be that the transform of e^{at} has a simple pole at s=a. Cross-entropy: the key property (minimised exactly when Q equals P, and the minimum is the entropy of P) is announced as the one point to remember, and is re-invoked verbatim in structure when KL divergence is defined at the end. Rejected misreadings: that the central limit theorem implies Gaussian⊛Gaussian=Gaussian (called backwards); that cross-entropy loss is just a one-hot bookkeeping identity (called unsatisfying and lame); that a normal distribution can be assumed without justification.
findings.why_it_works: Without a designated takeaway the reader compresses arbitrarily and usually keeps the most vivid rather than the most load-bearing item. Naming the wrong reading is stronger than stating the right one, because a plausible wrong model is not displaced by a correct model presented alongside it — it must be explicitly knocked down.

findings.observation: He shows the artefact rather than making a claim about it, when a claim is checkable.
findings.evidence: Convolutions (KuXjwB4LzSA): rather than asserting that FFT convolution is faster, he pulls up an interpreter, builds two hundred-thousand-element arrays, and reports measured averages of about 4.87 seconds against about 4.3 milliseconds. He also invites the reader to run the small 1,2,3 ⊛ 4,5,6 example in their own library to confirm he is not lying.
findings.why_it_works: Verification is cheapest at the moment of authoring and most expensive after publication. Committing to show real output forces the author to actually run the thing, which is exactly the discipline that a silently-broken renderer defeats.

findings.observation: Optional rigour is parked in a static side panel that the spoken line does not depend on, and the split is announced.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy: the Lagrange-multiplier argument for why F must be a logarithm, and a separate note on overfitting, are both put on screen for the curious while he says he does not want to derail into them. Convolutions (IaSGqQa5O-M): the √2 Jacobian factor is left as an on-screen note for calculus enthusiasts. Why-pi: the higher-dimensional-sphere-volume extension is left as an on-screen exercise.
findings.why_it_works: It resolves the rigour/pace conflict without compromise: the critical path stays readable at reading speed, and the reader who wants the proof is not told to go elsewhere. Crucially, nothing on the critical path ever requires pausing.

findings.observation: Motion in the corpus is always a parameter sweep attached to a stated monotone or qualitative claim; I found no instance of ambient, looping or ornamental motion carrying any explanatory load.
findings.evidence: Entropy: redistributing probability mass between bars is accompanied by the explicit claims that skew lowers total entropy and spread raises it, and that more symbols raises it. Convolutions (IaSGqQa5O-M): the slider s is the input of the convolution, and the swept area is the output value, shown side by side with the diagonal slice to prove the two visualisations agree. Laplace: he lets s wander the plane and asks the viewer to think about why the shape comes out as it does, then gives the answer (bigger imaginary part means more spiralling means more cancellation).
findings.why_it_works: Motion is the most attention-capturing channel available, so it should be spent only on the relationship the reader is meant to extract. A sweep with a named independent variable and a named consequence uses that capture; a loop with no variable spends it on nothing and trains the reader to ignore the channel.

findings.observation: Questions are planted before they are answered, and the plant is announced as a plant.
findings.evidence: CLT: he states at the outset that three assumptions underlie the theorem, refuses to say what they are, invites the viewer to predict them, and delivers them at the end. Cross-entropy: he asks what makes logarithms special among all decreasing functions and says he wants that question hanging in the reader's mind, then answers it. Convolutions (IaSGqQa5O-M): the video opens with an explicit quiz about the sum of two normal variables and closes by handing the answer to the sequel.
findings.why_it_works: An open question converts passive reading into search: the reader scans subsequent material for the answer, which is a far better encoding state than reception. It only works if the answer is actually delivered and explicitly connected back to the plant.

findings.observation: NEGATIVE FINDING — I looked for and did not find spatial narration of terms crossing an equals sign. There is no 'move this term to the other side' language anywhere in the corpus.
findings.evidence: Across all fifteen transcripts the manipulation verbs are: factor out / pull outside the integral, cancel, combine, break apart, replace X with Y, take the log of both sides and negate, collect like terms, rearrange (as an announced skip). Operations on equations are described as applied symmetrically to both sides (entropy: log both sides then negate), never as a migration of a term.
findings.why_it_works: Relevant as a constraint on the morph feature: the corpus supports morphs that depict extraction, substitution, annihilation and regrouping, but gives no support for animating transposition. Transposition is also the manipulation most likely to teach a false rule if animated as travel, since the sign change happens in the same instant as the motion and is easy to miss.

findings.observation: NEGATIVE FINDING — I expected and could not confirm systematic colour-coding of individual symbols. Colour in the narration codes value classes or cases, not symbol identity.
findings.evidence: The colour references I found are: negative values red and positive blue in the edge-detection kernel output; phase-direction colouring on the Laplace magnitude plot; blue and red dice; green and purple for upright versus upside-down tables in the LeWitt video. Nothing in any narration says a symbol keeps a colour across appearances. His finished videos plausibly do this, but the captions do not evidence it, so I flag this as inference, not observation.
findings.why_it_works: Worth adopting on independent grounds (it is a cheap persistent-channel binding, consistent with the width/height binding that IS evidenced), but it should not be presented as a 3B1B-derived rule.

candidate_rules.rule: Never let a symbol's first on-screen appearance come before a shot in which its referent was drawn or computed concretely. The introducing narration must be an act of naming something already discussed, not a definition.
candidate_rules.rationale: Universal in the corpus: P/Q after the robot arithmetic, e after the mole examples, m1/v1 while pointing at a block, h at the END of the entropy derivation. A symbol with nothing bound to it costs working memory and buys nothing.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Build a symbol table per knowledge point. For each symbol, record the index of the first shot whose drawFn or narration contains it. Assert that some strictly earlier shot's narration names, in plain words, the object it abbreviates. Fail the build on any symbol whose first mention is inside a formula.

candidate_rules.rule: Every symbol's introducing narration must contain a type/range clause: what kind of object it is, what values it can take, and (for RL) whether it is a probability, a log-probability, a return, a value, or an index.
candidate_rules.rationale: Laplace re-declares that s is complex and promises to keep re-declaring it; CLT stops to flag that variance has squared units and cannot be read as a distance. In RL, γ, α, ε, π(a|s), V, Q, G_t, δ_t and A(s,a) all coexist on screen with wildly different types and are routinely conflated.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Assert that the sentence introducing each new symbol matches a type-clause pattern (is a number / vector / matrix / distribution over / probability in [0,1] / index over / expected ...). Maintain a declared-type map and lint any shot where a symbol is used in a role inconsistent with its declared type (e.g. a probability being summed with a return).

candidate_rules.rule: Re-gloss any symbol in one clause before reusing it if it has not appeared in the last three shots.
candidate_rules.rationale: Meaning decays fastest right after introduction. He restates the cross-entropy gloss and the pole gloss on essentially every reappearance, and pre-emptively promises to re-bind s throughout.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Track last-appearance shot index per symbol. If gap > 3 and the symbol reappears, require the narration to contain its registered gloss string (or a fuzzy match above a threshold). Emit a warning listing the un-reglossed symbols.

candidate_rules.rule: No formula may appear in full before the shot that walks its mechanism in pictures. Its first full appearance must be followed, in the same or the next shot, by a decode pass that names every distinct glyph in it — or explicitly defers the ones it does not name.
candidate_rules.rationale: The attention formula appears only after keys, queries, the dot-product grid, softmax and masking are all understood; he then names numerator, √d and softmax-by-column and openly postpones V. Deferral is what stops an unnamed glyph reading as a comprehension failure.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Extract the set of distinct glyphs from the formula node. Extract the set named in the following narration. Require full coverage, or that each uncovered glyph appears in an explicit deferral phrase registered in the shot (e.g. a `defers: ['V']` field). Fail on any uncovered, undeferred glyph.

candidate_rules.rule: Every Σ, ∫, max, argmax and E in a shown formula must have three things named in words in the same shot: what the index runs over, what one term of the body means, and what the weights are.
candidate_rules.rationale: He reads Σ as a for-loop with domain, body and weights every time — the cross-entropy sum, the convolution sum, the entropy sum. These operators are the densest glyphs in RL formulas (the Bellman expectation equation contains three of them).
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Parse the formula for accumulation operators. For each, require a registered narration triple (domain, body, weight). Fail if any operator has fewer than three filled slots.

candidate_rules.rule: Every morph must be tagged with the rewrite law it depicts, drawn from a closed list: SUBSTITUTION, FACTOR_OUT, REGROUP, CANCELLATION, EXPAND_DEFINITION, DISCRETE_TO_CONTINUOUS, REPRESENTATION_SWAP, ROLE_SWAP. A morph with no law is deleted.
candidate_rules.rationale: Every argument-carrying manipulation in the corpus is one of these: the s→s−1.5 substitution; the s-dependent factor leaving the Gaussian integral; the n−n and 2C(n,4)−C(n,4) cancellations in Moser; Σ→∫ in the convolution analogy; ket-sum ↔ column vector in the Grover correction; the P/Q role swap that exposes cross-entropy's asymmetry. An untagged morph is decoration.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require a `law` field on every morph primitive; validate against the enum; fail the build on a missing or unrecognised value. Spot-check by asking whether the law can be stated as one sentence the reader could verify from the two static frames.

candidate_rules.rule: A morph plays exactly once per user-visible trigger and ends in a stable final state. No morph may loop, ping-pong, auto-repeat, or reverse. No element in a formula may pulse, breathe, glow cyclically, or use marching-ants strokes.
candidate_rules.rationale: A morph asserts A equals B. Replaying it asserts nothing and destroys the reader's ability to know whether they are looking at A or B. This is the direct encoding of the reader's verdict on the earlier decorative build, and it is consistent with the corpus, where every motion terminates in a state that is then discussed.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Grep the source for `infinite`, `alternate`, `iterationCount` other than 1, `yoyo`, `repeat: -1`, and for CSS `@keyframes` applied to formula spans. Assert every FLIP transition has a finite duration and no reverse leg. Manually: screenshot the page five seconds after load and again ten seconds after; the two images must be identical.

candidate_rules.rule: Both frames of a morph must be independently correct and readable as static images. Author frame A and frame B as stills first; add the morph only afterwards.
candidate_rules.rationale: He always discusses the endpoint state; the motion is never the only carrier of the claim. It also protects against the renderer-assumption failure — a frame you have looked at as a still is a frame you have verified renders.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Render each morph's start and end DOM to a snapshot. Require a reviewer (or a screenshot diff against a golden image) to confirm each still is legible and states something true. Reject any morph where frame A or frame B is meaningless alone.

candidate_rules.rule: Do not animate routine simplification. If the honest narration would be 'and simplifying gives', show only the result and say in one clause that the intermediate algebra was skipped.
candidate_rules.rationale: Laplace explicitly runs the fraction-combining algebra on autopilot and shows only where it settles; the Lagrange-multiplier derivation is skipped in the spoken line entirely. Animating no-claim steps trains the reader that motion is meaningless, which then devalues the morphs that matter.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Lint morph narrations for simplify / rearrange / expand / collect terms / it works out to, unaccompanied by a named consequence. Flag each for review with the default action being to collapse the morph into a static result plus a skip clause.

candidate_rules.rule: Never morph across a change of definition as though it were an algebraic rewrite. If the two expressions are different definitions rather than two forms of one quantity, either use a static side-by-side or state in the narration that this is a redefinition.
candidate_rules.rationale: Morph carries an implicit claim of identity. In RL the tempting-and-wrong cases are Bellman expectation → Bellman optimality (Σ_a π(a|s) versus max_a) and V^π → V*. Morphing these teaches that one is derivable from the other by rewriting.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require every morph tagged EXPAND_DEFINITION or ROLE_SWAP to carry the sentence asserting identity. Maintain a deny-list of symbol pairs (V^π/V*, Q^π/Q*, expectation/optimality operators) that may not appear as the two ends of a single morph without an explicit `redefinition: true` flag and matching narration.

candidate_rules.rule: When two formulas differ in one place, lay them out identically and state the difference as a single replacement: 'the only change is X in place of Y'.
candidate_rules.rationale: Laplace's s→s−1.5 and i→ωi; the discrete-to-continuous convolution; cross- versus self-attention. This is the highest-yield structure in RL, where SARSA versus Q-learning, on- versus off-policy, and TD(0) versus n-step targets all differ in exactly one slot.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each declared formula pair, diff the glyph sequences. Assert the diff has exactly one contiguous span. Assert the narration contains a replacement phrase naming both sides of that span. Assert the two formulas use the same layout template.

candidate_rules.rule: Every formula shot must be followed, within the same knowledge point, by a shot instantiating it at a small concrete case whose value is independently visible in a drawn object (a grid world cell, a backup diagram, a bar in a chart).
candidate_rules.rationale: 6-choose-4 counted as 15 intersection points in the drawing; the Laplace integral at s=1 landing on 1 by two independent routes; 1/i = −i checked against the spiralling sum. This gives the reader a correctness oracle and catches silent mis-parses of the general form.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require every knowledge point containing a formula to declare a `worked_instance` with (a) the substituted values, (b) the numeric result, and (c) the id of the drawn element where that same number is independently readable. Fail if any of the three is missing. Additionally, recompute the result in the build script and compare.

candidate_rules.rule: Assign each symbol a persistent visual channel (a position, an axis, a bar dimension, a colour) within a knowledge point and never reassign it. Reading the picture and reading the formula must be the same act.
candidate_rules.rationale: Width = p, height = −log q, area = the sum, sustained across entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence. s = a place on the s-plane for a whole video. Colour-per-symbol is my extension, not evidenced in the narration, and should be adopted on its own merits.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain a channel map per knowledge point: symbol → channel. Fail if any channel is bound to two symbols, or any symbol to two channels, within one knowledge point. Require the introducing shot's narration to state the binding.

candidate_rules.rule: Give every multi-glyph subexpression that recurs a one-sentence English name at introduction, and refer to it by that name thereafter rather than re-reading its syntax.
candidate_rules.rationale: The standardised sum named as 'how many standard deviations from the mean'; cross-entropy named by its question. In RL this applies to r + γV(s') ('the target'), δ_t ('how wrong the current estimate was'), the importance ratio, and the advantage.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Keep a glossary of named subexpressions per knowledge point. Assert each is named at first use and that at least half of its subsequent references use the name. Assert the SUM card's mechanism line uses the names, not the syntax.

candidate_rules.rule: Every animated element must carry a written argument annotation of the exact form 'as X varies, Y does Z'. If X, Y or Z cannot be filled in, delete the animation.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is the single mechanical test that separates the corpus's motion from the decorative build that failed. Every sweep in the corpus fills all three slots: as probability mass is redistributed, total entropy falls; as s moves up the imaginary axis, more cancellation shrinks the integral; as p moves, the locus of minima traces the entropy curve. Pulse rings, breathing circles and pacing tokens fill none.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require a non-empty `argues: {varies, watch, claim}` field on every animated primitive; fail the build if any is empty or contains filler ('emphasis', 'draws attention', 'looks nice'). Ban CSS animation and requestAnimationFrame on any element not registered in the animated-primitive table.

candidate_rules.rule: Any coordinate system, slice, ordering, layout choice or highlight that the author made for legibility must be explicitly disowned in narration as an authorial choice, not a property of the mechanism.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is his own diagnosed failure mode, stated in the Grover correction: he had to declare outright that the 2D slice was not part of the algorithm and that the algorithm does not care how anyone visualises it. Readers attribute every salient visual choice to the object.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each drawFn, list its arbitrary choices (axis ordering, chosen state ordering, which action is drawn first, the specific γ or ε used, chosen colour semantics). Require each to appear either in narration as a disowning clause or in a registered `arbitrary_choices` field that the SUM card surfaces. Review checklist item, not fully automatable.

candidate_rules.rule: State explicitly whether a formula is a characterisation or a procedure, and never let structure be read as an execution order.
candidate_rules.rationale: The Grover correction's core repair: linearity is a property of a transformation, not instructions for computing it. In RL this is the dominant misreading — the Bellman equation as a loop, the expectation over successors as the agent visiting all successors, the policy gradient as something the agent computes exactly.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Tag every formula as CHARACTERISATION or ALGORITHM. Require the narration of every CHARACTERISATION to contain a clause denying the procedural reading. Require every ALGORITHM to state its per-step cost. Fail on untagged formulas.

candidate_rules.rule: Audit every toy example for leaked properties: list what the simplification adds, and assert that none of the additions is the thing being explained.
candidate_rules.rationale: His stated cause of the Grover failure was a toy verifier that checked whether the input equals 12 — a function that visibly contains its own answer, in a lesson about not knowing the answer. RL equivalents: a 4-state chain that makes the discount look irrelevant; a deterministic grid world used while teaching stochastic transitions; a tabular example used while teaching function approximation.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require each example to declare `adds: [...]` (the properties introduced by simplifying) and `teaching: '...'`. Fail if any entry in `adds` overlaps the `teaching` concept. Reviewer step: for each toy, ask 'could a reader conclude the general case has this property?'

candidate_rules.rule: Render every formula through the actual production renderer and read the rendered output before writing any narration about it. Never assume a renderer's input dialect.
candidate_rules.rationale: Directly encodes the LaTeX failure. It also matches his practice of showing measured output rather than asserting it — real timing numbers on screen rather than a claim of speedup.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Automated: a build step that walks every formula node in the rendered DOM and fails on any residual TeX artefacts — a backslash followed by a letter, `$`, unbalanced `{}`/`\left`/`\right`, or `\frac`/`\sum`/`\alpha` appearing as literal text. Manual: a screenshot of every formula shot must be viewed before that knowledge point is marked done. Additionally assert every morph's start and end frames have equal sets of term ids, so no term silently vanishes.

candidate_rules.rule: Each knowledge point declares exactly one takeaway sentence. It must appear verbatim in the SUM core-claim slot and be restated near-verbatim in at least one later shot.
candidate_rules.rationale: He designates single facts to remember and then re-invokes them by name later ('remember that key property'). Without a designated takeaway the reader compresses to whatever was most vivid — which, in the failed build, was the animation.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require a `takeaway` string per knowledge point. Assert it appears in the SUM card and that some later shot's narration matches it above a similarity threshold. Fail if a knowledge point declares zero or more than one.

candidate_rules.rule: Each SUM misconception slot must state a wrong reading in the reader's own voice and then say why it is wrong — never merely restate the correct claim.
candidate_rules.rationale: He names and knocks down specific wrong readings rather than avoiding them: that the CLT implies Gaussian⊛Gaussian=Gaussian ('backwards'); that cross-entropy loss is just one-hot bookkeeping; that normality can be assumed without justification; that the quantum verifier hides the answer.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Assert the misconception field contains a first-person or second-person assertion (a claim, not a caution) followed by a refutation connective. Reject entries that are negations of the core claim ('it is not true that ...') with no independent content.

candidate_rules.rule: Plant every QUIZ question in narration before the shot that answers it, and mark the answering shot as the payoff.
candidate_rules.rationale: The CLT's three assumptions are announced as withheld and delivered at the end; the convolution video opens with a quiz and closes by handing it forward; cross-entropy plants the 'why logarithms specifically' question and answers it. An open question converts reception into search.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Require each QUIZ to carry `planted_in: <shot id>` and `answered_in: <shot id>`, and assert planted_in < answered_in < quiz position. Assert the planting shot's narration contains an interrogative.

candidate_rules.rule: Anything on the critical path must be comprehensible at reading speed. Optional rigour goes in a static side panel that the main narration never depends on, and the split is announced.
candidate_rules.rationale: Lagrange multipliers, the √2 Jacobian, overfitting, higher-dimensional sphere volumes — all parked on screen for the curious while the spoken line stays complete without them. The reader who does not pause must still get a correct, complete account.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Mark each element `critical` or `aside`. Assert that removing all `aside` elements leaves every knowledge point's narration self-contained (no dangling references). Assert every `aside` is static — no `aside` may contain an animated primitive.

candidate_rules.rule: Do not animate a term crossing an equals sign. Restrict morphs to extraction, substitution, regrouping, cancellation and representation swaps within one side, or to symmetric operations applied to both sides simultaneously.
candidate_rules.rationale: Negative finding: the corpus contains no transposition narration at all. Operations on equations are applied to both sides (take the log of both sides, then negate). Animating a term travelling across the equals sign teaches a false rule, because the sign change happens in the same instant as the motion and is easy to miss.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For every morph, compare the term ids on each side of the relation in frames A and B. Fail if any term id changes sides. Symmetric-operation morphs must show the operation applied to both sides in the same transition and are tagged separately.

anti_patterns: Motion with no independent variable. Every animation in the corpus can be written as 'as X varies, Y does Z'. Looping pulse rings, breathing circles, marching-ants dashes and a token pacing back and forth fill none of those three slots and are therefore not animation at all — they are visual noise competing with the one channel that should be reserved for arguments.

Repeating a transition. A morph asserts that two expressions are the same thing; replaying it asserts nothing and leaves the reader unable to tell which of the two states they are looking at. All motion in the corpus terminates in a state that is then discussed.
Animating routine algebra. He announces the skip and shows the endpoint instead. Dressing a no-claim simplification in motion both wastes attention and trains the reader that motion is meaningless.
Introducing a symbol cold inside a formula. Nowhere does a letter arrive before its referent has been worked concretely; the introducing sentence is always an act of naming, never a definition.

Presenting a compact published formula as a first impression. The attention formula, the Laplace definition, and the entropy formula all arrive after the mechanism, not before it, and are immediately decomposed.
Leaving a glyph unremarked. Unnamed symbols read to the reader as their own failure; he either names every glyph or explicitly schedules one for later.
Deferring to standard notation when it obscures. He declines the messy cross-entropy conventions, invents value-down/value-up names, and flags each deviation plus the crosswalk.
Letting an authorial rendering choice pass as mechanism. His own worst failure mode, corrected on camera: the 2D slice was his, not the algorithm's, and he had to say so explicitly.
Toy examples that leak the property being explained. The 'check if the input equals 12' function taught that the machine knows the answer, in a lesson whose point was that nobody does.
Reading a structural formula as a procedure. Linearity is a property of a transformation, not a set of instructions — the same trap as reading a Bellman equation as a loop.
Asserting a computation works without showing its output. He runs the timings and prints the numbers rather than claiming a speedup, and invites the reader to reproduce a small case.
Requiring the reader to pause to follow the critical path. Pausing is reserved for optional side panels; the main line is always complete at reading speed.

Restating the correct claim in place of naming the wrong one. He identifies the specific plausible misreading and knocks it down, because a wrong model is not displaced by a correct one merely presented alongside it.

Carrying normalising constants through an argument. Constants are stripped for the derivation and restored afterwards with an assertion that the reasoning survives; carrying them multiplies glyph count while hiding which structural feature does the work.
Multiple simultaneous unannounced simplifications. Even when he makes two at once (drop f(t), assume s real) each is announced separately.

lens: Pacing, cognitive load and the viewer's state of mind

findings.observation: Motion in his explanations is almost never ambient — it is a controlled sweep of exactly one modeled quantity, and the narration states in advance which quantity is moving, what to watch, and what the sweep will prove. The animation IS the argument; if you froze it you would lose the claim.
findings.evidence: Central Limit Theorem video: he says to notice what happens as he changes the starting distribution; at a sum of 3 the lower plot changes shape completely, at a sum of 50 changing the starting distribution has essentially no effect on the lower plot. The sweep of one parameter is the entire proof-by-demonstration of the theorem. Cross-entropy video: he moves P and traces where the minimum of the cross-entropy graph goes — the sweep GENERATES a new object (the entropy curve as the locus of minima). Entropy video: he 'sloshes' a probability distribution around so the reader watches total rectangle-area respond. Laplace video: he lets s 'wander around the plane' and immediately attaches an instruction to think about why the resulting shape appears. Across all 15 transcripts I found zero narration references to motion that is not a change in a semantic quantity.
findings.why_it_works: A sweep converts a universally-quantified claim ('for ALL starting distributions, the sum tends to a bell curve') into a single perceptual event the reader can verify with their eyes. Working memory holds one changing thing plus one invariant far more easily than it holds a verbal quantifier. Motion that carries no quantity, by contrast, occupies the same attention channel while paying nothing back, so it is strictly a tax.

findings.observation: He diagnoses his own worst failure as a FRAMING failure at the opening, not a detail failure — and concludes that a verbal caveat cannot defeat a structural implication of the example you chose. His fix was to replace the example with one whose structure intrinsically embodies the property, not one annotated with it.
findings.evidence: Grover post-mortem: he opened the original video by having viewers imagine a mystery number being searched for, and flashed a toy function that just checks whether the input equals 12. Viewers concluded the computer must already know the answer. He says he genuinely tried to forestall that objection and failed, and calls the opening misleading — quote: "That's on me." His replacement examples are Sudoku and SHA-256, where 'nobody knows the answer, including the machine' is a property of the example itself rather than an assertion by the narrator.
findings.why_it_works: Readers generalize from the structure of what they see, not from the disclaimer attached to it. A toy chosen only for simplicity smuggles in whatever structural claims its simplicity happens to make. Since the disclaimer competes with the picture and loses, the only reliable repair is to change the picture.

findings.observation: When confusion arises, he explicitly REFUSES to fix it by adding lower-level detail. He considers showing the missing mechanism, argues it would not add clarity, and instead re-picks the example and re-emphasizes an omitted structural property.
findings.evidence: Grover post-mortem: he names quantum compilation as the missing low-level step, previews it, and rejects it with an analogy that knowing the logic gates implementing addition teaches you little about how to add two numbers. His actual fixes were (a) a better example and (b) an entire section on linearity, built up from a single-qubit z-gate and a hiker walking northeast before being applied in 2^k dimensions.
findings.why_it_works: Confusion usually comes from a wrong mental model, not a missing fact. Adding facts to a wrong model increases load without changing the model. Rebuilding the model in a low-dimensional case that the reader can hold entirely in working memory is cheaper and actually addresses the cause.

findings.observation: He explicitly disowns presentational conveniences that a reader could mistake for mechanism — and the post-mortem shows what happens when he does not.
findings.evidence: Grover post-mortem: readers thought choosing a 2-D slice through the huge state space (a slice that happens to contain the answer axis) was a step of the algorithm. He says flatly that it is not, that the algorithm just interleaves two operations, and that the state vector staying in that plane is an emergent property, not an instruction given to the computer. Contrast with the transformers video, where he pre-empts this by declaring up front that he is projecting a 12,288-dimensional space onto a chosen 3-D slice for animation purposes.
findings.why_it_works: Every layout, projection, ordering, and color choice is silently read as content unless disowned. Because the reader cannot distinguish 'chosen for drawing' from 'part of the thing', the author must mark the boundary at the moment of introduction — afterwards is too late, as the failed video demonstrates.

findings.observation: Recaps are short, prerequisite-scoped, and explicitly framed as 'here is what I want in your head right now' — never comprehensive summaries of the prior material.
findings.evidence: The attention video opens by naming a quick recap and 'the important context I want you to have in mind', then lists only three things: text splits into tokens, tokens map to high-dimensional vectors, directions in that space carry semantic meaning. Everything recapped is consumed within the next few paragraphs. The cross-entropy video gives 'a very quick recap of the basics' in roughly four sentences. The Grover follow-up compresses a whole prior video's core into one sentence about bit strings being basis vectors.
findings.why_it_works: A recap is a working-memory load operation, not a review. Loading only the registers the next computation reads keeps the cost proportional to the benefit; loading everything spends attention on items that will never be touched and dilutes the ones that will.

findings.observation: He installs one designated takeaway per section, states it as a takeaway explicitly, and then repeats that same claim verbatim at spaced intervals — including when it is later used.
findings.evidence: Laplace video: he says if only one fact is remembered, let it be that the transform of an exponential has a simple pole above the corresponding value of s — and closes the video restating exactly that. Cross-entropy video: he flags 'the one key property I want you to remember' (cross-entropy is minimized when Q equals P, and the minimum equals the entropy of P), repeats it three separate times in different visual forms, and then re-invokes it verbatim to define KL divergence at the end. Attention video: 'the most important idea I want you to have in mind' about directions carrying meaning.
findings.why_it_works: Spaced verbatim repetition of one canonical sentence gives the reader a stable retrieval handle. Because the wording is identical, the third encounter costs almost nothing to recognize but strongly consolidates; paraphrasing each time would force re-parsing and lose the handle.

findings.observation: He uses a persistent, content-bearing progress gauge that the material itself feeds — not an abstract chapter counter or progress bar.
findings.evidence: Across the two transformer videos he keeps a running parameter tally for GPT-3 that accumulates as sections complete: the embedding matrix contributes ~617M, then the unembedding another ~617M for 'a little over a billion', then ~6.3M per attention head, ~600M per multi-headed block, and finally just under 58 billion for all attention — explicitly measured against the 175 billion total announced at the start. He also declares up front that GPT-3's weights fall into eight matrix categories and that the plan is to step through each.
findings.why_it_works: It answers 'where am I' with a number the reader already cares about, so orientation and content are the same act. An abstract progress bar costs attention and teaches nothing; a tally that must reach a pre-announced total creates both a location sense and a small open loop.

findings.observation: He marks difficulty in advance, grants explicit permission not to absorb it on first pass, and then — after the hard part — inserts a sufficiency checkpoint telling the reader what they have already earned and that the remainder is elaboration.
findings.evidence: Attention video: before the mechanism, he says many people find attention very confusing and not to worry if it takes time to sink in; after multi-head attention he repeats the same permission almost verbatim. Between them sits the key move — he tells the reader that if they understood everything so far and stopped there, they would come away with the essence of attention, and that all that remains is laying out that you do it many times in parallel. HONEST CAVEAT: this explicit difficulty-warning pattern appears in only about two of the fifteen files, so it is a deliberate tool for the hardest material, not a routine per-section habit.
findings.why_it_works: Anxiety about falling behind consumes the same working memory the explanation needs. Permission converts 'I am failing' into 'this is expected', and the sufficiency checkpoint reclassifies remaining material from 'more hard stuff' to 'decoration on something I already own', which drops perceived load sharply.

findings.observation: Optional depth is explicitly sorted out of the main line, labeled at its boundary with a named audience, and declared harmless to skip — and it is never a prerequisite for anything later.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy video: he pulls a Lagrange-multiplier derivation onto the screen explicitly for 'the extra curious', says he is hesitant to derail, and states the details are not too important. Laplace video: analytic continuation is flagged as firmly beyond what you need 'to drive the car'. Attention video: a notational discrepancy with the literature is put in an on-screen note for the curious, with the stated reason that it risks distracting from the main conceptual points but is called out so readers are not confused by other sources. Transformers video: readers comfortable with the deep-learning background are told they can feel free to skip ahead to the next chapter.
findings.why_it_works: Explicit tiering lets each reader spend their limited attention where it pays. Unlabeled optional material is worse than absent: the reader assumes it is required, tries to absorb it, and either stalls or loses the main thread.

findings.observation: Prediction prompts are framed as invitations, are answerable from what is already on screen, and are followed immediately by the answer. He essentially never gates progress on the reader solving something.
findings.evidence: Mechanical count across the corpus: 'take a moment', 'see if you can', 'take a minute', 'it's worth your time to ponder' appear frequently; the imperative 'pause the video' as a hard stop does not. Convolution video: the reader is asked to predict the effect of a kernel with positive values on the left and negative on the right — then he immediately walks the prediction through. Moser's circle video: he encourages pausing on the intersection-counting question, then says if you give yourself a moment, here is one thing you might notice, and supplies it. Central Limit Theorem video: he withholds the theorem's three assumptions to the very end and asks the reader to watch for them — the whole lesson becomes a running prediction task.
findings.why_it_works: A prediction attempt creates a retrieval slot that makes the subsequent answer stick, but only if the reader can plausibly generate a guess from present evidence. Gating on a correct answer converts the prompt from an aid into an obstacle, and readers who fail then read the rest in a degraded state.

findings.observation: He posts a concrete answerable question in the opening minutes and treats the lesson as a contract to answer exactly that question — then visibly returns to it.
findings.evidence: Central Limit Theorem video: early on he says here is the kind of question he wants the reader able to answer by the end — roll a die 100 times, sum the results, find the tightest range you can be 95% confident about — and near the end he works precisely that problem, arriving at roughly 316 to 384. The brief LLM video does a compressed version: a rhetorical multiple-choice about how long a billion operations per second would take to train a large model (a year? ten thousand years?) with the answer being well over a hundred million years.
findings.why_it_works: A concrete question gives every intermediate step a visible purpose, which is what sustains attention through a long derivation. The multiple-choice variant additionally calibrates the reader's prior so the true answer registers as surprising rather than as another number.

findings.observation: Section endings hand off a shaped hole. The last sentence before a transition either states the single takeaway or names the exact unanswered question the next section will answer — and he sometimes leaves a question deliberately hanging across several sections.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy video: he explicitly says he wants a question hanging in the reader's mind — why logarithms specifically, what makes logs special among all functions of that shape — and does not answer it until much later, via the constrained-optimization argument. Central Limit Theorem video ends by naming what comes next: why this particular function is the limit and why it contains pi. Entropy video ends a major section with a bare statement that this is the key idea, then opens the next question. Laplace video ends by naming the key takeaway and explicitly deferring the worked example so the reader can stand up, stretch and reflect.
findings.why_it_works: An open loop is a low-cost, high-persistence memory device: a well-posed question survives a break far better than a partial derivation. Ending mid-derivation, by contrast, forces the reader to hold arbitrary intermediate state across the boundary.

findings.observation: He voices the reader's objection in the same beat that provokes it, before answering — often in the reader's own indignant voice.
findings.evidence: Entropy video: he interrupts himself to say he hears some readers asking how the robot knows where to draw the dividing lines, then answers with the prefix-free property. Convolution video: he anticipates that some readers could rightfully complain the plan is idiotic, and articulates exactly why, before introducing the FFT. Moser's circle video: he raises the objection that the count might depend on where the points are placed, and shows the degenerate symmetric case. Colliding blocks video: he raises the sticklers' worry about whether small-angle approximation is rigorous enough, and gives the Taylor error term and the unresolved digits-of-pi caveat.
findings.why_it_works: An unvoiced objection runs as a background process, consuming attention and eroding trust in everything that follows. Voicing it in the reader's own register discharges it immediately and signals that the author is tracking the same difficulty, which is what keeps a skeptical reader engaged rather than defensive.

findings.observation: Every simplification is labeled as a simplification at the moment it is made, and is later paid back explicitly — sometimes the payback becomes the punchline.
findings.evidence: Central Limit Theorem video: the idealized Galton board is announced as deliberately unrealistic, with the stated goal being illustration rather than physics — and at the very end he reveals that the exact idealizations he made (independence, identical distribution) ARE the theorem's assumptions, and that a real Galton board violates both. Entropy video: the robot's probabilities are announced as contrived powers of two, and the payback comes when moving to natural language, where probabilities are not clean powers of two and fractional bits must be interpreted. Attention video: he twice says he is inventing the adjectives-modify-nouns example, and separately flags that the value matrix he has drawn as one square matrix will be modified in the multi-head setting — which he then does.
findings.why_it_works: A labeled simplification is a loan the reader consents to; an unlabeled one is a false belief they will have to unlearn later, usually at the worst moment. Paying it back at a named point turns the earlier lie into a second lesson instead of a correction.

findings.observation: He previews the SHAPE of the answer before showing the machinery that produces it, so the derivation has somewhere to land.
findings.evidence: Laplace video: he explicitly says it is helpful to preview what the new function does before pulling up the definition, shows the picture of poles spiking over the s-plane, and only then writes the integral — following it with an acknowledgement that the reader is by now itching to see the actual definition. Transformers video: a high-level end-to-end data-flow preview precedes any matrix. Convolution video: the dice-sliding picture precedes the summation notation, and he says outright that the notation is secondary in importance to the visual you hold in your head.
findings.why_it_works: Symbol manipulation with no target image is pure load. Giving the destination first turns each derivation step into a checkable move toward a known place, which lets the reader recover from losing a step instead of derailing.

findings.observation: He treats a complex static figure as something to be decoded in a stated order, supplying the reading order himself rather than assuming the figure is self-explanatory.
findings.evidence: Entropy video: introducing the binary-string tree diagram, he says it is probably intuitive if you pause and stare at it, but then calls out the important features in sequence — each layer is all strings of a given length, everything starting with 0 is on the left half, everything starting with 1 on the right, and the property that each string is a prefix for everything above it. Cross-entropy video: the bar diagram is introduced with an explicit and fixed encoding (bar width is P, bar height is negative log base 2 of Q) that is then held constant while one side is varied.
findings.why_it_works: A dense figure with no stated reading order forces the reader to search, which is expensive and unreliable. Naming the encoding once and then varying only one side of it turns the figure into a reusable instrument rather than a fresh puzzle each time it appears.

findings.observation: A visual convention, once declared, is enforced globally and named as a memory aid.
findings.evidence: Transformers video: he tells the reader to draw a sharp mental distinction between the model's weights, which he always colors blue or red, and the data being processed, which he always colors gray — and states why (weights are learned, data is the specific input). The convention then holds across two long videos.
findings.why_it_works: A stable color/position code offloads a categorical distinction from working memory to perception. It only works if it never breaks, which makes it a discipline constraint rather than a styling choice.

findings.observation: Sentence-level style: long but strictly linear sentences, very high second-person density, and questions as the main structural transition device.
findings.evidence: Measured across the corpus: mean sentence length 24-31 words with medians of 22-29; second-person words ('you', 'your', "you'll", "you're") run 19-39 per thousand words. Sentences are long via coordination and present participles that advance one step at a time (multiply this matrix by all the embeddings, producing one query vector per token), not via nesting. Question marks run roughly 0.3 to 4 per thousand words and typically sit at section seams. He uses deliberate placeholder vagueness ('somehow', 'kind of', 'loosely speaking') to let the reader park a black box without anxiety, then cashes it in later. CAVEAT: one file in the corpus (Exploration & Epiphany) has markedly different statistics — 16-word mean sentences, second person at only 5 per thousand and first-person-plural at 41 per thousand — and appears to be narrated by a guest, so it should not be pooled with the rest when inferring his personal style.
findings.why_it_works: Linear long sentences let a reader consume a multi-step process without holding an unresolved clause open; nested ones do not. Constant direct address keeps the reader cast as a participant performing the reasoning rather than an audience receiving a result, which is what sustains effort across a long argument.

findings.observation: He verifies claims against an independently computable check, out loud, and invites the reader to do the same — a habit of not asserting what has not been confirmed.
findings.evidence: Convolution video: after computing a convolution by hand, he invites the reader to open their favorite language and library to confirm he is not lying, and separately benchmarks two library functions live to show a three-orders-of-magnitude difference. Laplace video: he runs a sanity check by setting s to 1 and confirming the spiraling vector sum lands on the value that the earlier area-under-a-curve interpretation gave, and gut-checks a second case against 1 divided by i. Moser's circle video: derived counts are cross-checked by literally counting the intersection points in the drawn diagram. Exploration video: a derived family size of 12 is corroborated against the independent fact that a cube has 12 edges.
findings.why_it_works: An independent check catches exactly the class of error that internal reasoning cannot — a wrong assumption that is self-consistent. Doing it visibly also models the habit and licenses reader skepticism, which is what a rigorous audience wants.

candidate_rules.rule: Never animate anything that is not a change in a modeled quantity. Every animated shot must have a narration sentence naming (a) the quantity being varied, (b) what the reader should watch, and (c) what the change establishes. If you cannot write that sentence, delete the animation.
candidate_rules.rationale: Across fifteen transcripts, every reference to motion is a single-parameter sweep whose endpoint is the claim (sum size vs. bell-curve shape; P vs. the locus of cross-entropy minima; s vs. the pole picture). Motion with no referent spends the reader's attention channel and returns nothing, which is precisely the decorative-animation failure being fixed.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each shot with animation, assert its narration matches a template containing a varied-quantity token plus one of {notice, watch, as X changes/grows/shrinks, observe} plus a consequence clause. A shot whose narration contains no such construction fails the build.

candidate_rules.rule: Ban idle animation by construction: no infinite iteration counts, no alternate-direction loops, no keyframes that start on load without a step advance, no animated stroke-dashoffset, no pulse/breathe/glow/ripple. Every animation must be triggered by an explicit step advance and must terminate in a stable end state.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is the mechanical form of the previous rule and directly encodes the reader's verdict that looping rings, breathing circles, marching ants and a pacing token were exhausting and worse than nothing. A terminating, step-triggered animation cannot become ambient noise.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: grep the source for `infinite`, `alternate`, `setInterval`, `requestAnimationFrame` loops without a termination condition, and `stroke-dashoffset` inside `@keyframes`. Every hit must be either removed or accompanied by a comment naming the specific argument it carries; CI fails on unannotated hits.

candidate_rules.rule: One shot animates at most one degree of freedom. If two independent things change between the start and end state of a shot, split it into two shots.
candidate_rules.rationale: His sweeps vary exactly one thing while everything else is visibly pinned — the cross-entropy bar diagram fixes bar widths (P) and varies only heights (Q); the CLT demo fixes sum size and varies the source distribution, then fixes the distribution and varies sum size. The invariant is only legible because it is the only thing not moving.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Represent each shot's start and end as a state dict; assert the set of independently-set keys that differ has size 1 (dependent/derived values excepted, and declared as derived).

candidate_rules.rule: Never introduce a formula on screen before a sentence has already said, in plain language, what that formula will turn out to mean. Formula term-morphing may only run between two forms whose relationship the narration has already stated.
candidate_rules.rationale: He previews the poles picture before writing the Laplace integral, previews the transformer data flow before any matrix, and states outright that the convolution notation matters less than the visual you hold in your head. A morph between two symbol strings with no stated semantic relation is motion, not argument.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Each shot that renders a formula must carry an explicit `MEANING:` field; assert it is non-empty and that either the same shot's narration or the immediately preceding shot's narration contains it. For morph shots, assert a declared `MORPH_CLAIM` naming what the rewrite preserves.

candidate_rules.rule: Before authoring any content that uses a drawing primitive, render one live instance of that primitive and read back the actual DOM/SVG output. Never assert a rendering capability — including LaTeX support — that you have not personally observed rendering correctly.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is the direct fix for the second failure: assuming the morph function rendered LaTeX and shipping backslash garbage. It also matches his own habit of sanity-checking derived values against an independent computation rather than trusting the derivation.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain a fixture page rendering exactly one instance of every primitive and every distinct formula string used in the deck. A script asserts no rendered text node contains `\\`, `\frac`, `_{`, `^{`, `\left`, `\right`, `$`, or an unbalanced `{`. Run it as a pre-publish gate; a human reads the fixture screenshot once per new primitive.

candidate_rules.rule: Every example must structurally embody the property it is meant to illustrate. Never rely on narration to deny something the picture implies. Before shipping an example, write down the one structural claim a reader would infer from the visual alone with the narration removed — if any narration sentence contradicts that claim, replace the example.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is the explicit lesson of his Grover post-mortem: a toy verifier that just checks whether the input equals 12 made viewers believe the answer was hidden in the machine, and his attempt to forestall that verbally failed. His fix was Sudoku and SHA-256, where the unknowability is intrinsic rather than asserted.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Every example carries a `VISUAL_IMPLICATION:` field written before the narration. A reviewer (or a picture-only pass) checks it against every `NOT`/`isn't`/`doesn't mean`/`to be clear` sentence in the same knowledge point; a contradiction is a blocking defect, not a wording issue.
