candidate_rules.rule: Never fix a confusing shot by adding lower-level implementation detail. Fix it by (a) choosing a better example, (b) demoting to a smaller instance the reader can hold entirely, or (c) promoting an omitted structural property to its own shot.
candidate_rules.rationale: In the post-mortem he explicitly declines to add the missing quantum-compilation detail, arguing it would not add clarity, and instead adds an example swap plus a whole section building linearity from a one-qubit case and a walking-hiker analogy.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Any revision commit that responds to 'this shot is confusing' must not increase the shot's token count by more than a small threshold without also changing the example, reducing the dimensionality of the instance, or adding a preceding shot. Track it as a review question on each fix.

candidate_rules.rule: Disown every presentational convenience in the shot that introduces it. Any projection, slice, ordering, layout, or color choice that a reader could mistake for mechanism must carry an explicit sentence saying it is a drawing choice and not part of the thing being explained.
candidate_rules.rationale: Viewers took his 2-D visualization slice to be a step of Grover's algorithm; he had to publish a correction stating the algorithm has no care how you choose to visualize it. He avoids the same failure in the transformers video by declaring the 3-D projection up front.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain a conventions registry: every projection/slice/reordering/color-coding gets one entry with the shot id that introduces it and the disclaimer sentence. Assert every registry entry has a non-empty disclaimer and that the disclaimer string appears in that shot's narration.

candidate_rules.rule: Declare a visual convention exactly once, name what it encodes, and never break it. A quantity may not change color, axis, or position role between shots within a knowledge point.
candidate_rules.rationale: He tells readers to draw a sharp mental distinction between weights (always blue or red) and processed data (always gray), and holds it across two long videos; the cross-entropy bar diagram keeps width = P and height = -log Q fixed for an entire lesson.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Assert every semantic role in the conventions registry maps to exactly one visual encoding across the deck, and that no encoding is reused for two roles. Diff the registry on every commit.

candidate_rules.rule: Tag every simplification at the shot where it is made and give it a named payback shot. No simplification may ship without a payback; the build fails on an orphan.
candidate_rules.rationale: He announces the idealized Galton board as deliberately unrealistic and then, at the video's end, reveals those exact idealizations are the theorem's assumptions — the payback becomes the punchline. Unlabeled simplifications become false beliefs the reader must unlearn later.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Author `SIMPLIFY(id, claim)` at the lying shot and `PAYBACK(id)` at the repairing shot. A script asserts a bijection between the two sets across the deck.

candidate_rules.rule: Open every knowledge point with a scope contract naming assumed background, what is covered, and what is deferred. Close every section with either the designated takeaway sentence or the exact question the next section answers — never mid-derivation.
candidate_rules.rationale: The CLT video opens by stating it assumes minimal background, will go decently deep, and defers the why-pi question to a sequel; the entropy video even states the duration and the target feeling. His sections consistently end on a takeaway or a posed question, and he deliberately leaves one question hanging across several sections.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Assert the first shot of each knowledge point contains an assumed-background clause and a deferred-material clause. Assert the last sentence of each section either exactly matches the section's declared TAKEAWAY string or ends in a question mark.

candidate_rules.rule: Declare exactly one TAKEAWAY sentence per section, state it verbatim at the point of derivation and again at the section close, and reuse the identical wording wherever it is later invoked. Do not paraphrase it.
candidate_rules.rationale: He repeats the cross-entropy minimum property in identical wording at least three times and re-invokes it verbatim to define KL divergence; the Laplace video designates one fact as the single thing to remember and closes on it.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Each section declares `TAKEAWAY: "<sentence>"`. Assert the string occurs at least twice in that section's narration and at least once in its SUM card, with exact-match comparison (not fuzzy).

candidate_rules.rule: Recap only the prerequisites the next section actually consumes, as a short named list. Cap recaps at roughly 120 words, and cut any concept mentioned in a recap that is not used again within the next three shots.
candidate_rules.rationale: His recaps are three items long and every item is consumed almost immediately; the Grover follow-up compresses a whole prior video into a single sentence. A recap is a register-load, not a review.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Tag recap shots. Assert word count under threshold, and assert each capitalized/technical noun phrase in the recap reappears in the narration of one of the next three shots. Flag unused items.

candidate_rules.rule: Maintain one persistent content-bearing progress gauge per lecture that the content actually feeds — a running count, a checklist of N pieces named up front, or a diagram that fills in. Never use an abstract percentage or a bare chapter number as the primary orientation device.
candidate_rules.rationale: The GPT-3 parameter tally accumulates across sections toward a total announced at the start, giving location and content simultaneously; he also declares eight matrix categories up front and steps through them.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Assert the deck declares a gauge with a target value stated in the first knowledge point; assert the gauge's value changes in at least three distinct shots and its final value is stated in the closing shot.

candidate_rules.rule: Any shot that asserts something a careful reader would resist must voice that objection in the reader's own words before answering it. Shots containing hedges ('somehow', 'it turns out', 'you can show', 'it happens to be') must carry either an objection-and-answer pair or an explicit deferral naming where it is resolved.
candidate_rules.rationale: He routinely interrupts himself to voice the reader's complaint — how does the robot know where to divide, isn't this plan idiotic, doesn't the count depend on point placement, are small-angle approximations really enough — before answering. An unvoiced objection runs as a background process consuming the attention the explanation needs.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: grep narration for the hedge list; for each hit, assert the same shot contains a second-person objection construction ('you might', 'you could rightfully', 'some readers will ask', 'hang on') or a `DEFER(section_id)` tag.

candidate_rules.rule: QUIZ items must be answerable from material already shown in the same knowledge point, must be framed as an invitation rather than a gate, and must be followed immediately by the answer with reasoning. Never quiz on material tagged OPTIONAL.
candidate_rules.rationale: His prompts are consistently 'take a moment', 'see if you can', 'it's worth your time to ponder' — never a hard stop — and the answer follows immediately. The mechanical count found essentially no imperative 'pause the video' gating. A reader who fails a gate reads the remainder in a degraded state.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each QUIZ, assert every concept in its stem and options appears in a prior shot of the same knowledge point; assert no referenced shot is tagged OPTIONAL; assert an explanation field is present and non-empty.

candidate_rules.rule: Mark optional depth explicitly at both boundaries, name its audience, and state that skipping it is harmless. Nothing after an OPTIONAL block may depend on a concept first introduced inside it.
candidate_rules.rationale: He tiers explicitly — a Lagrange-multiplier derivation for the extra curious with details declared not too important, analytic continuation flagged as more than you need to drive the car, a notational footnote left as an on-screen note. Unlabeled optional material is worse than absent because readers assume it is required.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Assert `OPTIONAL` blocks have opening and closing markers and an audience phrase. Build a concept-first-mention index and assert no concept first mentioned inside an OPTIONAL block is referenced outside one.

candidate_rules.rule: Warn before the single hardest shot in a knowledge point, grant explicit permission not to absorb it on first pass, and place a sufficiency checkpoint immediately after it stating what the reader now owns and that the remainder is elaboration. At most one HARD shot per knowledge point.
candidate_rules.rationale: The attention video does exactly this twice, and the key move is telling the reader that stopping there would still leave them with the essence, with the rest being parallel repetition. Note this is a targeted tool, appearing in roughly two of fifteen files — overusing it would flatten its signal.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Assert at most one shot per knowledge point carries the HARD tag; assert the preceding shot's narration contains a permission phrase and the following shot's contains a sufficiency phrase naming what has been established.

candidate_rules.rule: Before publishing, run a sound-off pass and a picture-off pass. Read every narration paragraph with visuals hidden — it must still carry the argument. View every shot with narration hidden — exactly one thing must be seen to change, and the visual implication must match the declared one.
candidate_rules.rationale: The two documented failures are respectively a picture-off failure (motion carrying no argument) and a sound-off failure (a formula that rendered as garbage while the narration read fine). Testing each channel independently is the only way to catch a defect that the other channel is masking.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Partly mechanical: assert each section's TAKEAWAY string appears in narration alone, and assert each animated shot's start/end state diff is non-empty and single-parameter. The remainder is a two-pass human checklist run once per knowledge point before publish.

anti_patterns: Motion with no referent in the narration — anything that moves without a sentence naming what quantity is changing and what the change proves.

Infinitely looping or idle animation: pulse rings, breathing circles, marching-ants dashed strokes, a token pacing back and forth, ambient glow. Nothing in fifteen transcripts corresponds to this; every motion reference is a terminating single-parameter sweep.
Changing two or more things at once inside a single shot, which destroys the reader's ability to see which change caused which effect.
Relying on a verbal caveat to defeat a structural implication of the visual. His own post-mortem is that he tried this and it failed.
Responding to reader confusion by adding lower-level implementation detail. He explicitly considered and rejected this in the Grover follow-up.
Letting a presentational convenience (a projected slice, a chosen ordering, a color) go undisowned, so readers take it for mechanism.
Introducing a formula cold, before any sentence has said what it will turn out to mean.
Comprehensive recaps that restate everything from the previous section rather than only the registers the next section reads.
A numbered outline as the primary structure marker. He orients readers by open questions and by a content-bearing running tally, not by 'first we'll do A, then B, then C'.
Hard gating: 'pause and do not continue until you have solved this'. His prompts are always invitations with the answer following immediately.
Optional material left unlabeled, or worse, optional material that later content silently depends on.
Ending a section mid-derivation with unresolved intermediate state the reader must carry across the boundary.
Paraphrasing the section's key claim differently each time it appears, which destroys the retrieval handle that verbatim repetition creates.
Nested, subordinate-clause sentence construction. His sentences are long (24-31 words on average) but strictly linear, advancing one step per clause.
Simplifying without labeling the simplification, or labeling it without ever paying it back.
Assuming a rendering capability without observing it — the direct cause of the raw-backslash defect.
Assuming your own derived number is right without an independent cross-check; he routinely re-derives a value a second way or counts it off a diagram.

lens: Self-diagnosed failure modes — what Sanderson says went wrong in his own explanations, in mechanism terms, and the negative rules that follow

findings.observation: A reported confusion is almost never located where the confusion was created. He treats the reader's stated question as a symptom and hunts upstream for where the wrong model was installed.
findings.evidence: Grover post-mortem (Dlsa9EBKDGI): commenters all pointed at one mid-video step — how can the algorithm flip the sign along the answer's axis without already knowing the answer? He traces the actual cause back to the opening framing of the whole setup, minutes earlier, and says he suspects the origin is not a lack of low-level detail but how he framed the setup.
findings.why_it_works: A reader reports the point where a wrong mental model finally broke against the material, not the point where the model was formed. The break is downstream of the cause, so patching at the break is always patching the wrong place.

findings.observation: He explicitly considers and rejects 'add a layer of detail beneath the confusing step' as the fix. Going lower under a false frame produces more false frame.
findings.evidence: Same file: he weighs explaining quantum compilation (how a classical circuit becomes a quantum operator), previews what it would look like, and then declines — arguing that knowing which logic gates implement addition teaches you essentially nothing about how to add.
findings.why_it_works: Depth answers 'how is this implemented'. The reader's question was 'what kind of thing is this' — a category question. Resolution never answers a category question.

findings.observation: A degenerate toy example installs a false invariant. If the example satisfies the stated definition plus one accidental extra property, readers induct the extra property as part of the definition — and it will be exactly the property the whole lesson turns on.
findings.evidence: He briefly flashed a verifier function that literally checks whether the input equals 12, while simultaneously calling it a black box. In that example the answer really is sitting in the source code. He calls this a misleading way to open and takes the blame for it outright.
findings.why_it_works: Readers generalize from the intersection of the examples they were shown, not from the stated definition. One example means the intersection is that example, accidents included.

findings.observation: Examples are ranked by how forcefully they FORBID the likely misreading, not by how simple they are. He gives an explicit three-rung ladder.
findings.evidence: input==12 (bad) → Sudoku verification (much better) → SHA-256 preimage (better still), with SHA-256 best precisely because reverse-engineering it is believed impossible, so 'can verify' and 'can solve' are structurally forced apart. He states the design property the example must carry as: [quote] "The logic gates distill the rules of the game, but not the strategy."
findings.why_it_works: Simplicity is a virtue only where it does not destroy the property being taught. When it does, the simplest example is the most dangerous one.

findings.observation: A term of art whose everyday reading is false in context is worse than no term. He identifies one as a direct cause of the failure.
findings.evidence: 'Black box' was meant narrowly — you only ever interact with the operator by applying it to inputs, never by reverse-engineering it. Readers heard the ordinary meaning, you cannot see inside. The truth was the opposite: to build the quantum version you must go into the guts of the classical function.
findings.why_it_works: Readers apply everyday semantics first and the technical gloss second, if at all. When the two point in opposite directions, the everyday one wins and becomes load-bearing.

findings.observation: THE central finding for a drawing engine: readers cannot distinguish an authorial presentation choice from a step of the mechanism, because a picture renders both in the same visual grammar. He devotes a whole section of the post-mortem to un-teaching one such artifact.
findings.evidence: The original video visualized the algorithm inside a 2D slice of a huge space, and that slice was by definition chosen to contain the answer's axis. He insists the choice of slice is in no way part of the algorithm's instruction set; the algorithm merely alternates two operations and is indifferent to how anyone draws it. The state vector staying in that plane is an emergent consequence, not a step.
findings.why_it_works: Every drawing contains choices the mechanism does not require (basis, ordering, layout, framing, colour, what is centred). Unlabelled, these read as mechanism. This is exactly how decorative motion misleads: the reader assumes the motion means something and constructs a meaning.

findings.observation: The real gap was a missing STRUCTURAL property one level up, not a missing detail one level down. Supplying it dissolves the question rather than answering it.
findings.evidence: He names linearity as the thing he under-emphasized, and says half his reason for making the follow-up at all was as an excuse to teach it. Linearity is what licenses defining an operator purely by its action on basis states and getting all superpositions free — so nothing in the algorithm ever 'finds' the special axis.
findings.why_it_works: A step feels impossible when the reader's model requires an agent to perform a search that the formalism does not actually require. Naming the property that removes the agent removes the impossibility.

findings.observation: He refuses to assert a satisfying interpretive gloss as fact, and separates a property of a transformation from a procedure for computing it.
findings.evidence: He raises the popular 'it acts on all 2^k basis states at once, in parallel' reading, says it might be true, and then gives a deflating analogy: rotating a hiker walking northeast is linear, so the result equals rotating the north part and the east part and adding — which does not mean two rotations were physically performed. He leaves the interpretation flagged as interpretation.
findings.why_it_works: This is a defensible sentence that induces a wrong picture. Sentence-level truth is not the audit unit; the induced picture is.

findings.observation: After making a thing vivid, he goes back and deflates its importance with numbers rather than hedging adjectives.
findings.evidence: The post-mortem ends by saying Grover's may just not be useful: quadratic only; Sudoku goes from ~9^60 to ~9^30, SHA-256 from 2^256 to 2^128 — both still infeasible. He names seeing through hyperbole as an explicit goal.
findings.why_it_works: A vivid explanation implicitly overclaims significance; the correction has to be numeric because the overclaim was emotional, and adjectives cannot cancel it.

findings.observation: He names and rejects derivations that are formally correct but explanatorily empty — specifically, ones where the structure you invoked cancels out of the final expression.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy video (GlYgs6v2YfU): the standard 'it's cross-entropy against a one-hot distribution' story is worked through, all the zeros cancel, and he rejects it as lame — it explains the name and not the choice, so why not just call it log loss. He then supplies the real reason (the weighted average over many instances of the same context genuinely is cross-entropy; and requiring the loss to be minimized exactly when model matches data forces a logarithm).
findings.why_it_works: Mechanical check: after the derivation, does the object you named still appear? If it cancelled, you explained the terminology, not the design decision, and you still owe an argument.

findings.observation: He maintains a persistent, externally-stated acceptance criterion and re-audits against it after every step — including saying it still fails.
findings.evidence: Why-pi (cy8r7WSuT1I): the criterion is a named imagined sceptic asking what circles have to do with population statistics. After the classic proof: fails (feels like a trick, and doesn't answer that question). After the Herschel–Maxwell derivation: better, and he retro-motivates the earlier trick. At the end: still not satisfying, because that derivation presumes a spatial setting, so it is deferred to another video.
findings.why_it_works: A stable external test stops the author grading their own explanation by how good it felt to write. It also converts 'incomplete' from a failure into a scheduled item.

findings.observation: Steps that are genuinely unmotivated are labelled unmotivated at the moment they are taken, and retro-motivated later if a reason can be found.
findings.evidence: Why-pi: bumping a 1-D integral to 2-D is announced as barely motivated — roughly, who ordered another dimension, just watch what happens. Later, after the symmetry derivation, he returns and recasts that same step as the move that lets the defining property become visible, so it reads as necessity rather than luck. The exploration video (_BrFKp-U8GI) similarly labels a probe as pure guesswork, on a par with an artist dividing 79 by 12 to see whether it comes out even.
findings.why_it_works: Unlabelled arbitrariness reads to the reader as 'I missed something'. Labelled arbitrariness reads as honest search, costs nothing, and the later payoff converts it into inevitability.

findings.observation: Dead ends are kept in the explanation and explicitly labelled as dead ends.
findings.evidence: _BrFKp-U8GI derives a technically valid counting formula, then flatly says it does not help: counting lookalikes is no easier than counting family sizes, and you still have to walk the whole hallway. He calls it cute but useless, and names disappointment as normal.
findings.why_it_works: It shows the shape of a failed good idea (most of research), and it stops the reader assuming they missed the reason it worked.

findings.observation: Duration is used as a QUANTITY — and cut the instant that quantity has landed.
findings.evidence: _BrFKp-U8GI: a long travelling shot down a corridor holding all 4096 incomplete cubes, with narration saying explicitly that you know 4096 is big but cannot feel it until you see the corridor; the shot speeds up; he notes you would have to traverse it once per family; he notes you are only halfway; then he cuts it off and moves to strategy.
findings.why_it_works: Elapsed cost is a legible unit for 'infeasible'. In a non-time medium the same claim needs a substitute unit — an explicit step counter, an exhaustive enumeration the reader must scroll past — but the rule is the same: length must equal a number in the argument, and stop when the number is delivered.

findings.observation: Motion is used to demonstrate a NULL result — that varying an input does not change the output — which is a claim no static image can make.
findings.evidence: CLT (zeJD6dqJ5lo): at sum size 3 he wiggles the underlying distribution and the output changes completely; at 10 it mostly holds but he finds exceptions (a spiky bell curve); at 50 he says nothing he does to the input has any effect on the output shape. Three regimes, same interaction.
findings.why_it_works: Insensitivity is only demonstrable by sweeping and showing the hold. The three-regime version also delivers the boundary — where the theorem starts to bite — for free.

findings.observation: A sweep is justified when it deposits a persistent artifact that is then interpreted as an object in its own right.
findings.evidence: Cross-entropy video: P is held fixed and Q swept, showing a clear minimum; then P itself is swept and the locus of minima is traced out as a new curve, and the reader is asked what that new curve represents (it is the entropy of P).
findings.why_it_works: The sweep is not the payload; the trace is. The motion earns its place because at the end of it something new exists on screen that was not there before.

findings.observation: The cheapest legitimate 'animation' is re-reading an already-drawn structure along a different axis. Nothing moves; the reading order changes; that change IS the insight.
findings.evidence: _BrFKp-U8GI: a 24-row grid is built column by column (per shape, count its symmetries). The epiphany, staged as a moment of noticing, is that the identical cells can be counted row by row instead (per transformation, count the shapes it fixes) — which is computable in closed form. He also stages a rearrangement of one 24-cell block into four intact copies of a 6-member family; the rearrangement is the proof step.
findings.why_it_works: Re-indexing costs no new visual vocabulary and forces the reader to hold the same object in two readings — which is precisely what the mathematical content (Burnside's lemma) says.

findings.observation: In a multi-panel animated figure he states, per panel, which symbol is the input and which is a knob.
findings.evidence: Convolution demo (IaSGqQa5O-M): he says explicitly that on the three left panels x is the input and s is merely a parameter, whereas on the right-hand result panel s is the input and the output is the area of the lower-left panel.
findings.why_it_works: Without this a reader cannot tell which axis is the answer and which is a control, and will read the knob's sweep as part of the phenomenon.

findings.observation: Encoding changes are announced, and lossy encodings are declared lossy before being extended.
findings.evidence: CLT: he switches bar height→bar area as the carrier of probability and says why (to match how continuous densities are read). Laplace (j0wJBEZdwLs): he first plots only the magnitude of a complex-valued output, states outright that the output has direction too and that he is throwing it away, then adds hue for phase. Transformers (wjZofJX0v4M): a persistent global contract — learned weights are always blue/red, data flowing through is always grey — with an instruction to hold that distinction sharply.
findings.why_it_works: A silent re-encoding invalidates everything the reader trained themselves to read in the previous shot. One contract held across many shots outperforms per-shot cleverness.

findings.observation: Every cheat is named, its cost quantified, and its repair scheduled — then actually performed.
findings.evidence: Why-pi: he assumes a proportionality constant is 1, calls the move cheeky, states that the result will therefore be off by a constant factor, and schedules renormalization at the end. IaSGqQa5O-M: the diagonal-slice area is 'almost but not quite' the convolution — off by a factor of root two — and he states it, explains where it comes from, and then notes it just gets absorbed into a constant.
findings.why_it_works: An unnamed approximation silently becomes a false belief. A named one with a scheduled repair is a loan the reader can track.

findings.observation: An approximation is not accepted until its error is bounded and its failure condition is stated in checkable form — even at the cost of undercutting the video's own headline.
findings.evidence: Colliding blocks (6dTyOl1fmDo): after the small-angle approximation, he anticipates sticklers, gives the Taylor error as order theta-cubed, and then states the exact digit condition on pi under which the count would be off by one — concluding that the famous result is, technically, an unsolved problem.
findings.why_it_works: Converts 'close enough' into a falsifiable statement, and demonstrates that the standard is applied even when it costs the punchline.

findings.observation: He voices the reader's objection in the reader's own register, concedes it, and only then answers.
findings.evidence: Convolution (KuXjwB4LzSA): he anticipates the reader calling the polynomial-sampling plan idiotic, agrees that all the complexity merely moved, and only then introduces roots of unity and the FFT. Moser (YtkIWDE36qU): he raises the 'doesn't it depend where the points are' objection himself, demonstrates the degenerate symmetric placement where a region vanishes, and then states the genericity restriction.
findings.why_it_works: An objection voiced is disarmed. An objection ignored compounds, and the reader spends the rest of the piece maintaining it instead of following.

findings.observation: The tempting-but-wrong correspondence is shown failing before the correct one is offered.
findings.evidence: Moser: the natural guess that intersection points correspond to pairs of chords is proposed, then killed with a non-intersecting pair, then replaced by the correspondence with quadruples of boundary points — with the bijection argued in both directions.
findings.why_it_works: Readers who would have made the error watch it die; readers who would not learn what standard a correspondence has to meet.

findings.observation: Circular justifications the reader is likely to construct are named and severed.
findings.evidence: Gaussian+Gaussian (d_qvLDhkg00): he anticipates 'of course the sum is normal, the central limit theorem says so' and says that has it backwards — this very computation is the reason the CLT's limit is a Gaussian rather than something else. He also deflates his own field, noting the supposed ubiquity of normal distributions is often exaggerated.
findings.why_it_works: A wrong dependency direction feels like understanding and survives indefinitely unless explicitly cut.

findings.observation: An invented illustrative story used to make an uninterpretable mechanism legible is re-marked as invented at every shot that leans on it, not disclaimed once.
findings.evidence: Attention (eMlx5fFNoYc): the adjectives-updating-nouns story is flagged as made up at introduction, and re-flagged at least twice more — the true behaviour of the learned matrices is described as hard to parse each time he uses the story to interpret one.
findings.why_it_works: A single up-front disclaimer decays within a minute; the reader retains the story and drops the caveat. The caveat has to ride along with each use.

findings.observation: He audits his own rendered figure for artifacts, flags an unexplained visual feature as an open question, and then closes the loop later.
findings.evidence: CLT: he observes that at 3000 samples the histogram looks spiky and asks whether that is real or an artifact of randomness; he sets it aside and computes exactly; much later he returns and answers — the spikiness was real, and a sum of size 10 was simply not large enough.
findings.why_it_works: Any visible feature of a figure is a hypothesis the reader forms about the mechanism. Unexplained features become believed mechanism. This is the direct analogue of shipping a render you never looked at.

findings.observation: Derived results are checked against something independent, using several distinct kinds of check.
findings.evidence: _BrFKp-U8GI: a derived family size of 12 is corroborated because a cube has 12 edges, and the formula is separately tested on both extreme cases. Moser: 6-choose-4 = 15 is checked against counting the intersection points in the drawing. Convolution: he runs Python on screen to confirm a small convolution and to time two implementations (about 4.87 s versus 4.3 ms), saying the reader can verify he is not lying. Blocks: the predicted 31 collisions is checked against real footage of a physical demonstration. Entropy (l6DKRf-fAAM): the claimed bit savings is checked against a sampled stream. Even an anecdote is fact-checked in line and reported as probably apocryphal.
findings.why_it_works: Five independent check types — small hand case, edge case, independently known count, numeric run, physical reality. Each is cheap; the habit is what matters.

findings.observation: A non-essential embellishment is permitted only when it is doing an informational job the primary channel cannot do — and it is then confessed as an addition.
findings.evidence: Blocks: the collision sounds are physically impossible under the perfectly-elastic assumption. He says so, admits he likes them, and then gives the substantive reason: without them there is no way to convey visually how dense the burst of collisions in the middle is.
findings.why_it_works: This is the exact licence test for a decorative-looking element. It passed not because it was pleasing but because a specific quantity (density in time) had no other carrier.

findings.observation: He states outright when the visual route is the WORSE route, and justifies including it on other grounds — the strongest anti-decoration evidence in the corpus.
findings.evidence: Laplace: he says honestly that for the cosine case the symbolic reasoning is the easier way to the answer and the diagram is notably more complicated, then keeps the diagram for mechanism appreciation. Gaussian+Gaussian: he notes the direct integral works fine, and that for most pairs of functions the geometric method buys you nothing at all — it pays off here only because of a rotational symmetry unique to bell curves. Convolution: he explicitly declines to open with the image-processing examples despite calling them the most visually intriguing, because they are unrepresentative of the operation.
findings.why_it_works: A picture is licensed by the specific structural property it exploits, not by how good it looks. He is willing to say a picture is not the efficient path, and to reject the prettiest example.

findings.observation: Stated conditions are used to indict the piece's own opening hook.
findings.evidence: CLT: he deliberately withholds the theorem's three assumptions, tells the reader to watch for them, and delivers them at the end — then turns them on the Galton board, his own opening demonstration, showing it violates two of the three (bounces are neither independent nor identically distributed). He notes a bell curve nevertheless appears, gives a partial reason, and warns against assuming normality without justification.
findings.why_it_works: Without the audit, the most memorable instance in the piece is an invalid one, and it is what the reader keeps.

findings.observation: Misconceptions are stated as contrastive pairs — the wrong belief first, in the reader's terms, then the correction.
findings.evidence: It is not that the key value hides inside the function behind a curtain; it is an emergent property of the gates. It is the variance that adds, not the standard deviation. Linearity is a property of a transformation, not a set of instructions for performing it. The slice is our viewing choice, not part of the instruction set.
findings.why_it_works: The correction only lands against a named wrong belief; asserted alone it is absorbed as one more true statement among many.

findings.observation: Assessment is 'explain why', not 'select the right option', and the prompts probe live misconceptions rather than recall.
findings.evidence: IaSGqQa5O-M opens with a guess-the-distribution question and then says explicitly that guessing is not enough — the real quiz is being able to explain why. The cross-entropy video's closing prompts are: convince yourself two forms of an expression are equal; say in what sense a given diagram represents an expression; and ask what would happen if KL divergence were used instead of cross-entropy as a distillation loss (a genuine trap, since the two differ by a term that is constant in the trained model's parameters).
findings.why_it_works: A distractor that merely looks similar tests reading; a distractor that is what a competent reader would actually conclude tests the model.

findings.observation: Deviations from standard notation are declared as deviations and reconciled with the literature before the reader leaves.
findings.evidence: Attention: he invents 'value down' and 'value up' matrices, says twice that these are not the conventional names, and near the end explains how papers actually staple the value-up matrices into a single output matrix — calling it a distracting detail that he raises anyway so the reader is not lost elsewhere.
findings.why_it_works: A pedagogical shorthand that is never reconciled strands the reader precisely at the boundary where they go to read anything else.

findings.observation: One designated takeaway per unit, restated, rather than balanced coverage.
findings.evidence: Laplace: an explicit 'if there is only one fact you remember from this video' — the transform of an exponential has a pole above the corresponding point. Cross-entropy: the single property he asks the reader to retain (minimized when the two distributions coincide, and the minimum is the entropy of the true one) is restated at least three times in different visual forms. Attention also runs a persistent numeric tally of parameters, then uses it to correct a likely misconception — attention accounts for roughly 58 of 175 billion, so most parameters live elsewhere.
findings.why_it_works: Repetition of one claim across different representations beats coverage; the running tally gives the reader a checkpoint to test whether they are still following.

findings.observation: GAP — I did not find any explicit statement anywhere in this corpus about animation pacing, easing, loop duration, or a stated rule against decorative motion. Every anti-decoration finding above is indirect: he labels flourishes as flourishes, rejects the prettier example as unrepresentative, and admits when the visual route is worse.
findings.evidence: Searched all fifteen transcripts. The nearest explicit statement is in IaSGqQa5O-M, where he says of a 3-D collapse animation that he is having a bit of fun and that you would not draw this with pencil and paper — immediately followed by a promise that the same intuition will be load-bearing in a later proof.
findings.why_it_works: That pairing is itself the usable rule (a flourish must be cashed in later, and the author must be able to name where), but it is one instance, not a stated principle. Treat the derived rule as inference, not as his doctrine.

findings.observation: GAP — I found no discussion at all of tooling or rendering-pipeline verification. His verification discipline is entirely about content: results checked against hand cases, edge cases, independent counts, numeric runs, and physical demonstrations.
findings.evidence: The closest thing to a pipeline check is running Python on screen to confirm a convolution and a timing claim, which verifies a mathematical claim rather than a renderer. No transcript mentions checking that a visual actually drew correctly.
findings.why_it_works: The rule 'never claim a rendering primitive works without rendering one instance and reading it' is a legitimate extension of his content-verification habit into the medium, but it is an extension. Do not attribute it to him.

findings.observation: GAP — he never states in one sentence the principle that an explanation can mislead while every individual sentence in it is true. It is reconstructible from the Grover post-mortem with high confidence, but the synthesis is mine.
findings.evidence: In that file every original claim was literally true — the operator is used only by application; there is an axis for the answer; the step does flip along it; the 2-D slice does contain that axis. The misleading came from four sources, none of them false statements: a true-but-degenerate example; a term of art whose plain reading was false; a presentational frame indistinguishable from mechanism; and an omitted structural property (linearity) whose absence left the reader to fill the gap with a wrong causal story about the machine looking something up.
findings.why_it_works: This gives the audit unit: not 'is each sentence true' but 'what model does a competent reader build from this, and does that model have properties the real thing lacks'. Four named installation routes make the audit mechanical.

candidate_rules.rule: Never ship a repeating animation unless the repetition count, or the fact of non-termination itself, is a claim stated in the narration. Delete every pulse ring, breathing circle, marching-ants dash, and back-and-forth token.
candidate_rules.rationale: Motion is read as meaning. A loop with no N-dependence asserts that something is recurring, and the reader will spend effort constructing what. The one licensed non-terminating loop in the corpus is a spiral that visibly fails to converge — where non-termination IS the claim (the Laplace integral diverging on the left half-plane).
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For every animated element, the author must complete the sentence: 'the Nth repetition means ______.' If the completion contains no N, delete the loop. Mechanically: grep drawFns for CSS `infinite`, `alternate`, `repeatCount="indefinite"`, and `setInterval`; each hit requires a matching narration sentence naming what the repetition counts.

candidate_rules.rule: Never include an animated shot whose narration does not name both (a) the thing that is changing and (b) the quantity the reader should read off while it changes.
candidate_rules.rationale: Every load-bearing animation in the corpus has both. Sweeping a parameter and watching the entropy area change; sweeping the sum size and watching the output shape hold; sliding the offset and watching the overlap area. The pair (driver, readout) is what makes a sweep an argument rather than movement.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Per shot: extract the driver variable and the readout quantity from the narration string. If either is absent, the shot is decorative — either write the sentence or render the shot static.

candidate_rules.rule: Never let a presentational choice appear in a drawing without a narration line marking it as a choice. Applies to: chosen basis, chosen slice, node ordering, which state is centred, axis limits, colour assignment, and which of several equivalent forms an equation is written in.
candidate_rules.rationale: The single failure he dissects at greatest length. He drew Grover inside a 2-D slice picked to contain the answer's axis, and readers concluded that picking the slice was a step of the algorithm. He states flatly that the algorithm is indifferent to how anyone chooses to visualize it, and that the plane confinement is emergent, not instructed.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each drawFn, write a list of decisions the mechanism does not require. Every item on that list must appear in the narration prefixed by something equivalent to 'this is our view, not part of the method' — or be removed from the drawing.

candidate_rules.rule: Never use an example that satisfies an extra property the general case lacks, when that extra property is the one a reader is most likely to over-generalize. Rank candidate examples by how forcefully they forbid the misreading, not by how simple they are.
candidate_rules.rationale: The `input==12` verifier. It satisfied the definition and also, accidentally, put the answer in the source code — which was precisely the thing readers wrongly concluded was always true. His replacement ladder (Sudoku, then a cryptographic hash) is ordered by how structurally impossible the misreading becomes.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: For each example, enumerate its properties beyond the definition. For each such property, ask: if a reader assumed this held in general, would the lesson break? Any yes disqualifies the example. In RL terms: never illustrate a value function with a gridworld whose optimal policy is visually obvious from the reward map, if the point is that the policy is not read off the reward.

candidate_rules.rule: Never respond to reported confusion by adding detail below the confusing step until you have written down, in one sentence, the false belief the reader holds, and located the shot where it was installed.
candidate_rules.rationale: He explicitly weighs and rejects the downward fix, arguing that knowing which gates implement addition teaches you nothing about how to add. The real repairs were upstream framing and a structural property one level up.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain a defect log with three required fields per reported confusion: FALSE BELIEF (one sentence in the reader's voice), INSTALLED AT (shot id), FIX (framing / example / structural property / detail). A defect whose FIX is 'detail' and whose INSTALLED AT is more than one shot before the reported location is almost certainly misdiagnosed.

candidate_rules.rule: Never use a term of art whose ordinary-language reading is false in this context without an explicit 'this does not mean ___' in the same shot.
candidate_rules.rationale: 'Black box' meant only-applied-not-inspected; readers heard cannot-see-inside; the truth was the opposite. In RL the exposed terms are legion: 'model-free' (does not mean no model of value), 'greedy' (does not mean short-sighted in the colloquial sense), 'off-policy', 'return', 'state' (does not mean 'the situation'), 'reward' (does not mean 'good outcome'), 'optimal' (relative to a fixed MDP), 'bootstrapping'.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Maintain a per-knowledge-point glossary. For each term, write its plain-English reading. If that reading is false here, either drop the term or attach the negation sentence. Grep narration for each glossary term's first occurrence and verify the negation sentence is adjacent.

candidate_rules.rule: Never present a derivation as the REASON a construct was chosen if the construct cancels out of the final expression. Such a derivation explains the terminology only, and you still owe a separate argument.
candidate_rules.rationale: His explicit rejection of the one-hot story for cross-entropy loss: the zeros cancel, nothing of cross-entropy remains, so the derivation cannot justify the choice. Directly applicable to the standard CS234 moves — deriving TD(0) as a special case of TD(lambda), or the policy gradient via the log-derivative trick.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: After each derivation, ask: does the object named in the title still appear in the final expression? If it cancelled, tag the shot NAME-ONLY and require a second shot supplying the real reason for the choice.

candidate_rules.rule: Never claim a rendering primitive works until you have rendered exactly one instance of it and read the output — in the browser, at the size it will ship, in both themes.
candidate_rules.rationale: This is an extension of his content-verification habit into the medium, not a rule he states. The habit it extends is real and repeated: running the code on screen to confirm a convolution and a timing, checking a formula against a hand count, checking edge cases. He does not assert results he has not exercised.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Per project, keep a PRIMITIVES-VERIFIED list. A primitive may appear in more than one shot only after a dated entry recording that it was rendered and inspected. For the specific bug at hand: if formula morphing is FLIP-on-HTML-spans, the smoke test is one shot containing a single term with a subscript and a Greek letter, screenshotted; if backslashes appear, the primitive does not render LaTeX and every formula in the project must be authored as spans.

candidate_rules.rule: Never state a derived formula or a computed number without at least one independent check inside the same knowledge point.
candidate_rules.rationale: He checks constantly and cheaply, using five distinct kinds of check: a small hand-computable case, an extreme/edge case, an independently known count, a numeric run, and physical reality. None of these are expensive.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Every knowledge point whose payload is a formula must carry a CHECK field naming which of the five it used and what the two numbers were. For RL: verify a Bellman backup on a 2-state chain by hand; verify a policy-gradient sign by checking that the gradient increases the probability of an action that got positive advantage; verify a discount-factor claim at the endpoints gamma=0 and gamma→1.

candidate_rules.rule: Never leave a visible feature of a rendered figure unexplained. Either it is in the argument, or it is an artifact and must be removed, or it must be named as an artifact and resolved before the unit closes.
candidate_rules.rationale: He notices spikiness in his own histogram, asks aloud whether it is real or a sampling artifact, defers, and later returns to confirm it was real and explain why. An unexplained feature is a hypothesis the reader forms about the mechanism.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: After rendering each figure, enumerate every visually salient feature (spikes, asymmetries, gaps, colour bands, unrendered regions, stray labels). Classify each: ARGUMENT / ARTIFACT-REMOVE / ARTIFACT-EXPLAIN. Ship no figure with an unclassified feature.

candidate_rules.rule: Never change an encoding between shots without a narration line announcing the change, and never use the same visual channel for two meanings inside one knowledge point.
candidate_rules.rationale: He announces the switch from bar height to bar area, declares that plotting only a complex number's magnitude discards its direction before adding hue, and holds a global colour contract across a whole series (learned weights one colour family, flowing data another).
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Give every drawFn an explicit ENCODING declaration (what maps to x, y, length, area, hue, opacity, thickness). Diff consecutive shots' declarations; any diff without a matching narration sentence fails. Any single knowledge point in which one channel carries two meanings fails.

candidate_rules.rule: Never quantify significance with an adjective where a number is computable.
candidate_rules.rationale: He returns after the fact to replace 'much faster' with actual magnitudes (a quadratic speedup that still leaves an infeasible number of steps), and states that letting readers see through hype is a goal. For RL this bites on 'sample-inefficient', 'converges', 'high variance', 'much better than random'.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Grep narration for a banned-adjective list (much, dramatically, enormously, vastly, far more, a lot). Each hit must be adjacent to a figure, an order of magnitude, or a rate.

candidate_rules.rule: Never include a visual flourish unless a later, named shot consumes it. Record the consuming shot id at the time the flourish is authored.
candidate_rules.rationale: The one place he keeps something purely for fun, he says so and immediately promises the same intuition will be load-bearing in a later proof — and it is (the diagonal-slice reading returns to prove that a convolution of Gaussians is Gaussian).
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Any shot tagged FLOURISH must carry a CASHED-IN field pointing to a real later shot id. Unresolved FLOURISH tags at build time are a build failure.

candidate_rules.rule: Never approximate, idealize, or simplify without naming the cheat, stating its cost, and scheduling its repair — then performing the repair.
candidate_rules.rationale: He names the cheeky constant and says the answer will be off by a factor, then renormalizes; he names the root-two factor in the slice reading and absorbs it; he bounds the small-angle error and states the exact condition under which the headline result would be wrong. In RL: tabular assumptions, infinite-visitation assumptions, i.i.d. assumptions on replay buffers, and the Markov assumption itself.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Every simplification gets a CHEAT entry: what was assumed, what it costs, which shot repairs it. Unrepaired CHEATs at the end of a unit must be listed on the summary card as known limitations, not silently dropped.

candidate_rules.rule: Every misconception card must state the wrong belief in the reader's own words BEFORE stating the correction, as a contrastive pair.
candidate_rules.rationale: His corrections are always 'it is not A, it is B' where A is what a competent reader would otherwise conclude — the key value is not hiding behind a curtain; it is the variance that adds, not the standard deviation; linearity is a property, not an instruction set.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Every SUM misconception field must contain two clauses and a negation. A card containing only a true statement fails.

candidate_rules.rule: Never disclaim an invented illustrative story only once. Re-mark it as invented at every shot that leans on it.
candidate_rules.rationale: He re-flags the adjectives-updating-nouns story as made up at least three separate times, each time he uses it to interpret a matrix. A single disclaimer decays within a minute; the reader keeps the story and drops the caveat. In RL this covers any anthropomorphic gloss of what an agent 'wants', 'believes', or 'is trying to do'.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Tag invented stories with an id. Grep every shot whose narration invokes that id; each must contain a re-marking clause.

candidate_rules.rule: Never let the motivating example escape an audit against the conditions the unit later states. If the hook violates the conditions, say so.
candidate_rules.rationale: He withholds three assumptions, tells the reader to watch for them, delivers them, and then shows that his own opening demonstration violates two of the three — and warns against assuming the conclusion holds without justification.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Every knowledge point with stated conditions must contain a shot in which the opening example is re-tested against each condition, with an explicit pass/fail per condition. In RL this is unavoidable: most intuition-building gridworlds violate something the theorem needs.

candidate_rules.rule: Never end a knowledge point with more than one designated takeaway, and restate that one takeaway in a second representation before closing.
candidate_rules.rationale: He designates single facts explicitly ('if there is only one fact you remember'), and restates his key cross-entropy property three times in different visual forms rather than adding a second property.
candidate_rules.how_to_check: Each SUM card has exactly one core-claim sentence. Count the distinct assertions in the card's claim field; more than one fails. Verify the claim appears in at least two shots with different drawFns.

anti_patterns: Opening with a definition or formula before the problem that makes it inevitable — he says explicitly that these terms are trivial to define, and that defining them early would spoil the story; the definition is meant to arrive as the residue of an insight.

Opening with the most visually attractive example when it is unrepresentative — he declines to open the convolution video with image processing, despite calling it the most visually intriguing, because a couple of finicky details make it a poor model of the operation in general.
Responding to confusion by going one level deeper. He considers this and rejects it by name.
Letting a formally correct derivation whose structure cancels out stand as the motivation for that structure.
Asserting an operational story ('what it's really doing is X in parallel') for what is only a property of a transformation.

Leaving a broken pattern at 'be careful with patterns'. He treats the shallow moral as insufficient and insists on explaining where the pattern came from, the exact mechanism of the break, and the exact size of the shortfall.
Hedging with adjectives where numbers exist; and, symmetrically, letting a vivid explanation imply significance it does not have.
Smoothing a search into a straight line. He keeps a formula that works and is useless, and labels it useless.
Presenting a picture as evidence when the picture would look identical under a false hypothesis — hence the insistence that the slice is a viewing choice and the plane confinement is emergent.
Silently re-encoding, or reusing one visual channel for two meanings within a unit.
Covering many later uses of an invented illustrative story with one early disclaimer.
Using a term of art in a context where its plain-English reading is false, without negating that reading on the spot.
Claiming a result he has not exercised on a small case, an edge case, an independent count, a numeric run, or physical reality.
Ending a unit with balanced coverage instead of one repeated takeaway.

Motion whose only property is that it continues. Every sustained motion in the corpus is a parameter sweep with a stated readout, a trace that deposits a new object, a re-indexing of an existing grid, a step-per-event correspondence, a null-result demonstration, a length that measures a quantity, or a visible failure to converge.
